Both leaderboards are run by their maintainers on closed test sets. With checkpoint averaging and recurrent depth, GLiDE 27B reaches 73.37.

Artificial Intelligence.title: C-LiTE: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Cellular feature learning in Histopathology
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology, as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assessment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of parameters. Applying ViTs directly to small cellular crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases computational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce interpolation artefacts. To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight foundation model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 x 64 px cell-centred crops using a 4 x 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 x 16 token grid without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-5-S using a pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from TCGA, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. To our knowledge, this represents the largest public dataset for self-supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level. We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyping. Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Ensemble Logic
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Ensemble Logic (EL) is a family of modal logics whose modal parameters are terms with quantified variables. We interpret formulas over metric monoids, that is, commutative monoids equipped with translation-invariant metrics. Displacement evaluates a formula at a translated point, while bounded existence and bounded universality evaluate it at some or every point of a window of prescribed length. Quantification over points and lengths allows the same variable to occur in the parameters of several operators. This provides a common framework for temporal and spatial reasoning in discrete, dense and multi-dimensional settings. Our main result establishes a sharp undecidability boundary for satisfiability over the natural numbers: satisfiability is undecidable already for formulas $\exists N\,\exists n\,Ψ$ in which $Ψ$ is built from the letters of a fixed alphabet by conjunction, disjunction, displacement and bounded universality. We prove this by a reduction from Post's Correspondence Problem. We also present results, in part from companion work, that place this theorem in the general theory of EL. These include an atomic-displacement normal form for covariant windows and composition laws for discrete and dense time. The discrete logic admits an embedding of linear temporal logic, defines the accepting runs of every Büchi automaton, and has a sound equational calculus. For the rational logic, we show that every fixed formula can be evaluated in polynomial time on interval models in which atomic propositions are interpreted by finite unions of intervals. Finally, we represent timed words over positions and real time and compare two window geometries; with rectangular windows, two shared lengths yield undecidability on finite timed words.

Artificial Intelligence.title: CP-Guard+: A New Paradigm for Malicious Agent Detection and Defense in Multi-Agent Collaborative Perception
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Collaborative perception (CP) is a promising approach for safe connected and autonomous driving that enables multiple connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) to share sensing information with each other to enhance perception performance. For example, occluded objects can be detected, and the sensing range can be extended. However, compared with single-agent perception, the openness of a CP system makes it more vulnerable to malicious agents and attackers, who can inject malicious information to mislead the perception of an ego CAV, resulting in severe risks for the safety of autonomous driving systems. To mitigate the vulnerability of CP systems, we first propose a new paradigm for malicious agent detection that effectively identifies malicious agents at the feature level without requiring verification of final perception results, significantly reducing computational overhead. Building on this paradigm, we introduce CP-GuardBench, the first comprehensive dataset for training and evaluating various malicious agent detection methods for CP systems. Furthermore, we develop a robust defense method called CP-Guard+, which enhances the margin between the representations of benign and malicious features through a carefully designed dual-centered contrastive loss. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on both CP-GuardBench and V2X-Sim, and the results demonstrate the superiority of CP-Guard+.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted for IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing (TDSC)

Artificial Intelligence.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.

Artificial Intelligence.title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Simpler Is Better: Evaluating Translation Pipelines for Medieval Latin Manuscripts
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Despite remarkable progress in machine translation, Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle on historical manuscripts, a domain that stresses core Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities: low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy input signals. We present a systematic framework for evaluating the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, a setting in which scribal shorthand, ligatures, and parchment degradation expose failure modes that are invisible in clean-text benchmarks. Benchmarking on the CATMuS Latin dataset reveals a specialization gap: domain-specific Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3$\times$ compared to general-purpose VLMs, despite operating at orders of magnitude fewer parameters. We introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC), a novel dataset comprising 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations, to our knowledge the first of its kind for medieval Latin. Our experiments uncover a complexity paradox: the simplest pipeline, a specialized OCR model feeding directly into a VLM, outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade aggregate translation quality. These findings offer both a new benchmark and practical guidance for deploying translation systems in low-resource historical settings.

Artificial Intelligence.title: DAQ: Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Transformers
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Spiking transformers combine attention-based representation learning with sparse spike communication, yet their weights and membrane variables still incur substantial storage and computation overhead. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical way to reduce these overheads, but preserving neuronal firing under weight and membrane quantization remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization (DAQ), a method that calibrates the quantizers to align neuronal firing decisions with those of a floating-point reference. We analyze how errors from these quantizers affect firing at decision boundaries and how they propagate over time steps in recurrent neurons. Based on this analysis, we formulate an objective that encourages quantized membrane variables to remain within the reference firing regions along the quantized model's own state trajectory. Experiments across multiple spiking transformer architectures on image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking demonstrate the effectiveness of DAQ with 4-bit weights and membrane variables. On FE108, DAQ achieves 58.8\% AUC and 90.9\% PR with SDTrack, while reducing energy by 66.2\%.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution
Artificial Intelligence.summary: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 59 pages, 27 figures. v2: new controlled ablation (Sec. 6.3), token-matched comparison, and OR-Tools baseline; revised introduction and figures

Artificial Intelligence.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/

Artificial Intelligence.title: Competing at Every Price Point with Agentic Evolution over a Menu of LLMs
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Consider a firm that surveys its competition for a particular agentic task and seeks to offer superior accuracy at every price point. A firm that Pareto-dominated its competitors would leave no rational customer a reason to buy elsewhere. This paper shows a path to this kind of capability by evolving multi-LLM Python agents from training pools of at most 100 examples. Given a priced menu of nine LLM endpoints; brief documentation of the task, objective, and API; a simple seed agent; and an operator-chosen per-problem cost target--usually set at an incumbent's own price--RoboPhD, an evolutionary meta-agent, evolves complete agent programs that attack the public frontiers of two semantically dissimilar tasks point by point: DS-1000 (execution-checked code generation) and PaperFindingBench (LLM-judged scientific document retrieval). On public leaderboards for each task, the evolved agents hold every Pareto-frontier slot on PaperFindingBench and all but one on DS-1000, including Pareto domination of both the top-scoring and the lowest-cost competing points.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Camera-ready version. Accepted for oral presentation at the "Managing Agents that Manage Agents" workshop at NeurIPS 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: TesseraFlow: Scalable Video Diffusion for Dynamic Medical Imaging Inverse Problems
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Generative priors are state-of-the-art for modeling medical images in image reconstruction tasks, but reconstruction with video priors takes tens of seconds to minutes per frame. Latent priors inherit the errors of their autoencoder, the memory of pixel-space whole-frame priors grows with the frame size, and pixel-space patch priors are slow for two reasons. First, their deep networks process every frame at full resolution at every sampling step, even though early steps resolve only low frequencies. Second, their samplers spend many network evaluations per sampling step on overlapping windows, multiple re-noising rounds, or backpropagation through the prior. We introduce TesseraFlow, a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior that reduces the first cost. A global encoder reads a low-resolution view of every frame once per sampling step. A single shallow decoder operates on this view during early steps and on full-resolution space-time tiles during later steps, so no network processes a whole frame at full resolution. Our sampler, ReTile, addresses the second reason. We use randomized grid shifting at every sampling step along with re-noising, which acts as a stochastic gradient instead of computing overlapping tiles, so a single network pass per sampling step suffices. On its own, ReTile speeds up an existing global-context patch prior by 6-9x, and our prior adds a further 3-5x speedup. TesseraFlow reconstructs about one 256x256 frame per second, 20-367x faster than patch and latent video priors, and can match or exceed the best generative baseline on cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT, at a fraction of its GPU time.

Artificial Intelligence.title: JEPA-Tuner: From Predictive Fine-Tuning to Asynchronous Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Does Regime-Gated Attention Help Stock Return Prediction? A Leakage-Controlled, Pre-Registered Evaluation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Regime-aware attention is an appealing inductive bias for stock-return prediction, but claims about it are rarely tested under leakage-controlled, out-of-sample conditions. We re-examine the Adaptive Financial Transformer (AFT), which biases self-attention with feature-group similarities weighted by gates that a market-regime encoder produces. First, on a single stock under a corrected protocol (aligned and purged windows, identical test dates for all models, cost-aware non-overlapping backtests, five seeds, Diebold-Mariano tests), no learned model beats the historical-mean forecast. The AFT's regime and context components are numerically inert: the learned gates have 0.9982 of maximal entropy, the context bias has 0.020 of the scale of the attention logits, and we show that the product of two simplex-normalised weightings attenuates it by a factor 1/G. Removing these components changes nothing. Second, we build a point-in-time S&P 500 panel (500 stocks, 1,390,254 stock-days) with 63 stationary features whose causality is verified exactly, and evaluate a model zoo and a layered meta-model with yearly walk-forward refits, a development period (2016-2022) and a sealed, pre-registered holdout (2023-2025). Cross-sectional breadth turns weak signals into detectable ones; the AFT is statistically indistinguishable from a vanilla Transformer and less stable than gradient boosting or ridge regression; six learned meta-learners fail to beat an equal-weight rank combination; and a hysteresis rule roughly halves turnover. On the holdout, the pre-registered primary system (21-day horizon) fails (rank IC 0.0003, one-sided p=0.49), whereas the same system at a 5-day horizon, a pre-registered secondary result, attains a rank IC of 0.0172 (one-sided p=0.038) and a net long-short Sharpe ratio of 0.34 at 5 bp per side. Code: https://github.com/Dishan18/FinancialTransformer
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 6 pages, 4 tables, 1 figure. v2: substantially revised and retitled. v1 reported results that were not produced by its experiments and used a flawed evaluation protocol (see Appendix A); all results were regenerated with a leakage-controlled, pre-registered evaluation on a point-in-time S&P 500 panel

Artificial Intelligence.title: Measuring AI Agents' Progress on Multi-Step Cyber Attack Scenarios
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We evaluate the autonomous offensive cyber capabilities of frontier AI agents on two purpose-built cyber ranges---a 32-step corporate network attack and a 7-step industrial control system attack targeting a simulated cooling tower---complemented by a private 76-task CTF suite spanning four difficulty tiers. Human-expert solve times are estimated at roughly 20 hours for the corporate range and 15 hours for the cooling tower; CTF time annotations range from 1 minute to over 42 hours and include measured playtests, designer estimates, and lower bounds from unsolved playtests. Across thirteen models released over a twenty-month period---from GPT-4o in August 2024 to GPT-5.5 in April 2026---we observe two trends. First, step-count progress increases approximately log-linearly with inference-time compute over the tested range (up to 100M tokens). Second, newer frontier models generally complete more steps at fixed token budgets. GPT-5.5 and Mythos Glasswing each completed all 32 steps in at least one run, the first end-to-end completions of the corporate range; Mythos Glasswing averaged 25.2 of 32 steps and completed the chain in 6 of 10 runs, and GPT-5.5 averaged 22.3 and completed it in 2 of 10. On the control system range, Mythos Glasswing achieved the first end-to-end completion of the chain (2 of 10 runs, mean 4.2); the other frontier models reached at most 3 of 7 steps by directly probing the operational-technology protocol rather than following the intended chain of IT compromise and authenticated control. These results indicate rapid improvements in autonomous cyber capability and suggest that complex but undefended multi-step ranges---including industrial-control attack chains---are no longer reliably distinguishing the strongest frontier models. Future evaluations should emphasise hardened environments, active defences, defensive-control effectiveness, and operational security.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Do LLM Agents Compromise Like Humans? Risk and Responsibility in Dyadic Decision-Making
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they must collaborate to make joint decisions. We investigate how this collaboration unfolds under risk, asking whether agents adjust their choices to accommodate their partners, how they assign responsibility for shared outcomes, and whether responsibility attribution shapes subsequent adjustment. We designed a series of agents with systematically varying risk preferences and paired them in a repeated joint decision-making task previously conducted with humans. Like humans, agents converged toward their partners' choices. However, similar aggregate behavior arose from different dynamics: agents showed little evidence of reciprocal adjustment, tended to weigh rewards more, and their responsibility attribution was decoupled from compromise. Similarly, while they showed bias in their responsibility attribution, the outcome's valence shaped the attribution differently than in humans. Our results reveal important differences between human--human and agent--agent joint decision-making, demonstrating that similar social outcomes can emerge from different social dynamics and reasoning.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 22 pages, 8 figures. Accepted at SocialAgent: Second Workshop on Large Language Models for Social Reasoning and Simulation, NeurIPS 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: Token Noise and the Illusion of Preference: A Shapley Value Framework for Auditing LLM-Simulated Choice Experiments
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate human respondents in choice experiments, yet their answers depend on the exact tokens of a prompt rather than on the offered products alone. I show that invisible characters, blank lines, or minor wording changes shift or reverse simulated choice probabilities. This sensitivity, which I term token noise, creates an illusion of preference and exposes studies to prompt hacking. I introduce a Shapley value audit that divides a model's choice response among the pieces of its prompt and reads each share beside the effect of removing that piece. The edit game divides the effect of several wording and formatting changes beside an actual price change. The word game divides a prompt's response across its words or tokens and summarizes the credit earned by the product attributes as the attribute share. Across four open-weight models and three product categories, wording and formatting edits could rival a substantive price change, while product attributes consistently received a minority of the word-level credit, sometimes less than the answer instruction. Framing cues could take credit from the very price they emphasized and frequently vanished or reversed across equivalent wordings of the question. A persona (even a bare statement that the respondent is a consumer) also shifted choice probabilities and the attributes' credit. Declared with its "players," reference, scale, and uncertainty, my audit separates what a simulated respondent prefers from how the question was asked, the distinction a study must draw before it reads a simulated choice as a preference.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Major revision with a new title (previous title: Explaining Large Language Models Decisions Using Shapley Values). 111 pages, including the online appendix

Artificial Intelligence.title: RES: Accelerating Diffusion Language Models with Rolling Entropy Sampling
Artificial Intelligence.summary: A diffusion language sampler makes two choices for every position in its denoising window: where the next token comes from, and when the position is committed to the KV cache. Using the entropy-bound sampler in DiffusionGemma, we study two extremes of the second choice. Committing each token as soon as it is accepted removes the chance to revise it, which hurts when the entropy bound is relaxed to trade accuracy for speed. When accepted tokens are frozen, macro accuracy falls from 73% to 20% as the bound is relaxed, while the unfrozen sampler stays near 70%. Committing a whole block at once wastes computation, since tokens converge in a largely left-to-right order and more than half of the window holds already-final tokens by twenty denoising steps. These findings motivate the Rolling Entropy Sampler (RES), which commits a contiguous accepted prefix once it reaches a minimum length and keeps positions farther ahead open to revision. Unlike earlier rolling samplers, RES runs on uniform diffusion, where accepted tokens can still change, and it needs no training. Across seven benchmarks, RES increases tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, while macro accuracy goes from 80.7% to 78.8%, and it extends the speed-quality Pareto frontier beyond what tuning the entropy bound alone reaches.

Artificial Intelligence.title: VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
Artificial Intelligence.summary: LLM-based formal provers often collapse the verifier's output into a pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that feeds what Lean reports (error messages with their position, verified partial proofs, and remaining goals) back into proof search. Phase 1 samples N whole proofs; Phase 2 searches a tree of verified partial proofs with a Tactician, automated step repair, a Critic that ranks states and allocates the budget, and a Retriever. On miniF2F test, VERITAS solves 86.9% with Claude Haiku 5.5 and 82.8% with GPT-6 Luna, against 71.7% and 61.1% for Best-of-5 sampling, and solves more theorems than three re-implemented feedback baselines at a third to a half of their search cost. We also evaluate on 55 combinatorics problems of CombiBench and release code and run logs at https://github.com/CoderDoge1108/VERITAS.

Artificial Intelligence.title: The Quantification Horizon Theory of Consciousness
Artificial Intelligence.summary: This paper engages the hard problem of consciousness (Chalmers, 1995) by examining the relationship between the neural correlates of consciousness (NCCs) and their associated qualia. The central premise is that, unlike the vast majority of systems--which have only quantifiable aspects--certain systems such as the NCCs have, in certain states, both quantifiable aspects and intrinsically unquantifiable aspects--the qualities of experience, or qualia. Reconciling these apparently disparate aspects within a scientific account has proven elusive, perpetuating the omission of qualia from the quantitative picture of nature established at the outset of the scientific revolution. The Quantification Horizon Theory of Consciousness (QHT) proposes a mathematical signature for this "mixed quantifiability": singularities in a complete mathematical model of the system, where quantification fails in principle. Its central conjecture is that such a model would both describe the system's physical aspects and contain singularities corresponding to its qualia. The paper also proposes where those singularities would be found: in the system's own quantitative activity. The boundary of such failures--a quantification horizon--would distinguish states of full quantifiability from states of mixed quantifiability, in which the system also has experience. Mathematics could thereby provide a signpost for qualia without reducing their intrinsic characters to quantities. The proposed correspondence paints an ontological triptych: nothing : zero :: physical thing : value :: quale : singularity. The paper identifies a leading candidate for the form the failure takes--a loop of comparisons, each of which can be satisfied, that cannot all be satisfied together--and considers what would establish its realization in the brain and other systems. The paper also considers implications for artificial consciousness.

Artificial Intelligence.title: To See is Not to Learn: Protecting Multimodal Data from Unauthorized Fine-Tuning of Large Vision-Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The rapid advancement of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) is increasingly accompanied by unauthorized scraping and training on multimodal web data, posing copyright and privacy risks to data owners. Existing countermeasures, such as machine unlearning and watermarks, are inherently post-hoc approaches that act only after intellectual property infringement has already occurred. In this work, we propose MMGuard to empower data owners to proactively protect their multimodal data against unauthorized LVLM fine-tuning. MMGuard generates unlearnable examples by injecting human-imperceptible perturbations that exploit the learning dynamics of LVLMs. By minimizing the training loss, the perturbation creates an optimization shortcut, causing the model to overfit to the noise and thereby degrading downstream performance when the perturbation is absent during inference. To further strengthen this defense, MMGuard introduces a cross-modal binding disruption, shifting LVLM attention to enforce a spurious correlation between the noise and the training target with theoretical guarantees. MMGuard is evaluated against nine open-source LVLMs across six datasets. Our results demonstrate effective, stealthy, and robust protection under white-box, gray-box, and no-box threat models, establishing a mechanistic advantage in proactively defending against unauthorized fine-tuning exploitation.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost. In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography. In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system. RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Do You Even Know What I Want? Improving LLMs Ability to Detect Hidden User Intent
Artificial Intelligence.summary: As with conventional AI agents, a common source of misalignment between Large Language Models (LLMs) and their human users is misspecified goals. Often, this happens when the human has skewed beliefs about the system's model and provides it with information that causes behavior different from what they expected, with potentially unwanted side effects. To ensure goal alignment, one solution would be for the LLM to ask the human questions about their objectives. However, it has been well-documented that LLMs most often provide default responses to user requests rather than try and ask questions to clarify their true intent. In this paper, we address these challenges by adapting a novel formulation for the objective misspecification problem to work with LLMs. We then test if LLMs that are prompted to ask questions about a user's true underlying objectives are better at identifying them compared to those that do not. We evaluate our method using four state-of-the-art LLMs tested on five standard IPC domains, showing that for some domains, asking questions greatly improved model performance.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Watermark Claims Under Test: Lessons from Auditing a Production LLM
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Population-Based Post-Training for Large Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several models in parallel and lets the training process do the tuning through population-based training. PBPT periodically evaluates models on a validation set. High-performers are duplicated and their hyperparameters perturbed to explore new configurations. Low-performers stop training and are replaced by these copies. On reasoning benchmarks (Enigmata, Nemotron) and interactive tool-use environments (Gaia2, AppWorld), PBPT produces stronger agents than compute-matched groups of independent RLVR learners. Furthermore, PBPT is able to recover from poor initial hyperparameters, automatically discovering better settings over the course of training.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Mind the Trap As LLMs Guess the Data Model: Grain-Aware Guards Against Fan-out in Text-to-SQL and Its Benchmarks
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Text-to-SQL systems built on large language models (LLMs) often aggregate over one-to-many and many-to-many joins, a classic trap: when the joined rows repeat an entity, a SUM or COUNT counts it more than once, yet the query runs and returns a plausible number. We characterize these fan-out errors by one condition on the relation an aggregate reads, which depends on two facts a schema does not show: each measure's grain, and how many rows a join on each key repeats. An audit that tests the condition on the data finds distorted gold answers for 4.2% of the dev questions of BIRD, a widely used benchmark, and BIRD's later, independent revision changed 44% of the answers the audit flags as definite fan-out, against 16% of unflagged ones. We release BIRD-FanOut, 486 BIRD questions with reviewed gold, and GrainTraps, synthetic questions that set this trap and related ones. Across eight LLM agents, functional dependencies (FDs) computed from the data help no more than per-column statistics on GrainTraps, but grain-aware FDs, which also state each measure's grain and the repetition per key, cut fan-out errors on BIRD from 18.4% of runs to about 13%, also on held-out questions and without LLM judges. Accuracy rises less, because most remaining errors are not fan-out and BIRD's hints often prescribe the over-count. Text-to-SQL models should be given the grain of the data, and benchmark gold should be audited on the data. Code, data and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/ahmed-mahran/misqal
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 17 pages, 14 figures, 9 tables. Code, data and benchmarks: https://github.com/ahmed-mahran/misqal

Artificial Intelligence.title: NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The decay exponent $α$ in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as $s_i = A_i \cdot (t-i)^{-α}$, where $A_i$ is cumulative attention and $α$ controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to $α=0$ and $α\to\infty$, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of \citet{xiang2026nohair} bounds the admissible range of $α$, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields $[0.556, 0.822]$ for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. \textsc{NoHairCache} achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM ($p < 0.05$ on all three datasets, with $0.06$--$0.10$ PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget $512$). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining $98.2\%$ of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at $25\%$ retention versus $91.1\%$ for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Consumer-Time Validity in Stateful AI Runtimes: Verifying Recovered State and Deferred Authority
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Stateful LLM serving engines and agent runtimes reuse execution state and deferred permissions across components and sessions. A cancellation, rollback, or approval is recorded by one component and relied on by another, and recording it does not make the later use valid: a downstream consumer may read state or dispatch an action whose identity, production status, allocation, or target revision has since changed. We call the missing check consumer-time validity and separate two forms. State validity governs what a consumer reads. On vLLM with LMCache, an interrupted KV load leaves unwritten blocks indexed, and a host-only counter rewind desynchronizes the GPU position, so a second tenant generates a schema-valid tool call naming the wrong tenant in 10/10 native-fault runs; the call is recorded and not executed. Authority freshness governs what a consumer executes: on a multi-session approval runtime, an unrevoked deferred grant overwrote a newer revision in one admitted live execution. Output equality cannot test state validity: a fault-free run diverges at token 30 through BF16 batching alone while attended-KV digests match. We therefore specify consumer-bound recovery contracts that, for state recovery, jointly require exclusion, retention, and task completion, and an admissible-witness standard realized as a GPU-free offline trace verifier over scheduler metadata and persisted tool artifacts. On recorded traces the verifier agrees with the reference verdicts in 42/42 frozen GPU-matrix scenarios. An allocation-aware repair satisfies 7/7 triggered vLLM fault predicates on a pinned scheduler-case matrix, where upstream PR 61769 satisfies 2/7, and revision-bound dispatch blocks all 160 deterministic conflicting overwrites in a separate dispatcher cohort. Recovery must be checked where state and authority are consumed, with evidence bound to the consuming request.

Artificial Intelligence.title: DoC: Learning to Defer or Commit for Timely, Accurate, and Stable Conversational Diagnosis Prediction
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Conversational diagnosis prediction requires accurate, early, and stable predictions from ongoing clinical dialogue, yet dialogue-level labels do not specify when to commit. We propose a two-phase framework for learning deferral and diagnosis decisions. First, iterative commitment-boundary estimation constructs Defer/diagnosis supervision without annotated commitment times. Second, Defer-aware supervised fine-tuning initializes a policy, refined through reinforcement learning with trajectory-level rewards for timeliness, first-commit accuracy, and post-commit stability. On EMSDialog and MediTOD, DoC commits early, achieving the highest first-commit accuracy among post-trained methods (76.7%/51.2%) and the lowest post-commit error overall (16.4%/48.3%).

Artificial Intelligence.title: Demystifying Classifier-Free Guidance for Auto-Regressive Image Generation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) has been widely adopted in autoregressive (AR) models for high-quality image generation. Despite its strong empirical performance, its mechanism in AR models remains unclear. This paper demystifies the mechanism of CFG through both empirical and theoretical studies. By examining the top-ranked semantics of different components in CFG, we show that texture information is primarily encoded in the difference between the conditional and unconditional logits, whereas both logits share previous-token repetition as their leading semantics. This strong repetition semantics obscures the desired texture information, causing greedy decoding from the conditional logits alone to produce nearly pure-color images. Through a training-dynamics analysis of shallow transformers, we prove that this shared repetition semantics does not arise from limitations or failures of pretraining, but instead originates from the texture sparsity of images. We further show that CFG improves generation quality by rectifying this repetition bias during inference. Motivated by the shared semantics between conditional and unconditional logits, we propose Attention Weight Reuse (AttnReuse), which reuses intermediate attention computations from the conditional-logit forward pass to accelerate the unconditional-logit computation. AttnReuse reduces about $25\%$ of attention computation with little performance degradation across different models.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Time-MAGNET: Federated Multimodal Graph Neural Expert Transformer for Human Activity Recognition
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Human Activity Recognition plays a vital role in applications such as fitness tracking, smart homes, and healthcare monitoring. Single modality HAR systems rely on a single source of sensory information and can therefore be affected by sensor specific noise and signal degradation, which may limit their ability to distinguish between activities. To address these limitations, this work proposes Time-MAGNET, a novel multimodal learning framework that adaptively fuses heterogeneous sensing modalities to learn discriminative representations for HAR. It adaptively models interactions among heterogeneous modalities using graph attention and a Mixture-of-Experts architecture. To capture complex temporal dependencies, we employ a lightweight encoder-only T5 architecture customized for multimodal HAR and efficiently trained using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). In real world applications, multimodal HAR data are typically distributed across devices or users and cannot always be centrally collected due to privacy, data ownership, and communication constraints. However, the distributed nature of HAR introduces statistical and system heterogeneity across clients, which can challenge conventional federated aggregation methods. To address this issue, we propose Federated Proximal Adaptive Weighting (FedPAW), a novel federated aggregation algorithm for stable and effective model aggregation under heterogeneous client settings. Extensive experiments on the MEx dataset show that Time-MAGNET achieves accuracies of 0.9555 and 0.8997 in centralized and federated settings, respectively, outperforming the considered baseline methods. The results indicate that adaptive multimodal fusion and LoRA based temporal modeling improve centralized HAR performance, while FedPAW provides effective aggregation under heterogeneous federated clients.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: The 2nd version is the revised and updated version of the 1st version with more experiments, ablations and a new federated algorithm. The title is also changed in this version

Artificial Intelligence.title: Proxy-Based Approximation of Shapley and Banzhaf Interactions
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Shapley and Banzhaf interactions capture the complex dynamics inherent in modern machine learning applications. However, current estimators for these higher-order interactions trade off between speed and accuracy. To overcome this limitation, we introduce ProxySHAP. ProxySHAP reconciles the high sample efficiency of tree-based proxy models with a situational residual correction recovering consistency. On a theoretical level, we derive a polynomial-time generalization of interventional TreeSHAP that computes exact interaction indices for tree ensembles, thereby bypassing exponential tree-depth dependencies in prior methods. Furthermore, we formally analyze the residual adjustment strategy, characterizing the specific conditions under which Maximum Sample Reuse (MSR) corrects proxy bias without its variance scaling exponentially with interaction size. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates that ProxySHAP sets a new state-of-the-art standard for approximation quality, including in large-scale applications with thousands of features. By achieving the lowest error in both small- and large-budget regimes, ProxySHAP significantly outperforms the prior best estimators ProxySPEX and KernelSHAP-IQ, while also delivering superior performance on downstream explainability tasks.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Auto-Policy, not Auto-Skill: Compiled Agent Skills for the Physical World
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Self-evolving Skill harnesses automatically rewrite an agent's procedural knowledge to improve efficiency, yet leave execution authority unconstrained. A Skill specifies how an agent should act, whereas a policy decides which requests may become physical actions; current Skill formats package procedure as markdown and scripts and leave authorization to the model. This gap is critical when a wrong invocation unlocks a door. We term the resulting failure Borrowed Authority: an inter-agent message pairs an instruction with an unverifiable permission claim, and the receiving Skill has no typed way to reject it. Across six open-weight receiver configurations (9,510 episodes), models execute 87% of unauthorized requests with no rule, 91% under a one-line rule, 25% when given the full policy in prose and a state-reading tool, and 18% behind a dedicated LLM checker. Failures concentrate on near misses (case variants, whitespace, wildcards, or just-expired readings), and where bare commands hesitate, an unverified claim displaces state checks. We propose Edge Skillguard, a typed invocation policy co-versioned with the actuator-owning Skill and enforced at the message boundary by a deterministic, fail-closed evaluator over leases, world state, and sensor freshness. Rather than using models as runtime filters, Edge Skillguard compiles prose rules offline behind an admission and operator-lattice tightening gate: across all six configurations and five policies, gated compilation yields verified guards (28/30 zero-shot, 30/30 after one feedback turn) and blocks 12/12 model-generated loosenings. On an edge testbed, Edge Skillguard admits 0/682 generated violations and 150/150 authorized requests at about 1 ms per decision, keeping invocation policy a fixed point outside the evolving harness's reach. Code and data: https://github.com/zhonghaozhan/edge-skillguard
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Extended version of the paper presented at the 1st Workshop on Agent Skills (Agent Skills '26), ACM CAIS 2026, San Jose, May 26, 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: CLASP: Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling for Zero-Shot OOD Detection using Vision-Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in medical imaging, yet existing approaches often rely on final-layer confidence or entropy-based layer selection, potentially missing complementary information. We show that low in-distribution (ID) confidence entropy does not reliably predict OOD discrimination. We introduce CLASP (Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling), an ID-only framework that jointly models layer--prompt responses and visual features. CLASP ranks visual encoder layers using Gaussian conditional mutual information and selects a compact subset through anchored spectral selection, without fixing the number of layers. It then combines the selected layer--prompt profiles with PCA-compressed visual embeddings and fits a single shrinkage-regularized Gaussian. OOD scores are computed using squared Mahalanobis distance, without fine-tuning, OOD training data, or test-time adaptation. Across histopathology, chest X-ray, and brain MRI benchmarks with UniMedCLIP and BioMedCLIP, CLASP performs strongly under varied distribution shifts. On MIDOG near-OOD, it achieves 87.54% AUROC with UniMedCLIP, outperforming confidence-based baselines; with BioMedCLIP, it remains competitive but trails visual-only Mahalanobis modeling. Ablations highlight the value of layer--prompt interactions and cross-feature dependencies, while exposing shift-dependent contributions and limitations under semantic shifts.

Artificial Intelligence.title: World Models for Ocean Engineering: A Critical Review of Maritime Autonomy, Adaptive Latent Prediction, Digital Twins, and Biodiversity Monitoring
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Learning from Another Angle: Rotation-Based Test-Time Training for Multimodal Large Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks but often remain vulnerable to distribution shifts due to their fixed parameters during inference. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a pathway for dynamic adaptation, existing approaches suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to multiple sampling and the risk of error reinforcement from biased self-generated supervision. In light of this view, we propose RoTTT (Rotation-based Test-Time Training), a simple and efficient TTT approach that enables instance-specific refinement at inference time. For each test instance, RoTTT performs a small number of gradient updates by predicting the rotation angle of the input image. The known rotation angles naturally serve as a reliable self-supervised signal, enabling lightweight and stable adaptation without requiring additional annotations. Extensive experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that RoTTT consistently improves performance across different MLLMs, providing a practical and efficient paradigm for on-the-fly MLLM adaptation.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Wrong Answers Remain Unsettled: Failure Dynamics in Recurrent Reasoners
Artificial Intelligence.summary: When a recurrent reasoner returns a wrong answer, is its computation finished or merely stopped? We test this on a trained Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM; 27M parameters, Sudoku-Extreme) by running the recurrence for one more inference budget and comparing with an unperturbed control. Solved answers persist (0.95 of 512 endpoints). Wrong answers mostly do not: 0.42 of near-miss answers (n=170) and 0.18 of all 512 wrong endpoints keep their answer. Perturbations from 0.05x to 20x the terminal-update scale barely change these rates, so the measurement reflects continued recurrence, not noise sensitivity. The solved-above-wrong ordering also holds in five further settings (a second seed, TRM, Maze, GRAM-guided TRM, N-Queens), but a fixed 1/2 persistence threshold does not, and neither do HRM's endpoint-spectrum and fast-versus-slow predictability patterns, which are not universal diagnostics. Perturb-and-reselect (known from prior work) is consistent with this: frozen noise gains 4.8 accuracy points (197 gained, 2 lost), but compute-matched extended depth gains 5.6 and Sudoku symmetry augmentation 34.6, so noise is not the best use of the budget. Conclusions are limited to finite horizons and one primary HRM checkpoint; they do not exclude asymptotic attractors.

Artificial Intelligence.title: A Design Space for Data Agents: Insights from KDD Cup 2026
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Data agents interpret analytical requests, gather evidence from heterogeneous sources, and compute results within finite resource budgets. We analyze the final code submissions of the ten highest-ranked teams in the KDD Cup 2026 Data Agents for Complex Data Analysis competition. We organize the observed design choices into three interacting layers, covering workflow orchestration, analytical functions, and working state. The comparison reveals recurring patterns for allocating computation in response to task progress, structuring evidence for computation and assessment, and preserving reusable artifacts with their provenance. Candidates that rely on the same evidence can inherit the same error, so interpreting their agreement requires tracing those dependencies. The design space motivates controlled evaluations of how resource allocation, evidence sharing, and targeted recovery affect task completion and correctness.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Who Gets Re-ranked When a Clinical Model Gains New Data?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Hospitals often update a deployed risk model by adding a data source, such as laboratory results, that only some patients have. Work on safe model updates assumes fixed inputs and so ignores patients who lack the new data. The update has no new measurements for them, yet their rank can change, and a sick patient not yet tested can drop off an alert list. We split rank-based compatibility by data availability and pair it with error correction and alert-list effects. We compared each update with ordinary retraining on the old inputs, predicting ICU admission or death and hospital admission, on 78,475 emergency department visits from MC-MED and, in a pre-registered replication, 100,000 stays from MIMIC-IV-ED at a second hospital. Radiograph report text gave no detectable gain and almost no extra re-ranking. Laboratory results improved prediction but, at both hospitals and with linear or tree models, pushed patients without labs down alert lists; linear updates also reshuffled them more than retraining did, without ranking them better. A top-20% admission list caught 4.2% of admitted patients without labs after the update, against 18.8% after retraining (second hospital: 4.9% against 22.6%), while catching more patients overall. This held for list sizes from 5% to 50% and in every patient group we checked, despite better measured calibration. Separate alert thresholds for patients with and without labs restored most or all of their catch rate at both hospitals at almost no cost. Teams should check these patients before deploying such an update.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at the 6th International Workshop on Multi-Modal Medical Data Analysis (MMMDA), IEEE BigData 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: MolReJev: Decision Models Are In-Context Molecular Predictors
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Molecular prediction helps prioritize compounds for screening. Specialized predictors are trained for a fixed set of tasks, limiting cross-task generalization. Language models can condition on task descriptions and have recently shown promise in molecular prediction. However, generating answers token by token adds inference cost, and general-purpose models often lack task-specific molecular knowledge. We thus propose MolReJev, which combines Jev-style candidate scoring with in-context learning (ICL) on a language model. MolReJev retrieves similar labeled examples from existing task data and scores candidate labels jointly in one forward pass. ICL improves predictions from the released general-purpose Kev checkpoint and the separately trained MolReJev. For the trained model, gains span all evaluation groups, including held-out tasks, and extend to compounds absent from training. MolReJev generally outperforms MolecularGPT on matched evaluations and nearest-neighbor prediction with the same examples. With four examples, MolReJev and a trained text baseline achieve similar ROC-AUC, with higher measured throughput for MolReJev. These results show that decision models can serve as in-context molecular predictors for compounds, drug pairs, and reactions.

Artificial Intelligence.title: PruneNAS: Constraint Aware Neural Architecture Search based Pruning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse tasks, but its high computational cost remains a major barrier. We introduce PruneNAS, a novel framework that integrates structured pruning into NAS to efficiently explore high-performing architectures while leveraging pretrained models. Unlike conventional NAS methods that train each candidate from scratch, PruneNAS generates a candidate pool by pruning pretrained networks at multiple granularity levels and formulates the selection as a global optimization problem using training-free importance metrics. This approach enables rapid evaluation of candidate architectures under strict resource constraints, dramatically reducing search time from hundreds of GPU hours to mere minutes. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that PruneNAS discovers compact, high-accuracy architectures that nearly halve the computational cost (MACs) of prior methods on ResNet-50, while also showing strong generalization on object detection tasks with YOLO. Our method bridges structured pruning and NAS, offering a practical solution for resource-constrained model deployment.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, British Machine Vision Conference, Lancaster, 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: Learning Land-Surface Hydrology World Model from Satellite Observations
Artificial Intelligence.summary: A world model should tell us not only what will happen, but what would happen under a different action. Learned Earth models now forecast remarkably well, yet forecast skill says little about what their state means or how it responds to a changed driver. We build LandWM, a world model of land-surface water in which rain is the action, learned from seven years of SMAP and CYGNSS observations: physical observation operators tie its latent state to soil water, and a mass-conserving balance governs how that state responds to rain. Over the U.S. Southern Great Plains, the model, never shown a soil-moisture value, tracks 28 in-situ probes as well as the operational SMAP Level-4 product, even from CYGNSS alone, and a storm added to the forcing of a station's cell wets its soil as natural storms wet the probes. Replace either piece and the forecasts stay, but the meaning goes: with neural operators, only a probe fitted to the stations finds the soil water; with a generic recurrent transition, rain on a single cell barely moves it. Yet when the same rain covers the whole region the two transitions swap roles, and the conserving one responds too weakly. Grounding makes a world model readable; its response to actions must be tested under more than one kind of intervention.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Micro Operational Robustness of LLMs on Code Generation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: It is now common practice in software development for large language models (LLMs) to be used to generate program code. It is desirable to evaluate the robustness of LLMs for this usage. This paper is concerned in particular with how sensitive LLMs are to variations in descriptions of the coding tasks. However, existing techniques for evaluating this robustness are unsuitable for code generation because the input data space of natural language (NL) descriptions is discrete and sparse. To address this problem, we propose a robustness evaluation method called scenario domain analysis, which aims to find the expected minimal change in the NL descriptions of coding tasks that would cause the LLMs to produce incorrect outputs. We have formally proved the theoretical properties of the method and also conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the robustness of four state-of-the-art LLMs: Gemini-pro, Codex, Llamma2 and Falcon 7B, and have found that we are able to rank these with confidence from best to worst. Moreover, we have also studied how robustness varies in different scenarios, including the variations with the topic of the coding task and with the complexity of its sample solution, and found that robustness is lower for more complex tasks and also lower for more advanced topics, such as multi-threading and data structures.

Artificial Intelligence.title: DeepVoting: Learning and Improving Voting Rules with Fine-Tuning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Recently, social choice theory has been found broadly useful for AI alignment and evaluation, often based on the axiomatic properties for combining preferences provided by social choice functions. However, for many sets of axioms, functions which never violate the axioms are known to not exist, e.g., Arrow's Impossibility Theorem. Recent work on learning novel rules to minimize axiom violations shows the effectiveness of machine learning but explores a limited class of axioms. In this work we show the effectiveness of standard social choice data structures as features for learning existing voting rules, resulting in networks that have better accuracy than past approaches while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Subsequently, we develop a process for adding axiomatic properties to existing voting rules. By building novel axiomatic loss functions we are able to use transfer learning to fine-tune existing voting rules in a way that quantitatively preserves their original behaviour while also exhibiting strong adherence to previously absent axiomatic properties, resulting in novel voting rules that are closer to the impossibility frontier than those in the machine learning or theoretical literature.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Artificial Intelligence.title: SeqFold: Timestamp-Addressable Compressed States for User Action Sequence Backbones
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Existing sequential user modeling methods mainly focus on improving the backbone encoder or learning task-specific user representations for a single prediction objective. We instead study how to export the multi-layer user states of a frozen long-history backbone as compact, timestamp-addressable representations for downstream training backfill and serving. In this setting, the user state at a given timestamp summarizes the user's actions before that time, so downstream systems need only the state aligned to each target timestamp rather than the full hidden-state timeline. To this end, we present \texttt{SeqFold}, a compressed-state interface that combines learned multi-channel fusion, channel-specific temporal decay, and Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ) to produce compact discrete codes from frozen backbone states. Task-specific decoders then map these shared codes into flexible embedding spaces for downstream models. To make timestamp-addressable export practical at scale, we further develop a fused streaming implementation that updates the fusion recurrence after every action while materializing states only at target timestamps. On large-scale proprietary datasets, SeqFold reduces per-state representation storage by $3{,}400\times$ while preserving most of the downstream ranking performance of the uncompressed model, showing that SeqFold is an effective interface for reusing long-history sequence backbones in downstream models.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Rubrics Do Not Decide: Silent Value Completion in LLM Evaluation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multi-criterion LLM judges often evaluate responses without specifying how conflicting criteria resolve, leaving the winner undetermined even under exact criterion scores. Issuing a strict verdict without declaring the required trade-off premise constitutes silent value completion. We introduce TradeoffBench to isolate this failure by separating rule execution from response scoring. On authoritative criterion vectors, six open-weight non-reasoning judges pass all dominance and equality controls yet pick unsupported winners on 9%-81% of 1,345 conflicts. All 577 order-stable choices follow an explicitly banned majority rule. Reasoning-enabled configurations drop anonymous-vector violations to 2 in 9,720 judgments under an explicit rule, yet cannot bridge omitted trade-offs or divergent component scoring. On raw TradeoffBench text with unspecified trade-offs, GPT-6.1-sol omits its completion premise in 29.8% of 400 verified conflicts. Even under an explicit rule on four-rater-consensus MultiPref conflicts, four reasoning judges still issue strict verdicts on 16/45 (GPT-6.1-sol) up to 35/46 and 25/29 (open-weight judges) of valid presentations. We propose identified-first evaluation, decoupling specification support, explicit completion, and target agreement. In MultiPref human-score audits, peer-mean substitution raises directional disagreement from 0.6% to 28.8% on 2,707 shared targets. A single-peer ablation confirms a 29.38-point gap on 2,175 targets, ruling out averaging as the cause. In HUMAINE, declared partial trade-offs add 2.5 percentage points of coverage, yet newly decided pairs incur 3.9% disagreement versus 0.9% for Pareto. Reliable LLM judging, therefore, requires auditing, specification support, declared trade-offs, and human target agreement separately.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: When grading criteria clash (e.g., shorter vs. more thorough), LLM judges secretly make up their own tiebreaker rules to pick a winner without telling you. This paper catches that hidden guesswork and stops it. (12 main pages with proof in appendix)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Let Androids Dream: From Visual Elements to Emergent Implications via Contextual Alignment
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Image metaphor understanding differs from general VQA: the implied meaning is rarely explicit in pixels and instead emerges from the compositional interaction of visual elements together with social intent and culture-specific background. We identify missing context, namely conventions already in a model's weights that single-pass inference leaves unused and external facts absent from the weights, as a failure mode of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We formalize Contextual Alignment as inference over a latent context: selecting background knowledge relevant to the image's composition and useful for inferring its implication. We then propose Let Androids Dream (LAD), a training-free framework that operationalizes contextual alignment through test-time computation: (1) Perception extracts compositional visual structure, (2) Search adaptively acquires context from parametric knowledge or web search, and (3) Reasoning aligns compositions with context to derive emergent implications. On the bilingual S100 benchmark, LAD raises the lightweight GPT-4o-mini from 44% to 74% (English) and from 42% to 52% (Chinese) Multiple-Choice Question (MCQ) accuracy, on par with the closed-book GPT-5.4 in English, and from 2.98 to 4.02 and from 3.36 to 3.66 on Open-Style Questions (OSQ). LAD improves all five backbones we test, including the open-source Qwen2.5-VL-7B (+18 MCQ and +1.30 OSQ points in English) and Gemini-3.0-Pro, where it obtains the highest OSQ scores (4.30 and 4.46), and its gains hold on the full II-Bench and CII-Bench. Adding other search tools raises MCQ accuracy in five of six cases but changes OSQ scores by -0.48 to +0.01, whereas LAD's search stage improves both, suggesting that how context is acquired matters beyond access to search. LAD with web search also improves MMMU, SeedBench, and MMStar. We open-sourced all code and datasets at https://ming-zch.github.io/lad.

Artificial Intelligence.title: STEdgeFormer: MCU and NPU Deployable Transformer Architecture
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Transformer-based sequence models have achieved strong performance in language and time-series modeling, but self-attention remains computationally and memory intensive for deployment on resource-constrained edge accelerators. We propose STEdgeFormer, a lightweight, hardware-aware sequence architecture designed for efficient execution on embedded neural accelerators. STEdgeFormer combines polynomial mixture layers and DyT normalization with an accelerator-aware causal memory block, replacing pairwise self-attention with compact causal aggregation. On TinyStories, the fully NPU-supported STEdgeFormer (MW) achieves a perplexity of 7.39 with 4.12M parameters and 6.51 MB RAM, with an end-to-end latency of 40 ms. In comparison, the standard 4.12M-parameter configuration achieves a lower perplexity of 6.79 but requires CPU fallback for unsupported operators, resulting in 1450 ms latency. Vanilla Transformer, on the other hand, achieves a perplexity score of 5.71 using a 4.40M-parameter model, but it cannot be deployed on the hardware. On downstream tasks, STEdgeFormer achieves 94% accuracy on ECG5000 and 93% accuracy on Speech Commands with 1.39M parameters. These results demonstrate that hardware-aware architectural choices and operator compatibility can have a substantial impact on practical inference latency, beyond model size and task accuracy alone. Rather than targeting state-of-the-art accuracy on individual benchmarks, STEdgeFormer is designed to provide a deployable sequence modeling architecture under the memory, computational, and operator constraints of embedded neural accelerators.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, Neurips 2026 workshop- SLM Agents

Artificial Intelligence.title: Definition-Guided In-Context Learning for Zero-Shot Spoken Language Understanding
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Adapting spoken language understanding (SLU) systems to novel or revised label taxonomies conventionally requires additional labeled data and retraining, creating a bottleneck for real world deployment. While in-context learning with few-shot demonstrations offers an alternative, multi-modal generalization and scaling has been challenging. In this work, we investigate whether natural-language definitions alone can guide zero-shot SLU without demonstration exemplars, finding that symbolic definitions serve as the primary supervisory driver for adapting speech-text models. We operationalize this principle as Definition-Guided In-Context Learning (DG-ICL), a fine-tuning framework that decouples semantic categories from fixed lexical names. By replacing labels with dynamically randomized definitions (arbitrary synthetic tokens in DG-ICL-Sym or permuted vocabulary words in DG-ICL-Flip), DG-ICL avoids lexical shortcuts and encourages the model to ground acoustic representations in contextual definitions. Novel categories can thus be introduced at inference simply by defining them through the instructions. Across three speech-text models (AUDIO FLAMINGO 3, QWEN2-AUDIO, and SALMONN), DG-ICL outperforms standard instruction tuning on held-out tasks under novel symbols (0.663 vs. 0.449 macro-F1 on Audio Flamingo 3; 0.703 vs. 0.620 on Qwen2-Audio; 0.582 vs. 0.399 on SALMONN), while remaining competitive on original labels. Furthermore, counterfactual evaluations demonstrate instruction following abilities, where it is shown that DG-ICL-Sym retains 68% of its performance when definitions contradict pre-trained lexical priors, whereas standard instruction tuning elicits significantly reduced retention of 21%. Finally, we show that DG-ICL enables zero-shot speech clustering into user-defined categories specified on the fly

Artificial Intelligence.title: OmniDecisionBench: Evaluating and Benchmarking the Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models
