DomusFM has a small footprint and can be deployed on edge devices.

Artificial Intelligence.title: From Inference to Adaptation: Vision-Language Model Test-Time Adaptation via a Unified Optimal Transport View
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot capabilities yet remain sensitive to real-world distribution shifts. Although significant efforts are devoted to adapting VLMs at test time, they rely heavily on noisy pseudo-labels predicted from cross-modal embedding similarities during inference, which are unreliable under distribution shifts and mislead the adaptation. Moreover, existing methods largely overlook the critical relational structures across different modalities during test-time adaptation, whose supervision signals remain surprisingly robust under distribution shifts. In this work, we aim to jointly align the cross-modal semantics and intra-modal relational structures across modalities at test time to improve VLM adaptation. At the inference stage, we formulate the zero-shot image classification task as a cross-modal alignment problem via a Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) formulation, which considers both cross-modal semantics and intra-modal structures to generate robust pseudo-labels. At the adaptation stage, we propose a multi-level InfoNCE loss to leverage both the semantical and relational alignment supervision from the inference stage, empowering fine-grained adaptation of VLMs under distribution shifts with additional structural consistency. Finally, we bridge the inference and adaptation stages of our method by proving a mathematical equivalence between their objective functions, thereby revealing the mutual benefits of these two stages from a theoretical perspective. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our methods, outperforming the best-performing methods by up to 3% while maintaining a superior balance between effectiveness and efficiency.

Artificial Intelligence.title: KMed-31B Technical Report
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD$^2$). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.

Artificial Intelligence.title: RealICU: Do LLM Agents Understand Long-Context ICU Data? A Benchmark Beyond Behavior Imitation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Intensive care units (ICU) generate long, dense and evolving streams of clinical information, where physicians must repeatedly reassess patient states under time pressure, underscoring a clear need for reliable AI decision support. Existing ICU benchmarks typically treat historical clinician actions as ground truth. However, these actions are made under incomplete information and limited temporal context of the underlying patient state, and may therefore be suboptimal, making it difficult to assess the true reasoning capabilities of AI systems. We introduce RealICU, a hindsight-annotated benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) under realistic ICU conditions, where labels are created after senior physicians review the full patient trajectory. We formulate four physician-motivated tasks: assess Patient Status, Acute Problems, Recommended Actions, and Red Flag actions that risk unsafe outcomes. We partition each trajectory with 30-min windows and release two datasets: RealICU-Gold with 930-window annotations from 94 MIMIC-IV patients, and RealICU-Scale with 11,862 windows extended by Oracle, a physician-validated LLM hindsight labeler. Existing LLMs including memory-augmented ones performed poorly on RealICU, exposing two failure modes: a recall-safety tradeoff for clinical recommendations, and an anchoring bias to early interpretations of the patient. We further introduce ICU-Evo to study structured-memory agents that improves long-horizon reasoning but does not fully eliminate safety failures. Together, RealICU provides a clinically grounded testbed for measuring and improving AI sequential decision-support in high-stakes care. Project page: https://chengzhi-leo.github.io/RealICU-Bench/
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). Project page: https://chengzhi-leo.github.io/RealICU-Bench/

Artificial Intelligence.title: SkillLens: An Interactive Human-LLM System for Diagnosing and Refining Agent Skills
Artificial Intelligence.summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills, yet maintaining them requires developers to connect revisions with changes in behavior and task outcomes. Existing workflows fragment evidence across versions, evaluation cases, and execution traces. We present SkillLens, an interactive human-LLM system for diagnosing and refining agent skills. A formative study with five developers and researchers identified challenges in prioritizing failures, reconstructing case-level evidence, and preserving context across revisions. SkillLens links performance changes, case transitions, skill diffs, invocation sequences, traces, and outputs in a recoverable workflow, while keeping model-generated explanations and refinements under human review. Through a between-subjects user study with 20 participants, we show that SkillLens supports developers in diagnosing and refining agent skills through a more usable and less demanding workflow than the baseline. These findings highlight the value of linking version comparisons, case-level evidence, and human-reviewed refinement across skill iterations.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Synthetic Clinical Notes for Rare ICD Codes: A Data-Centric Framework for Long-Tail Medical Coding
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Automatic ICD coding from clinical text is a critical task in medical NLP but remains hindered by the extreme long-tail distribution of diagnostic codes. Thousands of rare and zero-shot ICD codes are severely underrepresented in datasets like MIMIC-III, leading to low macro-F1 scores. In this work, we propose a data-centric framework that generates high-quality synthetic discharge summaries to mitigate this imbalance. Our method constructs realistic multi-label code sets anchored on rare codes by leveraging real-world co-occurrence patterns, ICD descriptions, synonyms, taxonomy, and similar clinical notes. Using these structured prompts, we generate 90,000 synthetic notes covering 7,902 ICD codes, significantly expanding the training distribution. We fine-tune two state-of-the-art transformer-based models, PLM-ICD and GKI-ICD, on both the original and extended datasets. Experiments show that our approach modestly improves macro-F1 while maintaining strong micro-F1, outperforming prior SOTA. While the gain may seem marginal relative to the computational cost, our results demonstrate that carefully crafted synthetic data can enhance equity in long-tail ICD code prediction.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: We withdraw this paper because we identified issues in the current version that require substantial revision. The results and conclusions should not be considered final. A revised version may be submitted after these issues have been addressed

Artificial Intelligence.title: Can Your AI Twin Meet People for You? It Can Hold a Conversation. But What Does It Need to Judge Like You?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Should your AI twin go meet people on your behalf? We built LLM twins of 710 real people from their other conversations in the CANDOR corpus, sent them to meet each other in 5,680 simulated first conversations, and checked every rehearsal against what the real people said after meeting for real (355 held-out, participant-disjoint pairs, against baselines that include each person's rating history). The rehearsals work: a twin's conversation predicts real liking ($ρ$=0.277), carries information that questionnaires and rating history do not have (partial $ρ$=0.16 [0.05, 0.26]), and recovers most of what the same reader gets from the real conversation (0.321). Swap controls show that this signal travels through the conversation, not through the persona card. What, then, does a twin need to judge like you? Not your voice: making twins talk more like their owners, with person-specific activation steering and a LoRA trained on their own speech, did not help in a pre-specified test and lowered accuracy in an exploratory second round (-0.183 [-0.294, -0.066]). Nor simply your stated ratings: a persona-prompted twin that holds the conversation does not yet carry its owner's judgment, and when told its owner's past ratings it anchors on them instead of weighing them. Learning helps: a small appraisal head trained on other real conversations, which combines the twin's post-call answers with its owner's rating history, lifts rehearsal-based prediction above the history baseline out of fold (+0.059 [0.001, 0.115], against +0.022 without the twin's answers; pre-specified primary contrast +0.056 [-0.001, 0.111]). We propose an attribution protocol for twin-based social simulation and identify learned appraisal as the component twins need next.

Artificial Intelligence.title: PopMelodyGen: A Copyright-Aware Platform for Controllable Pop-Melody Generation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large-scale redistributable symbolic pop-melody data remain scarce due to copyright restrictions, creating a bottleneck for both practical deployment and reproducible research in music generation. We present PopMelodyGen, a copyright-aware platform for controllable pop-melody generation that combines rule-based synthesis with neural generation. Our approach first uses an expert synthesizer to produce large-scale labeled synthetic melodies from explicit musical knowledge and templates, providing scalable pretraining data with auditable provenance. A neural model is then pretrained on this corpus and adapted with a small licensed real-pop corpus to improve melodic naturalness while preserving controllability. The platform supports interactive melody creation with accompaniment playback and export for creators, as well as batch construction of annotated symbolic datasets for researchers. PopMelodyGen demonstrates a practical training and deployment paradigm for creative AI when large-scale reusable real-world data are limited.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: AAAI 2027 Demonstration Program (accepted); extended version with appendix

Artificial Intelligence.title: DeCo: Decoupled Traffic State Modeling with Cross-Variable Coordination
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Accurate forecasts of traffic flow, occupancy, and speed are essential for congestion management and travel planning. These variables exhibit distinct spatiotemporal patterns, and their coupled dynamics characterize the evolution of traffic conditions, such as the onset and dissipation of congestion. Existing methods often either neglect this coupling or struggle to capture the distinct dynamics of all three variables within a unified model. In this paper, we propose DeCo, a decoupled traffic state modeling framework with cross-variable coordination for forecasting flow, occupancy, and speed. Specifically, DeCo first trains a dedicated forecaster for each variable to specialize in its unique spatiotemporal dynamics. It then estimates a residual correction for each forecast by jointly leveraging the predicted trajectories and recent observations of all three variables, thereby exploiting cross-variable coupling and mitigating systematic prediction errors. We extend the flow-only PeMS03 and PeMS07 benchmarks to all three variables on their original sensors and release the aligned data. Experiments on PeMS03, PeMS04, PeMS07, and PeMS08 show that DeCo achieves the lowest mean absolute error for every variable on every dataset, up to 4.9% below RAGC, the strongest baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/lixus7/DeCo.

Artificial Intelligence.title: GUITAR: Structured Failure Diagnosis of GUI Agents via State Transitions
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Understanding where and why Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents fail is essential for building more reliable systems, yet current evaluation relies on step accuracy, a metric that treats each screen independently and overlooks the underlying structure of GUI environments. This leads to two critical blind spots: (1) functionally equivalent screens are evaluated in isolation, obscuring systematic failure patterns across shared screens; and (2) the long-tailed GUI distribution renders failures on rare but critical screens invisible under standard metrics. To address these issues, we propose \textbf{GUITAR}, a state-centric diagnostic framework that performs structured failure analysis over both states and transitions, using a State Transition Graph (STG) by mapping visually diverse screens to shared functional states. Across 8 agents and 6 tasks from AndroidControl and Mind2Web, GUITAR reveals that 60.4\% of failures occur in 20\% of states, localizing errors to a small set of bottlenecks. Bottleneck-targeted guidance improves SR by 2.8\% and retains a 1.88\% average gain across 7 agents under three-fold trajectory-held-out evaluation with fully automatic STGs. These findings demonstrate the diagnostic and actionable value of structure-aware evaluation within the evaluated mobile and web tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/sqzhang-lazy/GUITAR

Artificial Intelligence.title: The Evaluation Substrate Matters: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Serving Substrates
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) usually coordinate heterogeneous models and tools to solve complex tasks, creating a growing need for reliable evaluation. However, a multi-agent workflow that is fastest in one serving environment can lose its advantage in another, even when its models, prompts, and task remain fixed. This makes a benchmark result conditional on how the workflow is executed. We introduce MASSys, a benchmark for measuring this dependence in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. MASSys executes the same candidate-task pairs across serving substrates and load regimes, using five workload families spanning software repair, research synthesis, financial analysis, interactive control, and diagram generation. It records task quality alongside delivery, latency, cost, resource pressure, and failure evidence. In a controlled motivation diagnostic, the Star workflow falls from first to fourth in mean-latency rank under KV-cache pressure, while Chain rises from fourth to first. The substrate sweeps further show that increasing load creates long runtime tails and timeout pressure. In several task families, quality among evaluated outputs changes less than effective quality over submitted jobs: the system delivers fewer usable results even when the surviving outputs remain competitive. Tool and runtime traces reveal that these outcomes involve both model serving and non-model execution. Together, the results motivate evaluating MAS designs over explicit operating conditions and reporting which tasks are delivered, how well they are solved, and where execution breaks down.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Code: https://github.com/MAS-Sys-Bench/MAS-Sys ; Project page: https://mas-sys-bench.github.io/MAS-Sys-Page/ ; Trace dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/MAS-Sys/MAS-Sys-Traces

Artificial Intelligence.title: How Many Counterfactuals Does It Take? Probing VLM Hallucinations Through Circuits and Causal Effects
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Visual Language Models (VLMs) are known to produce hallucinated predictions that are not grounded in visual evidence, yet existing approaches lack a principled understanding of how robust such predictions are under counterfactual perturbations. In this work, we study the sample complexity of counterfactual robustness for hallucinated outputs in VLMs. We define a causal influence metric based on log-probability differences between factual, counterfactual, and activation-patched runs, and use it to characterize the stability of hallucinated predictions. By leveraging circuit discovery techniques (CD-T), we identify model components responsible for these predictions and track their activation differences across counterfactual samples. We then derive empirical bounds on the minimum number of counterfactual samples m required to reliably detect instability in hallucinated outputs, using concentration inequalities and variance estimates of the causal influence distribution.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: This version contains methodological limitations in the counterfactual evaluation and causal analysis that affect the interpretation of the reported findings. We are withdrawing it to avoid potential misinterpretation of these results

Artificial Intelligence.title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

Artificial Intelligence.title: ArchPilot: A Proxy-Guided Multi-Agent Approach for Machine Learning Engineering
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Recent LLM-based agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in automated ML engineering. However, they heavily rely on repeated full training runs to evaluate candidate solutions, resulting in significant computational overhead, limited scalability to large search spaces, and slow iteration cycles. To address these challenges, we introduce ArchPilot, a multi-agent system that integrates architecture generation, proxy-based evaluation, and adaptive search into a unified framework. ArchPilot consists of three specialized agents: an orchestration agent that coordinates the search process using a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-inspired novel algorithm with a restart mechanism and manages memory of previous candidates; a generation agent that iteratively generates, improves, and debugs candidate architectures; and an evaluation agent that executes proxy training runs, generates and optimizes proxy functions, and aggregates the proxy scores into a fidelity-aware performance metric. This multi-agent collaboration allows ArchPilot to prioritize high-potential candidates with minimal reliance on expensive full training runs, facilitating efficient ML engineering under limited budgets. Experiments on MLE-Bench demonstrate that ArchPilot outperforms SOTA baselines such as AIDE and ML-Master, validating the effectiveness of our multi-agent system.

Artificial Intelligence.title: SparseTokenGS: Gaussian-based Sparse-View CBCT Reconstruction via Reusable Token Pool
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography is widely used for fast, low-dose volumetric imaging and lesion localization in dentistry and image-guided interventions, but it introduces severe artifacts. Feed-forward Gaussian methods transfer the reconstruction cost to training and decode each coordinate from projection-aligned features and neighboring anchors. However, information from the whole scan is written only when the field is constructed and cannot be retrieved during coordinate decoding, leaving the volume inconsistent within the scan. This is a common limitation of such methods: once the field is fixed, decoding uses only local features and reconstruction quality drops substantially. We propose SparseTokenGS, a Gaussian-based method for sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography reconstruction via a reusable token pool. Anchor Token Fusion and Point-Token Attention query this shared pool at the anchors and at the query coordinates, respectively. The local Gaussian prior is retained, and the volume is reconstructed in one forward pass, without per-scan optimization or a projection-domain loss. On three public chest and dental datasets, SparseTokenGS achieves the highest reconstruction performance among the compared methods. On clinical dental scans, reconstruction from only six projections reaches 29.51 decibels in peak signal-to-noise ratio and a structural similarity of 0.842 against the full-view reference, and off-the-shelf tooth-and-pulp segmentation keeps these structures separable for root-canal localization. Experiments on volcanic rock and chicken show performance after same-object adaptation. A reusable token pool gives feed-forward reconstruction a mechanism that keeps scan-wide context available through decoding and can benefit future rapid clinical lesion localization and analysis. The code is available at: https://github.com/FrankDengAI/SparseTokenGS.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 10 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging

Artificial Intelligence.title: Unlearning Model Identity: Ablating LoRA Weights from Question-Based Identity Tuning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large Language Models are trained on diverse corpora containing outputs from proprietary teacher models and provider-curated sources. Models subsequently inherit embedded self-identity traits, persistently asserting specific proprietary names. Service providers of open-weight models frequently require the removal of model identity for downstream applications, such as custom interfaces, without exposing provider affiliations to end-users. Effective identity modification is therefore critical for customized model alignment and deployment. This study proposes a method to localize parameter-level representations of self-identity within low-rank adaptation modules to perform targeted weight ablation. By generating probing questions designed to elicit self-naming outputs and fine-tuning the base model on these responses, the approach identifies and ablates high-magnitude weights within the parameter set. Experimental results demonstrate that distilled identity traits reside within a localized subset of low-rank weights, achieving a complete removal rate in Qwen3.5-2B and a 10% rate in Gemma4-E2B while preserving general task capabilities. These findings confirm that ablating top-tier adaptation weights suppresses distilled self-identification without compromising broader model performance.

Artificial Intelligence.title: WorldCrafter: Consistent Video World Model with Implicit 3D-aware Memory
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Video world models enable interactive exploration of dynamic environments, yet struggle to respect prior observations over long horizons and across viewpoints. We present WorldCrafter, a video world model that learns a camera-queryable implicit 3D-aware memory for this purpose. The key insight is to let the requested viewpoint shape how multi-view evidence is compressed into the video generator's limited token budget. Trained jointly with the video generator, a memory encoder and pose-conditioned readout module integrate historical observations into a fixed set of target view-specific tokens before denoising, without explicit depth-based correspondences. By combining this memory with recent temporal context and few-step distillation, WorldCrafter enables streaming scene exploration from a single input image or text prompt. Experiments across static and dynamic scenes show substantial gains in long-horizon consistency and camera-control accuracy while preserving visual quality during minute-scale exploration.

Artificial Intelligence.title: HaM-World: Soft-Hamiltonian World Models with Selective Memory for Planning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: World models enable model-based planning through learned latent dynamics, but imagined rollouts become unstable as the planning horizon grows or the dynamics distribution shifts: an unconstrained predictor feeds each predicted state back as input, so the latent distribution contracts until distinct states merge. We argue that this drift and contraction reflect two missing structures in planner-facing latents: a history-conditioned predictive state summarizing past observations and actions, and geometric organization that separates configuration, momentum, and task semantics. We propose HaM-World, a structured world model that decomposes the latent state into a canonical-like (q,p) subspace and a context subspace c, while using Mamba selective state-space memory as the history-conditioned input to the same latent dynamics. The (q,p) subspace evolves through an energy-derived Hamiltonian vector field plus learnable residual/control dynamics, while c captures semantic, dissipative, and non-conservative factors. The planner uses this single latent state for prediction, reward/value estimation, imagined rollouts, and CEM search. On six DeepMind Control Suite tasks, HaM-World ranks first on four and second on the other two, with the highest six-task Avg. AUC (91.9, +10.3% over TD-MPC2). Within the horizons the planner unrolls, it reduces imagined-rollout error to 45% of TD-MPC2's and wins 11/12 k in {3,5,7} MSE cells. Under 12 OOD perturbations spanning dynamics shifts, action delay, and observation masking it attains the highest return in every condition (+10.2% on Finger Spin, +13.6% on Reacher Easy). Ablations show that both selective memory and the Soft-Hamiltonian prior contribute to the gains. Mechanism diagnostics support the intended design, showing bounded action-free energy drift, structured energy variation under policy rollouts, and coherent control-induced energy transfer.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 27 pages including references and technical appendix. Accepted as a poster at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/HaoyunT/HaM_World

Artificial Intelligence.title: Mitigating Backdoors in Masked Diffusion Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models because they can predict multiple tokens in parallel rather than generating tokens sequentially. However, recent studies have shown that MDLMs are vulnerable to backdoor attacks: when an input contains an attacker-chosen trigger, a backdoored model generates a targeted output, such as malicious code, while otherwise behaving normally. Despite this threat, backdoor defenses for MDLMs remain largely underexplored. We present UNMASK, the first defense framework for MDLMs that detects trigger-containing inputs, localizes the trigger tokens, and removes the backdoor from the compromised model. UNMASK exploits two fundamental properties of backdoor triggers, specificity and dominance, to assign a suspiciousness score to each input token. By leveraging two distinctive capabilities of MDLMs, parallel token prediction and token reconstruction at arbitrary positions, UNMASK computes these scores both effectively and efficiently. We further provide a theoretical analysis supporting the design of UNMASK. Evaluations across 40 settings spanning two attacks and four models show that UNMASK detects 99.3% of trigger-containing inputs at a 5% false-positive rate, substantially outperforming the strongest adapted baseline, which achieves 54.8%. UNMASK also achieves over 99% trigger-localization accuracy and reduces the average attack success rate from 95% to 1%, while largely preserving the model's utility on clean inputs.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Make Position Uninformative: Exchangeable Self-Distillation Flattens the Lost-in-the-Middle Curve
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Retrieval-augmented language models answer well when the relevant document comes first or last and poorly when it sits in the middle. Some fine-tuning recipes lift the middle by lowering the start. We show how training contexts teach positional bias. With a uniform answer slot and shuffled distractors, the optimal reader ignores position. Building on this result, Exchangeable Self-Distillation (ExSD) trains a small adapter on shuffled contexts to reproduce the model's answer when it reads the answer document alone. It needs no gold answers and only a few thousand examples. On six models from 1.5B to 32B parameters, ExSD raises both average and worst-position accuracy against the frozen model, including on a held-out test split. In controlled LoRA comparisons, it significantly improves both criteria over Pos2Distill. Against CORD, mean differences are not significant, while worst-position accuracy improves significantly in the 20- and 30-document settings. ExSD also matches or beats gold-answer fine-tuning, changes behavior on other tasks far less, and transfers to unseen tasks. Head probes show greater reliance on content over position.

Artificial Intelligence.title: LoopSeek: Decoupling System One Search from System Two Answering for Long Video Understanding
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Long video question answering requires finding relevant evidence before reasoning over it. With a limited frame budget, single-pass frame selection can miss critical evidence, while adaptive search often relies on repeated text generation to decide where to look. We introduce LoopSeek, a framework that decouples evidence search from answer generation through a division of labor between a non-thinking System I and a generative System II. Our key insight is that search can be expressed as a sequence of small, typed decisions, allowing System I to find the evidence that System II needs. Four System I role agents navigate a tree of video windows and coordinate through probability outputs to select frames, assess evidence, and revise the search without generating text. To align search with System II, System I learns from annotated evidence on questions that System II answers correctly only from that evidence, and the verifier's evidence estimates steer the search without calling System II, which stays frozen and answers once from the selected frames. On five long-video benchmarks, with a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B reading 32 frames, LoopSeek improves average accuracy from 53.5 to 63.9 over the uniform baseline and takes 32--80\% less GPU time per question than agentic methods.

Artificial Intelligence.title: MaPPO: Maximum a Posteriori Preference Optimization with Prior Knowledge
Artificial Intelligence.summary: As the era of large language models (LLMs) unfolds, Preference Optimization (PO) methods have become a central approach to aligning LLMs with human preferences and improving performance. We propose Maximum a Posteriori Preference Optimization (MaPPO), a methodology for learning from preferences that explicitly incorporates prior reward knowledge into the optimization objective. Building on the paradigm employed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and its variants of treating preference learning as a Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) problem, MaPPO integrates prior reward estimates into a principled Maximum a Posteriori (MaP) objective. This not only generalizes DPO and its variants, but also enhances alignment by mitigating the oversimplified binary classification of responses. Additionally, MaPPO introduces no additional hyperparameters, and supports preference optimization in both offline and online settings. In addition, MaPPO can be used as a plugin for DPO variants, including widely used SimPO, IPO, and CPO, and produce consistent improvements. Extensive empirical evaluations of different model sizes and model series on three standard benchmarks (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, and Arena-Hard) demonstrate consistent improvements in alignment performance without sacrificing computational efficiency.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Artificial Intelligence.title: SocialMemBench: Are AI Memory Systems Ready for Social Group Settings?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Memory systems for AI assistants were built for single-user dialogue, a design mismatched to multi-party social group settings. This matters for the social assistants being built today: group-acting agents in chat platforms, and proactive personal assistants whose model of a user must include their social context. Existing memory benchmarks evaluate dyadic or workplace dialogue; none targets social groups, where memory must anchor facts in shared history rather than professional roles, separate group norms from individual exceptions, and attribute correctly even after a member leaves. We introduce SocialMemBench, a benchmark of human-verified synthetic social group networks across five archetypes and three size tiers (4-30 members), with 430 personas and 1,031 QA pairs across nine question categories. Our evaluation exposes five failure modes, framed as testable hypotheses, and we provide evidence on two through the research probes Subject-Mem and SMG. Our results support three connected takeaways. First, social-group memory must preserve distinctions that ordinary fact recall misses, such as who dissented from a decision and what one member knows about another. Second, across 43 networks the four evaluated frameworks (Mem0, LangMem, Graphiti, Cognee) score 0.12-0.18, well below uncompressed retrieval (0.346) and full context (0.370) with the same answerer, and changing the answerer or retrieval budget does not close the gap. Third, explicitly representing social information mitigates specific failure modes but leaves others open: Subject-Mem targets single-stream conflation, lifting attribution from 0.25-0.46 to 0.78, and SMG targets norm-individual conflation, lifting group-decision accuracy to 0.70, while the other three modes remain open. We release the dataset, the evaluation pipeline with both research probes, and the audit viewer as a testbed for social-memory research.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to EACL 2027 (main conference). 23 pages, 5 figures, 18 tables. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/qunlexie/SocialMemBench Code: https://github.com/Qunlexie/SocialMemBench

Artificial Intelligence.title: Visual Foresight for Agentic Reasoning Before Action in Urban Navigation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of action consequences, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, a training-free agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with visual foresight for reasoning before action. Our central idea is to use predicted future views to assess proposed actions in the context of persistent medium-horizon subgoals and observed experience. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. To enable visual foresight, a predictive world sandbox uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to generate future views of proposed movements, providing visual cues for reasoning about their consequences beyond the current observation. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions using the subgoal and accumulated experience to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Distilling Visual Agents from Limited Interaction Experience
Artificial Intelligence.summary: How much interaction experience is needed to distill a capable visual agent? We study learning from few tasks and recorded interaction histories. Our framework selects representative trajectories using skill-context coverage and ordered visual-decision similarity. On-policy distillation (OPD) learns through fresh interaction on selected tasks or fresh student responses at fixed histories. Across Navigation, Sokoban, and spatial mapping, even one online training task supports transfer to other tasks. Four fixed trajectories raise a 4B student's success from 49.17% to 82.08% on standard Navigation and from 60.16% to 85.55% on Sokoban, recovering over 90% of the measured gap to a 27B teacher on these panels. On an independent Navigation panel, replay improves success from 45.83% to 76.67%, retaining 91.36% of the same-task online gain without new interaction during optimization. Training repetitions, matched supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a 9B extension further support the value of compact experience.

Artificial Intelligence.title: VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Fast World Planner: Advantage-Aware Action-Chunk Policy for Online Planning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is central to online planning for model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), but its iterative refinement incurs planning latency. Reducing refinement iterations often degrades performance, motivating stronger policy guidance learned from the planner. However, existing methods typically learn from the planner through action-level alignment, which does not directly capture the complete $H$-step planner proposal. Moreover, planner imitation leaves further target improvement to online refinement. To address these limitations, we propose FaSt World PlANner (SWAN), an advantage-aware MPPI-based MBRL framework that explicitly represents and improves the complete $H$-step planner proposal to improve policy guidance for efficient online planning. For proposal representation, SWAN combines k-MPPI, a multimodal MPPI extension, with a mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) action-chunk policy to capture multiple modes and correlations across time and action dimensions. For proposal optimization, we introduce Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization (APO), which reuses MPPI evaluations to construct an improved target using advantage estimates and trains the policy toward this target while preserving planner alignment. Experiments across 31 high-dimensional continuous-control tasks from DMControl, HumanoidBench, and MyoSuite show that SWAN substantially improves control performance and sample efficiency while using 50% fewer MPPI refinement iterations than state-of-the-art planning-based MBRL methods. Finally, SWAN demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree Go2, achieving stable velocity-tracking locomotion with high-frequency control. (see our demo at https://swanfastworldplanner.github.io/)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Internalized Experience: How Training Data Shapes Memory Formation in LLMs
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Parametric memory enables large language models (LLMs) to retain information from past experience and reuse it in subsequent tasks. Yet how training data supports the internalization of reusable task rules remains unclear. We introduce FSMem (Finite-State Machine Memory), a state-transition framework for constructing training data and studying how data content and organization shape memory formation. We evaluate rule reuse across synthetic worlds, classical planning, and code execution through valid-action identification and execution-outcome prediction, complemented by next-operation prediction in code. Our experiments reveal several systematic learning patterns. Under matched training conditions, even unchanged task rules become harder to internalize when learned alongside a larger variety of action types; by contrast, scaling the training data to provide broader state-action coverage generally improves rule learning. We further find that training at a single execution depth produces depth-specialized behavior, with models performing best when training and test executions have similar lengths. Motivated by this finding, we construct cumulative corpora that combine short and long trajectories, which can outperform long-trajectory-only training while using fewer training tokens. Together, these results demonstrate that the same task rules can be internalized differently depending on how execution experience is constructed, and that understanding these learning patterns can guide the design of more effective training data for parametric memory.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Action-Conditioned Transition Irreversibility for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Reinforcement Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Reinforcement-learning agents shape the observations they encounter; consequently, detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) states requires analysing action-conditioned trajectories rather than treating inputs as independent samples. We propose Action-Conditioned Transition Irreversibility (ACTI), a detector that evaluates forward and backward transition likelihoods, calibrates this comparison against the in-distribution profile at each timestep, and smooths the score over a short window, using no future information. We tested ACTI across six environments and fifteen detectors within OOD-RL-Bench, using the four anomaly mechanisms that qualified in every environment, with ten policy replicates per environment. All primary metrics are matched-time: each score after anomaly onset is compared with a clean twin rollout's score at the same timestep. Our method secured the top macro matched-time AUROC, outperforming the dynamics-model baseline (PEDM), while scoring transitions roughly two orders of magnitude faster. Compared to the state-only variant, ACTI achieved a small but consistent AUROC gain and a shorter detection delay. The capacity-matched forward-only baseline, ACTI-Forward, secured a statistically significant advantage in AUPRC alongside a reduced detection delay. The discrepancy in AUROC did not reach statistical significance. Ablation studies suggest instead that performance improvements stem from action conditioning, calibration at each timestep, and smoothing of the transition-likelihood scores. Based on these results, we recommend using ACTI-Forward.

Artificial Intelligence.title: FlowPlan-G2P: A Structured Generation Framework for Transforming Scientific Papers into Patent Descriptions
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Researchers routinely publish inventions as scientific papers, yet turning them into patent descriptions remains difficult because statutory enablement demands rigid, legally structured disclosure. Prior patent drafting methods either assume patent-native inputs such as claims or generate sections from outline chunks via local retrieval without an explicit document-level representation of technical dependencies. We propose FlowPlan-G2P, a graph-mediated framework that (1) induces a directed concept graph of invention elements and functional relations, (2) partitions it into ordered section subgraphs scored by connectivity, homogeneity, and domain-constraint penalties, and (3) synthesizes patent descriptions using section-specific drafting strategies. On Pap2Pat-EvalGold, Zero-Shot achieves the highest BERTScore at 0.87 yet receives only 1.5 out of 5 on expert legal compliance compared to 4.7 for FlowPlan-G2P, where lexical overlap and expert ratings rank systems in opposite order. Under expert-aligned Pat-DEVAL evaluation, open-weight Llama-4-Scout with \textsc{FlowPlan-G2P} reaches an overall score of 4.3 compared to 2.3 for Few-Shot Sonnet-4.5. We release our code publicly at https://github.com/repoofideas/flowplan_g2p.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Agent Money Benchmark: Can AI Agents Be Trusted to Spend Money?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.

Artificial Intelligence.title: S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with a 500-Million-Persona Resource
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Simulating economic responses at society scale requires decision rules that respond to household circumstances and accounting rules that track the consequences. We introduce S$^2$-MAS, a multi-agent simulation framework that combines 500 million synthetic household personas with trainable decision policies, reusable financial scenarios and explicit state transitions. After training on 2.93 million financial examples, YN-mini achieves 74.554% accuracy and 38.375% question-macro F1 in its MLX implementation on held-out consumer financial choices. These scores exceed the question-specific majority baseline by 2.783 and 6.206 percentage points, respectively. In a purchase-funding simulation, 12 million households each make a choice under two conditions. The 24 million choices generate 288 million monthly ledger states in 3 h 59 min on 14 GPUs. Jointly increasing purchase goals and approved credit limits produces heterogeneous changes in consumption, cash and repayments. Much of the variation in consumption arises from households switching between deferral and purchase. In a separate retrospective study of 1,060 households, standalone YN-master-9B reduces the mean absolute error in annual consumption by 3.42% relative to the deterministic fully rational benchmark. Its mean forecast is 19.7% below observed mean consumption. Further tests measure how year labels and information about later outcomes affect decisions. Together, these experiments establish an executable alternative for studying heterogeneous household behavior with learned policies and explicit financial accounting.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 55 pages, 13 main figures and 8 supplementary figures. Revised Figures 5 and 8, streamlined tables, and edited the text for clarity. Project resources: https://github.com/KataDavidXD/s2-mas

Artificial Intelligence.title: BitShare: Sensitivity-Aware Binning and Bit Sharing for Compacting LLM Weight Storage
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Bridging Teacher-Student Capability Gaps with Recurrent Computation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from large language models to smaller students, yet stronger teachers do not always yield better students. Recent studies report diminishing or even negative returns from teacher scaling. We hypothesize that these limitations arise in part from insufficient student capacity to absorb the teacher's knowledge. We therefore investigate loop and recurrent computation as a way to expand the student's effective capacity by modifying its computation graph while keeping the backbone parameter count fixed. Under teacher-forced KD during pretraining, weight-shared looping improves performance but retains teacher-size saturation, whereas cross-token recurrence avoids the observed reversal with larger teachers. In mathematical post-training under both teacher-forced KD and on-policy distillation (OPD), recurrent students scale better with increasing teacher size than looped and vanilla LLMs do. Crucially, we show that a pretrained LLM can be readily fine-tuned into a looped or recurrent architecture jointly with OPD, without repeating pretraining. Our recurrent Qwen model improves with larger teachers and consistently outperforms looped and vanilla LLMs. This suggests a new post-training paradigm that integrates architectural conversion into distillation, avoiding a separate conversion stage while substantially improving student performance and maintaining near-vanilla inference latency.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Econometric vs. Causal structure learning for time-series data: Implications for policy interventions using COVID-19 data
Artificial Intelligence.summary: This study compares regression-based and causal structure-learning approaches to recovering temporal dependencies in UK COVID-19 data and assesses their suitability for policy analysis. We evaluate four econometric methods and eleven structure-learning algorithms using a common lag-expanded dataset that permits edges only from past to current variables. The dataset comprises 866 daily observations and 45 variables, represented by 55 numeric series after categorical encoding. Maximum lags of 1, 7, 14, 17 and 21 days are examined; all four econometric methods and ten structure-learning algorithms successfully return structures at every lag specification. We compare graph structure, complexity, fit and temporal-edge stability across lag specifications. The resulting graphs vary substantially in density, complexity, fit and stability. Agreement with the knowledge graph is limited, while low structural Hamming distance sometimes reflects sparsity rather than recovery of known relationships. Edge recurrence also varies markedly by method, revealing sensitivity to the allowed history window. Diagnostics for VAR models using all lagged predictors indicate residual dependence, non-normality and instability; estimation becomes infeasible at longer lag orders. Policy evaluation raises further concerns: few mobility-to-infection links emerge, few meet the empirical coverage criterion, and none do so in longer-lag analyses. Common temporal constraints therefore do not resolve methodological disagreement. Learnt dependency structures should not be treated as policy-ready causal models without stronger identification assumptions, robustness checks and sufficient empirical support for the interventions assessed.

Artificial Intelligence.title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Evaluating embodied-AI policies in closed loop across simulation benchmarks such as LIBERO and RoboTwin requires repeated integration, as each benchmark defines its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention. Evaluation can also be slow: with a StarVLA checkpoint, the 5,000 episodes of RoboTwin Easy take 17.5 hours on four RTX PRO 5000 GPUs. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluators identifies two bottlenecks: alternating between one simulator and inference leaves the GPU at only 14.3% average utilization on LIBERO-Long, while rendering at every control step on RoboTwin means an action-chunk policy reads only one of every 16 rendered observations. We present RoboScope Kit, an evaluation toolkit that integrates each model and benchmark once through a unified interface, keeping each benchmark's native evaluator and scoring, and accelerates evaluation through two mechanisms. (1) Scheduling: simulator workers and policy replicas scale independently, with autotuning sizing both pools to each workload and host. (2) Runtime optimization: the simulation runtime skips unconsumed simulation and rendering work without changing the policy's inputs or outcomes. On a single RTX 4090, RoboScope Kit runs LIBERO-Long 6.2$\times$ faster and 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes 13.2$\times$ faster than StarVLA, and 2.1-7.3$\times$ faster than RLinf and vla-eval. Scaling to four RTX PRO 5000 GPUs, it evaluates all 5,000 RoboTwin Easy episodes in 66 minutes (15.8$\times$ faster). LIBERO-Long success rates stay within 0.3 percentage points of StarVLA, and every RoboTwin episode matches its exact outcome and terminal step.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 37 pages, 9 figures, 31 tables. Project page: https://mint-sjtu.github.io/RoboScope-Kit/ Code: https://github.com/MINT-SJTU/RoboScope-Kit

Artificial Intelligence.title: What If TSF: Evaluating Scenario-Guided Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled time series forecasting to move beyond numerical observations and incorporate external information in multimodal settings. Such information can improve forecasting performance, but accuracy alone may not reveal whether models appropriately respond to it: a model may ignore relevant information, fail to distinguish scenarios with different implications, or overreact to irrelevant or weak signals. We introduce What If TSF (WIT), a benchmark for evaluating whether models effectively respond to future scenarios. WIT constructs controlled scenario sets by fixing the forecasting state while systematically varying future scenarios, enabling three complementary evaluations: Factual Comparison, which measures the predictive utility of factual scenario information; Relational Comparison, which evaluates whether forecasts satisfy expected direction, contrast, intensity, and restraint relations across scenarios; and Grounded Comparison, which provides a complementary empirical assessment of scenario-induced revision trajectories where comparable real cases are available. Experiments show that factual accuracy gains do not consistently translate into appropriate responses to alternative scenarios, demonstrating the need to evaluate multimodal forecasting beyond predictive accuracy.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Active Learning for Communication Structure Optimization in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Optimizing the communication structure of large language model based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) has been shown to improve downstream performance and reduce token usage. Existing methods typically train on randomly sampled tasks. We show that this optimization is sensitive to the choice of training tasks: downstream accuracy varies widely across random task sets, and adding more random tasks does not consistently improve it. To actively identify the most valuable tasks from a pool of task-answer pairs, we propose an ensemble-based information-theoretic task selection framework. It estimates task informativeness by how much a candidate task changes the distribution over graph parameters, using ensemble Kalman inversion as an efficient and derivative-free approximation of the Bayesian update. The resulting estimator is especially suitable for black-box and noisy multi-agent systems and remains effective with ensembles much smaller than the parameter dimension. To further reduce the number of tasks whose informativeness must be evaluated, we introduce representative pre-selection and surrogate modeling. We validate the framework in benign and adversarial settings and across multiple task formats. It outperforms random training, demonstrating more effective task selection and greater overall cost efficiency.

Artificial Intelligence.title: MedCoast: Semantic Abstraction of Reasoning Trajectories for Test-Time Biomedical Question Answering
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Biomedical question answering often requires multi-step reasoning under limited inference budgets. While test-time search methods such as Tree-of-Thought can improve reasoning performance, directly searching over free-form language is computationally expensive and highly redundant, as many reasoning trajectories contain semantically equivalent intermediate steps expressed in different surface forms. We introduce MedCoast, an offline-to-online reasoning framework that converts sampled chain-of-thought trajectories into a compact space for structured process supervision. Offline, we recursively cluster semantically similar reasoning steps under shared prefixes to construct an abstract reasoning tree that captures recurring clinical reasoning patterns. We then derive node-level supervision from progress toward correct solutions, and train a lightweight process reward model (PRM) to evaluate partial reasoning states. At inference time, the learned critic guides test-time exploration by prioritizing promising reasoning prefixes. Across seven biomedical QA benchmarks, MedCoast often improves over self-consistency under fixed inference budgets, with gains of up to 15 points. Despite using a reward model more than 50 times smaller, MedCoast achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art reward models in several settings, highlighting its potential for resource-constrained biomedical reasoning.

Artificial Intelligence.title: AsyncMixVLA: Runtime Asynchronous Robot Policy Switching for Adaptation to Dynamic Environments
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, enabling general-purpose robotic control. However, environmental perturbations, such as objects moving during execution, can undermine their reliability. Different policies exhibit complementary failures under mid-rollout perturbations, motivating selective switching between policies for recovery. Such switching can stall the robot during inference of the newly invoked policy or, if performed asynchronously, act on stale observations. We present AsyncMixVLA, an adaptive inference framework for proactive, asynchronous switching across heterogeneous VLA policies. A learned trigger balances recovery potential against intervention harm to selectively escalate to a higher-compute policy. AsyncMixVLA overlaps its inference with committed outgoing actions and aligns its context to the anticipated takeover state. On LIBERO-Long with mid-rollout perturbations, AsyncMixVLA improves perturbed task success from 69.5% to 77.1% over the lightweight policy. It achieves 84.9% overall success, comparable to 84.5% for synchronous switching, while reducing median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms. Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1% success across three unseen perturbation families, compared with 71.3% for the stronger constituent policy in aggregate.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Manuscript prepared for the DAC 2027 Research Track (IEEE conference format)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Automatic Vehicle Detection using DETR: A Transformer-Based Approach for Navigating Treacherous Roads
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Automatic Vehicle Detection (AVD) in diverse driving environments presents unique challenges due to varying lighting conditions, road types, and vehicle types. Traditional methods, such as YOLO and Faster R-CNN, often struggle to cope with these complexities. As computer vision evolves, combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Transformer-based approaches offers promising opportunities for improving detection accuracy and efficiency. This study is the first to experiment with Detection Transformer (DETR) for automatic vehicle detection in complex and varied settings. We employ a Collaborative Hybrid Assignments Training scheme, Co-DETR, to enhance feature learning and attention mechanisms in DETR. By leveraging versatile label assignment strategies and introducing multiple parallel auxiliary heads, we provide more effective supervision during training and extract positive coordinates to boost training efficiency. Through extensive experiments on DETR variants and YOLO models, conducted using the BadODD dataset, we demonstrate the advantages of our approach. Our method achieves superior results, and improved accuracy in diverse conditions, making it practical for real-world deployment. This work significantly advances autonomous navigation technology and opens new research avenues in object detection for autonomous vehicles. By integrating the strengths of CNNs and Transformers, we highlight the potential of DETR for robust and efficient vehicle detection in challenging driving environments.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Surprising Success, Repeated Failure: Entropy-Guided Credit Assignment for Exploration in LLM Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models (LLMs) through outcome-level feedback, yet recent approaches to finer-grained credit assignment often require auxiliary models, additional sampling, or privileged information. Although policy entropy provides a readily available signal, prioritizing uncertain positions under both reinforcement and penalization concentrates penalties where failed responses still retain alternatives for recovery, which can suppress opportunities for exploration. To address this, we introduce Entropic Advantage Policy Optimization (EAPO), an entropy-guided credit assignment method that treats success and failure asymmetrically. Specifically, motivated by the observation that success under uncertainty is less repeatable while confident failures tend to recur, EAPO couples normalized policy entropy with the sign of the response advantage to reinforce surprising success and correct repeated failure. It assigns stronger reinforcement to high-entropy decisions in successful responses and stronger penalties to low-entropy decisions in failed responses, while attenuating penalties at uncertain positions to preserve opportunities for recovery. By redistributing the response advantage across tokens, EAPO derives token-level credit directly from existing rollout signals without additional supervision. We validate EAPO on a range of reasoning tasks across both base and reasoning backbones, demonstrating that it achieves the best overall performance. We further show that EAPO promotes more effective exploration, broadening problem coverage and diversifying successful reasoning strategies.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Learning response-aware patient dynamics for respiratory support
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Respiratory support can shape the short-term physiological trajectory of critically ill patients, but patients receiving the same intervention may follow different physiological trajectories. Clinical patient dynamics models typically predict future states from recent physiology and recorded interventions, while physiological change is mainly represented through the predicted future state. We propose a response-aware patient dynamics model that explicitly represents physiological change during autoregressive state updating. The model decomposes predicted physiological change into state-dependent baseline dynamics and respiratory-support-associated deviations, with room air providing a reference for the decomposition. We provide a formal analysis of this reference-anchored formulation. A response pathway encodes the predicted physiological change and uses it to update the latent patient state across the forecast horizon. Across ICU cohorts from two independent institutions, the proposed model achieves comparable overall trajectory prediction to patient dynamics baselines, with more consistent improvements when physiological states are changing.

Artificial Intelligence.title: CLASP: Deciding Structure and Claims Before Decoding for Whole-Slide Pathology Report Generation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Whole-slide pathology report generation has advanced through stronger slide encoders, retrieved knowledge, and, recently, slide-level multimodal LLMs. However, these generators leave every report-level choice to the decoder: how long the report is, how it is organised, and which findings it states and where. On the standard PathText-BRCA benchmark, we find that these choices dominate n-gram overlap, as reports from the query's hospital selected without learning approach the state of the art, while decoders under-generate and fall back to the most frequent findings. We present CLASP, a decide-then-decode generator that makes these choices explicitly, once per slide. Before decoding, an Exemplar Structure Prior (ESP) takes the sentence plan and length from reports of image-similar cases, a Calibrated Claim Decision (CCD) selects the findings from calibrated slide posteriors, and a Claim-to-Sentence Placement (CSP) assigns each finding to a planned sentence. A Plan-Conditioned Decoder (PCD), refined by structure-anchored sequence training, then writes the report under these decisions. With 35M parameters, CLASP outperforms retrained report generators and slide-level LLMs of up to 7B parameters, matches the strongest published results, and generalises to lung cancer from unseen hospitals. Its decisions change what the reports state, not only their length, transfer to an LLM decoder, and can withhold what H&E cannot show: withholding receptor status leaves 23% fewer contradictions with clinical records than the same network without decisions.

Artificial Intelligence.title: MACE: Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation of Frozen Vision-Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: In plant phenotyping, crop disease diagnosis has traditionally relied on expert assessment of visible symptoms and on models tailored to specific crops or diseases, and both are difficult to scale across field conditions. Recent methods provide frozen vision-language models with source-grounded knowledge bases that summarize the typical symptoms of each disease but describe little of how symptoms vary across individual cases. We introduce MACE (Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation), a training-free method that supplements the knowledge base with a memory of symptom descriptions paired with known disease labels. MACE matches a description of the query image against this memory and retrieves only text descriptions and disease labels, so the query is the only image that the diagnosis model sees. Across ten crops, MACE with Claude Sonnet 5.5 improved accuracy over the knowledge-base baseline from 42.8% to 62.2% in distribution and from 50.7% to 57.0% on held-out image collections. Retrieved disease labels accounted for most of the gain, and adding the corresponding text descriptions improved in-distribution accuracy by about six percentage points.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Project page: https://mace-bench.github.io/

Artificial Intelligence.title: Naive Prompt Optimization: Rethinking the Need for Complex Prompt Search
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Efficiently improving autonomous agents across diverse tasks is central to accelerating recursive self-improvement (RSI) in agentic AI, with prompt optimization emerging as a promising approach capable of delivering performance gains comparable to those achieved by fine-tuning model weights, while reducing computational costs in both optimization and serving. However, recent developments increasingly favor unnecessarily complex prompt optimizers. We introduce Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO), a lightweight single-lineage method that iteratively revises prompts using a teacher model with rollout feedback. NPO achieves comparable or better performance than GEPA with fewer rollouts in IFBench and HotpotQA, and its advantage increases with stronger teacher models, suggesting that stronger teacher reasoning may partially substitute for optimizer-side search complexity. In interactive games, NPO remains broadly competitive with GEPA despite its much simpler mechanism, while GRPO still performs better on some tasks less amenable to prompt-only optimization. We also show that NPO-optimized prompts elicit similar performance improvements when applied verbatim to other student models, especially across models within the same family. Overall, our preliminary results show that simple, linear prompt optimization can rival substantially more sophisticated and complex search procedures.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 24 pages, 17 figures, accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Responsible Use of Meta-Agents

Artificial Intelligence.title: LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Automated subject cataloging assigns controlledvocabulary headings to bibliographic records, but LCSH has no standard public benchmark. We introduce LCSHBench: 22,346 books in 15 languages from the openly licensed Harvard, Columbia, and Princeton catalogs. Records enter only when at least two independent cataloging agencies assigned LCSH; we release per-catalog provenance plus union and unanimous answer views. A concordance study of 465,187 works cataloged by all three libraries shows why this design matters: libraries usually agree on the underlying topic (93.3% share a concept-level heading) but often differ in exact expression (39.4% have identical heading sets). LCSHBench therefore scores both exact and concept matches, with set and rank metrics broken down by language and heading type, across open-vocabulary generation and full-vocabulary retrieval. As a first demonstration, a low-rank fine-tune of a 300M on-device embedder improves cross-lingual retrieval and beats a 3,072-dimensional hosted embedder on development exact recall@200 (0.659 vs 0.623). The language panel shows the gain is not uniform, and held-out-test and end-to-end confirmation remain future work.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Beyond Unit Tests: Path-Aware Rubric-Guided LLM Autograding of Notebooks
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Jupyter notebooks support open-ended, multi-step assessments in which students build one logical flow across interdependent steps, combining code, written analysis, and generated outputs such as plots. These reflect authentic scientific practice but are hard to grade consistently, since students may make different yet equally valid choices at each step, so a later answer can only be judged in light of the choices a student made earlier. We present an LLM-based autograder for such flow-structured notebook questions. It generates a rubric from a reference solution, then applies a softening pass that relaxes criteria tied to the reference so legitimate alternative paths are not penalized. Each question group is graded in a single model call, so later answers are judged against the student's own earlier choices, using question-type tags and schema-constrained, low-temperature outputs. Evidence is scored multimodally: code, text, numerical outputs, and figures from code cells. We deployed the tool in a machine-learning course, integrated with Gradescope, with a pre-submission format check and prompt-injection defenses, and evaluate it both in that live course and against archived submissions graded by staff in earlier terms. We report agreement, cross-model variance, cost, student perceptions, and injection resilience. With low-temperature models, agreement with human scores is often strong, including on the open-ended items the design specifically targets, while run-to-run stability depends sharply on the model's temperature support.
