We compare our task-manifold representation against Cartesian XYZ and principal component analysis (PCA) under random testing, systematic traversal, and genetic search strategies. Results demonstrate that the feasible task domain improves test-generation efficiency and enables systematic reference-cell coverage. Crucially, random and genetic search strategies detect a broader spectrum of failure patterns than baseline representations, revealing that complete reference-cell coverage alone does not exhaust intra-cell behavioral dynamics. Furthermore, differential testing between defective and patched controller versions reveals that targeted evolutionary search detects aggregate failure-rate shifts from software repairs. Finally, a cross-platform study on a 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 arm in MoveIt 2 confirms workflow transferability to kinematically redundant manipulators. Together, these findings highlight the necessity of combining feasibility-aware domain modeling with complementary search strategies for systematic testing of robot software.

Robotics.title: SCAP: Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining
Robotics.summary: Single-modality action-expert pretraining controls competition from visual shortcuts before vision--language--action (VLA) adaptation. Yet single-modality pretraining can impair the vision--language interactions needed for subsequent joint prediction. We construct a diagnostic model in which VA or LA pretraining can disable an initially active pathway for joint vision--language modeling. In this model, subsequent training with complete visual and language inputs cannot restore the pathway, even with unlimited adaptation. We therefore introduce Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining (SCAP), a new action-expert pretraining stage that precedes full-input training. During this stage, visual and text tokens are randomly masked before entering the VLM. In this unified diagnostic model, SCAP can preserve the joint vision--language modeling pathway during pretraining and subsequent full-input training. Compared with direct full-input training, it can also reduce reliance on visual shortcuts and increase reliance on language instructions. SCAP consistently improves performance across four different VLA architectures. In real-robot experiments, it achieves 76.67% average success across three instruction-conditioned manipulation tasks, outperforming full-input pretraining by 25 percentage points.

Robotics.title: InterBand-EMG: A Cross-Band Foundation Model for Generalizable Hand-Pose Estimation
Robotics.summary: Surface electromyography (sEMG) enables continuous hand-pose estimation, but learning representations that generalize across users and movements remains challenging. We introduce InterBand-EMG, which combines band-specific quantization with cross-band reconstruction and structured masked code prediction to learn transferable EMG representations for hand-pose tracking. We also introduce SynapMyo, an eight-channel EMG-to-pose dataset comprising 1,227.74 hand-hours from 499 users across 68 movement categories. Experiments on emg2pose and SynapMyo show that InterBand-EMG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in joint-angle accuracy across all three generalization settings on both datasets. The source code and the SynapMyo dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance of this paper.

Robotics.title: BladeR: Scalable, Shape-Guided 3D Reconstruction of Wind Turbine Blades from UAV Imagery
Robotics.summary: The structural integrity of wind turbine blades is critical for safe, efficient energy production. Accurate 3D reconstruction allows precise localization and quantification of wear and early damage detection. While drone-based inspections are standard, their high-resolution imagery poses challenges such as weak texture, lighting variability, and high computational cost. We present BladeR, a scalable pipeline for high-quality 3D reconstruction from inspection imagery. A hierarchical sparse reconstruction strategy leverages GPS/IMU data and blade shape priors to guide advanced keypoint matchers on full-resolution images. For dense reconstruction, a tiled Gaussian Splatting framework processes 45 MP images at native resolution, isolates the blade from background, and adaptively enhances detail recovery along the leading edge. Validation against commercial and open-source baselines shows significant improvements in model completeness and detail.

Robotics.title: Ego2Ego: Generative Visual Perspective Taking Across Collaborators
Robotics.summary: Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration. However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person. We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person's egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator's camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator's perspective. This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap. We address these challenges with Ego2Ego -- a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants. Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person's current view from the ego person's visual memory. Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone. By generating the collaborator's egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.

Robotics.title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
Robotics.summary: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.

Robotics.title: A context-adaptive policy framework for robust and reactive robotic manipulation via uncertainty-aware imitation learning
Robotics.summary: Generating robust and reactive manipulation strategies that can adapt to changing context information is a challenging task in robotics. Over the years, Learning from Demonstration (LfD) has emerged as an intuitive and effective solution for generating reactive policies, particularly by following dynamical-system(DS)-based approaches. However, most state-of-the-art DS-based approaches focus on addressing the robustness limitations, overlooking the modulation of policies in response to the environment. As a result, they tend to be inflexible with respect to parameterization by task-dependent variables. In this work, we build on existing work on policy fusion and uncertainty quantification to propose a context-adaptive policy framework that combines task-parameterized, robust and reactive manipulation. For this, we use LfD to acquire a policy that is conditioned on the robot state and low-dimensional task-dependent parameters reflecting the environment. We combine the learned policy with additional uncertainty-aware policies using a Mixture of Experts (MoE) formulation to improve its out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness and convergence behavior. The approach is evaluated on the LASA handwriting dataset and on a real 7-DoF robot in three scenarios: force-conditioned grasping, manipulation of deformable food items and object-centric grasping.

Robotics.title: Highly Deformable Proprioceptive Membrane for Real-Time 3D Shape Reconstruction
Robotics.summary: Reconstructing the three-dimensional (3D) geometry of surfaces is essential for robot perception and physical interaction. Vision-based approaches reconstruct surfaces at high resolution from an external viewpoint but often require a clear line of sight. A conformable membrane that reconstructs its own deformation offers a complementary route. Based on optical waveguide shape sensing, this work presents a stretchable proprioceptive silicone membrane that reconstructs localized contact and in-plane stretching under large deformation. The membrane integrates edge-mounted light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and centrally distributed photodiodes (PDs) in an elastomeric waveguide using liquid-metal interconnects. A neural network maps the optical intensity measurements to a dense point cloud of the membrane surface. Optical acquisition and model inference run in real time at about 90~Hz. Under localized pressing of up to about 25~mm depth, the membrane achieves an overall shape reconstruction error of 1.580~mm. It also localizes finger contacts with a mean error of 1.779~mm. Extreme strain tests show that the optical signals remain informative for in-plane outline reconstruction up to 75\% strain, approaching the mechanical limit of the liquid-metal circuit. These results indicate a practical route to proprioceptive shape sensing in deformable robotic systems.

Robotics.title: Going with the Flow: Koopman Behavioral Models as Pseudo Planners for Visuo-Motor Dexterity
Robotics.summary: Contemporary visuo-motor dexterity models often rely on expressive policy classes with diffusion and transformer backbones to achieve strong performance. However, these architectures require significant data and computational resources, and remain far from reliable, particularly for multi-fingered dexterity. Importantly, they model skills as reactive mappings and rely on fixed-horizon action chunking, creating a rigid trade-off between temporal coherence and reactivity. To address these issues, we first introduce Unified Behavioral Models (UBMs), a framework to represent dexterous skills as coupled dynamical systems that capture how visual features of the environment (visual flow) and proprioceptive states of the robot (action flow) co-evolve. As such, UBMs ensure temporal coherence by construction rather than heuristic averaging. Unlike world models that attempt to predict the impact of arbitrary robot actions on the environment, UBMs target behavioral dynamics that encode how demonstrated robot behavior is related to desired impacts on the environment. A UBM can be viewed as a pseudo planner: given an initial condition, it computes the desired robot behavior over the entire skill horizon, while simultaneously "imagining" the resulting flow of visual features. We propose Koopman-UBM as a first instantiation of UBMs in the form of a structured latent linear system. K-UBM's inherent structure enables reactivity and adaptation via automated online replanning: the model acts as its own runtime monitor, automatically triggering replanning when predicted and observed visual flow diverge beyond a threshold. Across seven simulated tasks and four real-world tasks, our approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art baselines, while offering considerably smoother executions, fast inference, efficient learning, robustness to occlusions, and automated online replanning.

Robotics.title: Empathetic Motion Generation for Humanoid Educational Robots via Reasoning-Guided Vision--Language--Motion Diffusion Architecture
Robotics.summary: This article suggests a reasoning-guided vision-language-motion diffusion framework (RG-VLMD) for generating instruction-aware co-speech gestures for humanoid robots in educational scenarios. The system integrates multi-modal affective estimation, pedagogical reasoning, and teaching-act-conditioned motion synthesis to enable adaptive and semantically consistent robot behavior. A gated mixture-of-experts model predicts Valence/Arousal from input text, visual, and acoustic features, which then mapped to discrete teaching-act categories through an affect-driven policy.These signals condition a diffusion-based motion generator using clip-level intent and frame-level instructional schedules via additive latent restriction with auxiliary action-group supervision. Compared to a baseline diffusion model, our proposed method produces more structured and distinctive motion patterns, as verified by motion statics and pairwise distance analysis. Generated motion sequences remain physically plausible and can be retargeted to a NAO robot for real-time execution. The results reveal that reasoning-guided instructional conditioning improves gesture controllability and pedagogical expressiveness in educational human-robot interaction.

Robotics.title: PRISM-SLAM: Probabilistic Ray-Grounded Inference for Scale-aware Metric SLAM
Robotics.summary: Monocular SLAM historically suffers from scale ambiguity and tracking failure in dynamic environments. While recent vision foundation models (VFMs) provide remarkable zero-shot depth priors, naively integrating these deterministic predictions ignores predictive uncertainty and frame-to-frame scale inconsistencies. We propose PRISM-SLAM, a real-time framework that rigorously integrates VFM priors into a structured Bayesian factor graph to achieve scale-aware, metric-consistent localization and mapping. Specifically, we introduce a Plücker Ray-Distance Factor to anchor monocular observations in absolute space within a globally consistent metric coordinate system, mathematically resolving scale drift by making the metric scale Fisher-identifiable. To handle environmental dynamics, we derive an epistemic uncertainty proxy from temporal depth consistency and formulate a Dynamic Scene Uncertainty Gating (DSUG) mechanism. This soft-gating approach probabilistically down-weights dynamic distractors without incurring the heavy computational overhead associated with traditional semantic segmentation masks. By employing a multi-process architecture that asynchronously processes VFM inference and geometric tracking, PRISM-SLAM provides verified metric output at 30 FPS using solely RGB input, bridging the gap between foundation models and real-world robotic applications. Evaluated on the TUM RGB-D and 7-Scenes benchmarks, PRISM-SLAM achieves a metric $SE(3)$ Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) nearly identical to its oracle-aligned $Sim(3)$ error. This demonstrates that our system can produce deployment-ready metric trajectories by delivering robust metric SLAM solutions without any post-hoc scale correction. Project page: https://prismslam-cmd.github.io/prismslam_pr/

Robotics.title: Ace! Motion Planning of Professional-Level Table Tennis Serves with a Robot Arm
Robotics.summary: Table tennis, a dynamic, compact, and popular sport, has for many years received significant attention as a robotics benchmark. Most of the research has focused on the rally aspect -returning an incoming ball-requiring high-speed vision, agile motion planning, and tight closed-loop control. On the other hand, getting robots to serve competitively remains a rather unexplored research problem, which in fact requires pushing physics modeling and control to the extremes. In this work, we present the first-ever approach capable of generating official rule-compliant serves that produce ball spins of up to 550 rad/s and speeds of up to 6.7 m/s, matching and even surpassing the capabilities of elite table tennis players. In official matches against these competitors, our serves score direct points in up to 21% of attempts and push the win rate of robot-initiated rallies above 50%. The motion plans for serving are generated in simulation by combining optimization-based control and Bayesian optimization, and are executed zero-shot in open-loop on our hardware.

Robotics.title: Flying over The Uncertain Nature (FORTUNE): Intelligent and Humanistic 3D Path Planning for Low-Altitude Collaboration
Robotics.summary: Low-altitude intelligent agents are driving demand for timely, socially responsible collaborative sensing in dynamic urban environments. Yet jointly handling heterogeneous spatio-temporal sensing demands, real-time uncertainty, and human-centered constraints in a unified multi-uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) framework remains challenging. We study 3D multi-UAV path planning and joint task assignment under heterogeneous spatio-temporal uncertainty of ground points of interest (PoIs). Unlike studies assuming static, known PoIs, we formulate a unified model capturing persistent (Type-I), temporally predictable (Type-II), and emergent unpredictable (Type-III) demands. Following the low-altitude-for-good principle, we explicitly model altitude-dependent societal and environmental costs, including noise and public safety risks, jointly optimizing sensing effectiveness and socially compliant operations. To solve the resulting large-scale mixed-integer nonlinear problem, we propose FORTUNE, a hierarchical offline-online framework. Offline, a Transformer-based predictor forecasts Type-II activation windows, while an enhanced sparrow search algorithm (ES2A) with priority-aware decoding and danger-aware evolution generates globally coordinated flight plans. Online, lightweight trajectory refinement accommodates new Type-III PoIs while preserving global mission coherence. Experiments on real-world traffic and synthetic datasets show FORTUNE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks, validating effectiveness, scalability, and practical applicability in dynamic low-altitude systems.

Robotics.title: SiMDex: Mining Similar Egocentric Videos for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Manipulation
Robotics.summary: Recent years have witnessed an explosive trend of scaling ego-centric human videos for robot manipulation, yet it remains unclear which data actually benefits dexterous manipulation. We present SiMDex, a similarity-based data mining framework that casts human data selection for VLA post-training in dexterous manipulation as a recommendation problem. For each robot demonstration, SiMDex runs a recall-ranking-re-ranking cascade over ~32M egocentric human samples: two stages, recall and ranking, select a task-relevant subset in a morphology-agnostic action space, and re-ranking verifies it on pixels, with no change to VLA architecture or training. Against a strong baseline trained with an equal amount of randomly sampled human data, SiMDex uses only ~1.49M mined samples (<5% of the pool) yet improves the overall success rate from 47.7% to 61.7%, showing that selective curation outperforms indiscriminate data mixing.
Robotics.comment: 38 pages, 12 figures, 16 tables. Project page: https://lin-nie.github.io/SiMDex/

Robotics.title: Readiness Barrier Functions: Forward-Invariant Control Authority for Overactuated Multirotor Allocation
Robotics.summary: Allocators that greedily maximize a readiness metric over the actuator fiber bundle of an overactuated multirotor jump between disconnected optimal strata, demanding actuator rates no motor can deliver; effort-minimizing allocators are continuous but cannot keep wrench-rate authority above any certified level. We reconcile the two by treating authority as a forward-invariant quantity: a control barrier function on the log-determinant of the drag-aware authority co-metric, enforced at torque level by a quadratic program in the allocation null space. A single design inequality makes the certified set compact and strictly interior to the actuator box; the readiness cost of a rotor deactivation is $\ln(n/(n{-}m))$ for symmetric designs. An alignment ratio states when tracking stays exact, otherwise the wrench error is $\mathcal{O}(ρ^{-1/2})$, and a robust variant handles motor-parameter uncertainty with a closed-form floor shift independent of the airframe matrix. On a hexarotor and a fully-actuated octorotor the closed-form gap matches simulation to machine precision. Over $300$ randomized missions, greedy maximization violates the certified floor in up to $51\%$ of authority-scarce missions, while the proposed filter never leaves the certified set and, in the hardest moment reversal, commits a $79\times$ smaller wrench error. The robust variant holds the floor on all $150$ perturbed plants. A high-fidelity simulation with measured propeller and motor data shows where the floor holds under unmodeled aerodynamics, electrical limits, and delay, and where it stops applying.
Robotics.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters

Robotics.title: LF-GICP: Parameter-Free Degeneracy-Aware LiDAR Odometry via a Voxel-Normal Localizability Field
Robotics.summary: Scan-to-map LiDAR odometry drifts unboundedly along the unobservable axes of geometrically degenerate environments like tunnels and corridors, and existing degeneracy handling requires environment-specific parameter tuning. This paper presents a parameter-free approach. We show that in voxelized GICP the Gauss--Newton (GN) Hessian masks translational degeneracy, because covariance regularization keeps the translation block artificially well-conditioned. We bypass this with a regularization-free voxel-normal localizability field and two of its statistics: a normalized fraction $f_0$ detecting directional anisotropy, and an absolute per-voxel mass $λ_0$ distinguishing information absence (tunnels) from dilution (dense open scenes). A temporal-median gate combines both to trigger Fisher-information correspondence weighting. Calibrated once by fixed rules on two short sequences and then frozen, LF-GICP achieves the lowest KITTI relative translation error ($0.865\%$) under an identical evaluation protocol against re-run baselines, outperforms them on GEODE tunnels and MulRan, leads the HeLiPR mean, and generalizes across four sensor types without re-tuning. We further demonstrate empirically that straight, uniform tunnels remain unobservable along their axis for LiDAR-only registration.

Robotics.title: DIDO: Distilling Interaction-Centric Dynamics into One-Step Denoising for World Action Models
Robotics.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) use video generation models to predict future visual dynamics for robotic manipulation, but iterative denoising introduces additional latency for closed-loop control. We empirically find that visual content converges at different rates during denoising. Static background structure forms early, whereas the gripper and manipulated object remain blurry after the first step, with their interaction dynamics emerging only through subsequent denoising. Consequently, naively truncating a multi-step video model to one step preserves scene structure but loses the interaction-centric dynamics most critical for manipulation. To address this issue, we propose DIDO, which distills the converged dynamics of a multi-step video model into a single denoising step. DIDO combines distribution matching distillation with interaction-centric representation guidance. Beyond compressing multi-step generation into one forward pass, DIDO explicitly models the gripper, manipulated object, and their interaction using supervised bounding-box visual reasoning tokens. Additionally, DIDO aligns the target object's representations across multiple model layers with features from a pretrained DINOv3 encoder. This interaction-centric guidance helps the distilled model preserve both the relevant entities and their future dynamics in a single step, while substantially reducing inference latency. DIDO achieves an average success rate of 99.0\% on LIBERO, 76.6\% on LIBERO-Plus, and 92.0\% on RoboTwin, while also demonstrating effective transfer to long-horizon and generalization tasks in real-world robotic manipulation.

Robotics.title: LexiconVLA: Learning Reusable Atomic Action Codebooks for Manipulation
Robotics.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models struggle to reuse recurring atomic actions across manipulation tasks. Our diagnostic study reveals that reliable task completion does not imply consistent execution of constituent atomic actions across task contexts. We present LexiconVLA, a retrievable atomic-action lexicon for cross-task reuse. Global and detail codebooks capture shared interaction structure and fine-grained execution variation respectively, preserving both reusable patterns and execution details. Visual-Atomic Action Alignment couples trajectory reconstruction from visual state changes with visual outcome prediction from action codes, grounding the lexicon in motion and its effects. We learn these codebooks with trajectory reconstruction and visual alignment on our AtomAction Dataset of 57,803 segments from 69 tasks. A planner and scene-aware adapter translate new goals into code-conditioned subtasks for a shared policy, without skill-specific experts or deployment-time parameter updates. Across five policy backbones on 26 RLBench tasks, LexiconVLA largely maintains performance on 18 seen tasks while improving success on 8 tasks held out from policy training. With BridgeVLA, unseen-task success rises from 16.67% to 34.17% (+17.50 percentage points), and overall success reaches 71.08%, the highest among methods with reported results. Real-robot experiments demonstrate stepwise execution and failure recovery.

Robotics.title: LocoPilot: Single-Operator Bilateral Teleoperation for Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning
Robotics.summary: Learning loco-manipulation policies requires demonstrations that capture coordinated base and arm motion on the target embodiment. Robot-free interfaces allow demonstrations to be collected independently of the target robot, increasing flexibility but without directly capturing platform-specific commands, proprioception, and body-mounted observations. On-robot teleoperation allows to capture these signals directly, but requires an interface capable of commanding the complete system concurrently. This paper presents LocoPilot, a single-operator bilateral teleoperation and data-collection framework implemented on a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator, an Intel RealSense D435 wrist camera, and an Intel RealSense D405 head camera. A second 6-DoF Piper L arm, used as the leader and two handheld controllers provide simultaneous control of the base, body posture, manipulator, and gripper. The follower arm interaction forces are estimated without a dedicated force/torque sensor and rendered to the operator through a passivity-constrained haptic channel. A ROS~2 pipeline records synchronized multimodal observations together with a unified 11D action shared by teleoperation and policy deployment. Compared to prior work, LocoPilot uniquely unifies robot-in-the-loop legged data collection, force feedback without motion-capture instrumentation, and the same action interface at deployment. We evaluate the interface across multiple loco-manipulation tasks and validate the complete collection-to-deployment pipeline by fine-tuning MolmoAct2 on pick-and-place demonstrations and deploying on the physical robot without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics. Code available at: https://github.com/iit-DLSLab/LocoPilot

Robotics.title: RynnUnify: Towards Unified Embodied Brain
Robotics.summary: We introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video--language reasoning. With capabilities spanning spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and grounding, RynnUnify connects an understanding of the physical world with visual anticipation of how it evolves across successive subtasks. Building on these capabilities, we further develop an agentic extension through reinforcement learning to selectively use video predictions for reasoning about unobserved states and interaction outcomes. We also develop a world-action extension of the full RynnUnify model, translating its understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory reasoning. Experiments show that RynnUnify achieves the highest average embodied understanding score among the evaluated unified multimodal models and improves the Rynn-VP overall score by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano. Its agentic extension improves the Rynn-GEU average by 6.0 points over direct reasoning, while the world-action extension achieves 51.5\% success on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7\% average success across three real-robot tasks. Together, these results establish RynnUnify as a shared foundation for embodied understanding, visual planning, and robot control, taking a step toward a unified embodied brain.

Robotics.title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
Robotics.summary: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on vision-language backbones, tying policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While recent world-action models mostly scale the video backbone and its data, we argue that the choice of latent space is just as critical, and that the policy should be trained natively in that space. We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; it predicts future features with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art average RoboTwin 2.0 success under both clean-only and full training, and state-of-the-art LIBERO-Plus success with corrected instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competitors; with full training, its success scales with model size up to 2.1B. Its S and B policies run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming both on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, and La-JEPA outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to $π_{0.5}$. A design study shows that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction improves the policy even when skipped at inference. Tailoring the policy's design, including its latent space, to control can thus matter more than the knowledge transferred from a pretrained generative backbone, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.
Robotics.comment: 31 pages, 6 figures. v2: full-RoboTwin results with scaling to 2.1B parameters, leave-one-out ablation, revised figures and text. Code: https://github.com/mt-clemente/lajepa

Robotics.title: Fault-Geometry-Aware Control Allocation for Emergency Quadrotor Landing under Single-Motor Loss of Effectiveness
Robotics.summary: Partial single-motor loss of effectiveness (LoE) changes the remaining control-authority geometry of a quadrotor and can change which control allocator performs best during emergency landing. We compare three allocators in Crazyflie software-in-the-loop simulation: bounded weighted least squares (reported as PINV), a finite-candidate residual allocator (QP-lite), and the same residual allocator with scoring parameters tuned offline by the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM). For this study, fault geometry is represented by the known failed-motor index. At $η= 0.496$ remaining effectiveness, matched development trials select CEM for M1, M3, and M4 and PINV for M2; the M3 selection is a one-trial margin (29/30 versus 28/30). After freezing this routing map, the policy achieves 117/120 safe first-contact touchdowns on fresh seeds and 115/120 in a separate randomized-order integrated-supervisor evaluation. For the critical M2/PINV branch, Firth regression gives a nominal $η_{50} \approx 0.4956$ with a within-model 95% bootstrap interval of approximately $[0.4955, 0.4956]$. One-factor-at-a-time $\pm 10\%$ plant perturbations shift $η_{50}$ by up to $0.05495$ for thrust coefficient and $0.04974$ for mass; the most frequent violated first-contact criterion also changes from vertical speed in many conditions to angular rate for mass $-10\%$ and thrust-coefficient $+10\%$. At fixed $η= 0.496$, PINV has a higher M2 safe count than frozen CEM in 9/11 tested plant states and ties in 2/11; the two ties are both 0/30. The experiments therefore distinguish motor-conditioned allocator selection from sensitivity to plant-model mismatch.

Robotics.title: Recursive Bayesian Monitoring of SLAM Failures for LiDAR-Based UAV Navigation
Robotics.summary: SLAM failures remain difficult to avoid in autonomous robotic systems, and undetected failures can propagate to unsafe planning, control, and mission-level decisions. Existing monitoring strategies often depend on prior maps, estimator-internal variables, or redundant sensing, which limits their applicability to deployed and resource-constrained robots. This paper presents a scene-geometry consistency monitor for detecting geometry-manifested SLAM failures using only the geometric output of the SLAM backend. The targeted failures include cumulative drift-induced failures, abrupt misregistration failures, and backend map corruption when they become observable as inconsistency in reconstructed scene geometry. The proposed method represents revisited local regions with recursive latent voxel geometry and evaluates each current observation against a trusted continuation explanation and a weak non-propagated reference explanation. The resulting voxel-wise evidence contrasts are aggregated into a fixed-boundary monitoring signal for online failure declaration and downstream safety response. Experiments on self-collected sequences, GEODE benchmark sequences, multiple robotic platforms, and different SLAM backends show that the monitor responds to failures when they are manifested in backend scene geometry. It achieves 4/4 valid post-onset declarations with no pre-onset alarms on four self-collected sequences, detects geometry-manifested failures in all five corrupted GEODE runs while remaining alarm-free in five geometrically consistent runs, adds only 0.1--0.2\% absolute CPU load, and supports a closed-loop UAV detect--isolate--recover workflow.

Robotics.title: Terrain-Aided Navigation Without Raycasting: A Sliding Grid Approach for Point Cloud Processing
Robotics.summary: We investigate the use of a point cloud measurement in terrain-aided navigation. Our goal is to aid an inertial navigation system, by exploring ways to generate a useful measurement residual for effective nonlinear state estimation. We compare two such measurement models that involve the scanning of a digital terrain elevation model: a) one that is based on typical ray-casting from a given pose, that returns the predicted point cloud measurement from that pose, and b) another computationally less intensive one that does not require raycasting and we refer to herein as a sliding grid. Besides requiring a pose, it requires the pattern of the point cloud measurement itself and returns a predicted point cloud measurement. We show that the sliding grid achieves comparable accuracy to raycasting, especially at higher altitudes, while being orders of magnitude faster computationally. By eliminating the need for raycasting, the sliding grid removes the dependency on dedicated GPU hardware or high-performance CPUs, making it well-suited for real-time terrain-aided navigation on resource-constrained embedded platforms.

Robotics.title: 2D or 3D? Rethinking Token Pruning in 3D VLAs with Cross-Modal Correlation Awareness
Robotics.summary: 3D vision-language-action (VLA) models process both image and point cloud tokens at each control step, increasing the cost of action prediction. Token pruning can reduce this cost, but a token's contribution depends on which other tokens remain. We present 2Dor3D, a framework that jointly selects which 2D and 3D tokens to retain under a fixed token budget. Our analysis shows that either modality can compensate for the other within a patch, that neighboring correlations help explain differences in pruning risk, and that shared tokens couple pruning decisions across patches. In one box-closing observation, two patches with nearly identical interaction scores differed eightfold in the action deviation caused by removing their image token. Guided by these findings, 2Dor3D transfers cross-modal prediction residuals to retained tokens, uses neighborhood correlation entropy to explore more retention choices at local outliers, and updates pruning costs after each proposed exchange between coupled regions. A fused GPU kernel packs the selected tokens into a shorter sequence for subsequent Transformer layers. Across RLBench and LIBERO, 2Dor3D speeds up end-to-end inference by $2.06$--$2.10\times$ on MLA and $1.86$--$1.91\times$ on FiS-VLA, with task success rates 0.5--0.6 percentage points below the corresponding unpruned models.

Robotics.title: Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching
Robotics.summary: Off-policy reinforcement learning of pretrained flow policies remains challenging due to the instability of optimization arising from the multi-step sampling process. Recently, Q-learning with Adjoint Matching (QAM) addressed this by recasting policy improvement as a stochastic optimal control (SOC) problem guided by a learned critic. However, QAM inherits a fundamental fragility of critic-guided improvement, since small critic errors can be exponentially amplified and often lead to performance collapse. This paper introduces Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching (TRQAM), a stable off-policy fine-tuning algorithm that adaptively controls the path-space KL between the fine-tuned and pretrained policies through projected dual descent. Specifically, we adapt a trust-region parameter $λ$ inside the sampling process of the flow policy and prove that $λ$ exactly weights the path-space KL in the SOC objective. As a result, our method can tightly control the deviation from the pretrained policy within a prescribed KL budget, achieving stable off-policy RL. Through experiments on 50 OGBench tasks, TRQAM consistently outperforms prior methods in both offline RL and offline-to-online RL. In particular, TRQAM achieves an overall success rate of 68% in offline RL, substantially improving over the strongest baseline at 46%.

Robotics.title: EgoPhys: Physics-Informed Digital Twins for Deformable Objects from Egocentric Video
Robotics.summary: Humans naturally understand object physics through everyday interactions, but predicting how deformable objects, such as soft objects and fabrics, respond to manipulation remains a major challenge for computer vision and robotics. Existing deformable physical twin methods typically rely on controlled multi-view or depth capture and costly per-object physical refinement. We present EgoPhys, a framework for constructing predictive deformable physical twins from a single egocentric RGB interaction. EgoPhys combines persistent correspondences with per-frame monocular 3D observations to fit a sequence-specific spring-mass model from moving-camera observations. Because a short interaction weakly constrains fine-grained local stiffness, EgoPhys amortizes this refinement across training interactions using a compact state-conditioned residual model that predicts bounded local corrections around the sequence-specific estimate and remains frozen at test time. Experiments show improved held-out future prediction over adapted deformable-twin baselines, with the amortized residual further improving prediction while reducing local-refinement cost by approximately 10-59x over dense per-spring optimization. The resulting twins also support deformable-object action selection, with representative physical robot manipulation providing a qualitative proof of concept.

Robotics.title: FIRE3D: Feed-forward Interactive 3D Scene Reconstruction Within A Minute
Robotics.summary: We present FIRE3D, a unified framework that transforms a single RGB image or casual video into interactable 3D scene assets for games and interactive applications in under a minute for up to twelve textured instances including preprocessing. At the core of FIRE3D is a feed-forward inference pipeline that predicts a compositional scene representation from posed RGB-D observations estimated from the RGB capture, including the 6-DoF pose, bounding box, mesh, and texture for detected objects. By modeling the scene as a collection of discrete entities, FIRE3D produces amodal object assets that can be independently edited and used in interactive applications. Our framework requires no test-time optimization, runs substantially faster than the compared reconstruction systems, and provides object-level completeness beyond existing feed-forward 3D approaches. We demonstrate leading detection accuracy, strong geometry reconstruction, and competitive rendering quality on the evaluated benchmarks, with substantial runtime gains.

Robotics.title: Co-Design Gym: A Unified Benchmark for Embodiment-Policy Co-optimization
Robotics.summary: Finding an optimal behaviour policy within a given environment is a widely studied problem in domains as diverse as games, robotics, energy infrastructure, communication networks, and multi-agent systems. Numerous benchmarks have been developed to support such research, but the vast majority assume that the agent's embodiment (design) is fixed, focusing instead on policy learning alone. Lifting this assumption gives rise to a broader class of problems in which optimizing embodiment and policy separately is highly suboptimal. An agent's embodiment strongly shapes which control policies can be discovered, while the optimal embodiment is in turn defined by the policies it admits. To help the research community study this class of problems explicitly and systematically, we introduce Co-Design Gym - a suite of benchmark environments for jointly optimizing embodiment and policy. Our environments span domains such as robotic manipulation and locomotion, multi-robot cooperation, deformable and soft dynamics, video games, electricity grids, wireless networks, F1 racing, multi-agent warehouses, and optimal control, offering 20 environment families (domains), with over 85 distinct co-design presets in total. We further contribute a systematic evaluation of representative co-design algorithms, characterizing the current state of the art. Together, these contributions lay the groundwork for cumulative, comparable progress in co-design.
Robotics.comment: Aviraj Newatia and Yordan Tsvetkov contributed equally

Robotics.title: GenSight: Unified Video Generation and 4D Perception for Embodied World Modeling
Robotics.summary: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures, but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world. We present GenSight, a unified embodied world model that brings future video generation and dense perception into a single pretrained video diffusion transformer. GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.

Robotics.title: UA-Depth: Uncertainty-Aware Depth Restoration for Material-Agnostic Object Manipulation
Robotics.summary: Robotic manipulation requires accurate metric depth, yet commodity RGB-D cameras often fail on non-Lambertian objects such as transparent, reflective, and translucent materials, producing holes, structured noise, and biased depth. Most restoration methods produce only a single depth map, treating noisy and reliable regions uniformly for downstream tasks while ignoring regional uncertainty. We present UA-Depth, an uncertainty-aware depth restoration framework that iteratively co-refines depth and pixel-wise uncertainty, and uses uncertainty-gated features to suppress unreliable cues for stable updates. To strengthen zero-shot behavior, UA-Depth leverages a frozen depth foundation model as a prior to initialize missing or unreliable depth, and applies two-stage MAD-weighted log-depth scale normalization to reduce outlier bias in relative-to-metric alignment. We introduce an eight-dataset zero-shot benchmark across diverse scenes, materials, and sensors. Across these benchmarks, UA-Depth achieves the best mean rank among representative baselines, with particularly strong gains on datasets dominated by transparent and reflective objects. Beyond depth metrics, we demonstrate downstream improvements in category-level 6D pose estimation and 6D grasp synthesis by exploiting the predicted uncertainty. \emph{Code, models, and data for training and evaluation will be released upon publication.}

Robotics.title: Belief-Driven Quantum Magnetometer Control for GPS-Denied Navigation
Robotics.summary: Autonomous vehicles increasingly need to navigate without satellite positioning. Magnetic anomaly navigation (Mag-Nav) with quantum magnetometers offers a passive, unjammable fix, but the low size-weight-and-power (SWaP) sensors that small drones can carry are weak, and they are operated open loop at a fixed setting. Interferometric (Ramsey) magnetometers face a trade-off: long interrogation times are more sensitive but become ambiguous when the expected field is uncertain. The navigator's own position belief, pushed through the anomaly map, predicts that field. We close this loop. The filter's predictive field distribution sets the Ramsey phase and interrogation time at every epoch, through a closed-form rule that moves between an ambiguity limit and a decoherence limit. We evaluate it on real U.S. Air Force flight data (real tracks, inertial drift, measured fields, and a survey map tested 18 months after it was flown), with only the Ramsey sensor modelled. Against fixed-setting baselines, 63 of 72 independent flight windows favour belief driven sensing ($p = 2 \times 10^{-11}$). Error falls by 20-27% for low-SNR sensors and 30-44% for mid-contrast sensors. An ablation separates the two ingredients. Phase alignment drives the gain in steady flight, and the rule matches the best fixed setting without the hindsight tuning that setting requires. After a lost start, interrogation time adaptation is essential, cutting median error by 37-42% even against hindsight-tuned phase-aligned settings. Gains are small for high-quality sensors with accurate maps. On an IBM superconducting qubit, the rule's interrogation time stays within $1.3\times$ of the empirical optimum. Coupled with information-aware routing, belief-driven sensing lowers mission error by 15-40%.

Robotics.title: ScaleEvals: Scaling Generalist Policy Evaluation through Reset-Free Autonomous Play
Robotics.summary: Real-world evaluation of generalist robot policies is bottlenecked by manual resets, human grading, and small fixed task suites with limited diagnostic coverage. We present ScaleEvals, a scalable reset-free protocol that evaluates policies through continuous physical play across a robot fleet. A VLM AutoPrompter generates scene-grounded tasks with difficulty estimates, language prompts, and skill tags, enabling performance analysis across diverse rollouts. A VLM AutoGrader assesses task progress, achieving 90.7% agreement with human graders. Scores are aggregated via a soft-win Bradley-Terry model, while tag-stratified ANOVA provides interpretable capability diagnostics. Across 3,000+ physical autonomous rollouts on DROID and YAM, ScaleEvals achieves 23.0 net rollouts/hr per station while reducing active human labor by 98%. By ranking five SOTA generalist policies, ScaleEvals correlates with held-out manual evaluation ranking on DROID (r=0.94, rho=0.90, p=0.018), and remains internally consistent on a second embodiment, YAM (r=0.839, rho=0.80). Beyond aggregate rankings, we observe behavioral compositionality: recombining verb-, skill-, and object-conditioned evidence predicts policy order on unseen prompts. Across 10 tasks and 240 prospective physical rollouts, we recover three-policy orderings of 96% pairwise concordance, demonstrating ScaleEvals can predict not just which policy leads, but where rankings reverse.

Robotics.title: Occupancy Planar Patch: Incremental Probabilistic Bounded-Plane Reconstruction from LiDAR Data
Robotics.summary: Online surface reconstruction from LiDAR scans requires observation models that respect the sensor's physical measurement geometry. Unlike unordered point sets, LiDAR returns carry anisotropic range noise along known rays, which also implicitly identify free space. We introduce the Occupancy Planar Patch (OPP), an incremental bounded planar patch representation that evaluates surface likelihoods and free space directly in range-space, allowing sensor noise, plane uncertainty, and ray clearance to be explicitly modelled during reconstruction. A single ray-to-patch association weight jointly updates plane geometry, refines surface boundaries, and blends camera imagery. The method is evaluated using six sequences from the Oxford Spires and Multi-Campus datasets. OPP achieves the highest precision and lowest reconstruction error among evaluated methods, while producing stored maps among the most compact. By conservatively admitting surfaces only where geometric evidence is certain, OPP prioritises structural precision over unconstrained completeness, which is well suited for architectural modelling. Geometric reconstruction operates in real time, requiring 81 ms per frame on a representative sequence, with texture projection adding 134 ms.

Robotics.title: A Hybrid Multi-Goal Path Planning Framework for Powered Wheelchairs in Dynamic Environments: From Simulation to Real-World Validation
Robotics.summary: Autonomous powered wheelchairs (PWs) operating in human-centered environments must combine efficient multi-destination path planning with continuous collision avoidance strategies in the presence of static and dynamic obstacles. This study presents a hybrid framework integrating Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP)-based global task ordering, Potential-Field (PF) guidance, and local Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and A-star (A*) planners. PF guidance transfers global path information to local planners, helping the robot stay aligned with the global path during obstacle avoidance. Local planning is enhanced with direction-aware, extended-neighborhood A* or RRT using environment-aware sampling and two-step extension. The TSP-PF-RRT and TSP-PF-A* methods are evaluated in normal, crowded, and extra-crowded simulation environments using point-based and elliptical robot models. The elliptical model accounts for platform dimensions during collision avoidance phase. Hardware tests on the physical PW use motion capture (MoCap) for ground-truth measurements, while outside-MoCap experiments rely on onboard LiDAR and RGB-D sensing. Results show that incorporating the wheelchair geometry changes the observed collision behavior, yielding comparable collision avoidance performance between the two hybrid planners under the elliptical model.
Robotics.comment: This work is under review at the International Journal of Social Robotics. The manuscript extends arXiv:2610.42049 by introducing an elliptical wheelchair model, enhanced local planning methods, and hardware validation

Robotics.title: Knowing What You Carry: Scalable Physics-Anchored World Models for Robotic Planning with Liquid Payloads
Robotics.summary: Payload-carrying robots, such as delivery robots and autonomous trucks, must choose motions that keep them and their payload safe, so their planners predict the outcome of each candidate motion. Modern planners compare thousands of candidates per step on a GPU, using world models such as batched simulators or learned predictors. Most of them assume a rigid payload, but a liquid payload keeps moving after a maneuver, and its state is rarely measured. Near a safety limit, small prediction errors can make an unsafe plan look safe. Coupled fluid simulations are accurate but too costly for every candidate, while low-order slosh models are cheap but accurate only away from resonance. We study this trade-off on a ground vehicle with a partly filled tank near its rollover limit. First, we build PLiMB (Parallel Liquid-MultiBody), a GPU-parallel slosh simulator that, to our knowledge, couples FLIP liquid two-way with many multibody vehicles for the first time. It provides training data and a high-fidelity reference. Second, we propose a scalable physics-anchored world model that combines a modal-slosh and roll prior, an estimate of the hidden liquid state from the vehicle's own motion history (no sensor in the tank), and a learned correction. Without simulating the fluid, it scores thousands of candidate plans in one batched pass within a 20 Hz control tick on one GPU. We judge each world model by the plans it leads a planner to choose. Near the rollover limit, planners that treat the liquid as a rigid payload or use published low-order slosh models repeatedly pick unsafe plans when a safe one exists. Ours never does in our standard tank and makes about half as many in a wide tank whose sloshing mode lies in the maneuver band. There, the liquid state left by earlier driving can change the best plan, and reading it from the vehicle's history halves our model's near-limit prediction error.

Robotics.title: Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency
Robotics.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.

Robotics.title: CoReMatch: Recurrent Continuous Coordinate Refinement for Real-Time Robotic Feature Matching
Robotics.summary: Feature matching underpins many robotic perception tasks, including visual localization, mapping, SLAM, and autonomous navigation. Existing semi-dense matchers predict confidence on fixed grids, limiting correspondences to predefined locations and requiring costly high-resolution grids for precise localization. We present CoReMatch (Coordinate Refinement Match), a recurrent framework that refines correspondences directly in continuous coordinate space rather than predicting discrete confidence maps. CoReMatch progressively improves correspondence estimates by propagating information across iterations. At the coarse stage, a Deep Aggregated Transformer captures global context and iteratively updates correspondence coordinates, while a lightweight regression head further sharpens their localization. Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show that CoReMatch strikes a strong balance between accuracy and efficiency, outperforming Efficient LoFTR in accuracy while running more than 10x faster on embedded edge hardware. These results demonstrate that recurrent coordinate refinement offers an efficient and scalable approach to real-time feature matching for robotic perception.

Robotics.title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
Robotics.summary: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.
Robotics.comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables: a 4-page paper with appendices. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

Robotics.title: Probing Invisible Actuation Shifts for Test-time Calibration of Visuomotor Policies
Robotics.summary: Visuomotor policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs) are increasingly deployed on robots whose cameras and controllers differ from those used to collect their training data. Such deployment introduces two kinds of shifts. Visual shifts, such as a moved camera, change the observed images; actuation shifts, such as a retuned controller, latency or an added payload, change only how commanded actions translate into robot motion. Invisible to the policy, actuation shifts sharply degrade its success, even under domain randomization. In this work, we propose PEA, a test-time calibration method that identifies actuation shifts through active probing before task execution. Specifically, before each episode, the robot executes a short probe that moves one arm axis at a time with known commands, so that gain, delay and drift leave separable traces. A closed-form identifier estimates them from the response, and PEA compensates every subsequent command so that the robot executes the motion the policy intends. The identifier requires no policy training and thus applies to any frozen visuomotor policy. Since visual shifts remain visible to the policy, PEA further adapts the frozen policy with a removable low-rank adapter, addressing coupled visual and actuation shifts. Experiments on LIBERO with a WAM and a VLA show that, without any policy training, the identifier of PEA recovers most of the success lost to actuation shifts and generalizes to shifts unseen during training (e.g., from 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy).

Robotics.title: SG-DOR: Learning Scene Graphs with Direction-Conditioned Occlusion Reasoning for Pepper Plants
Robotics.summary: Robotic harvesting in dense crop canopies requires effective interventions that depend not only on geometry, but also on explicit, direction-conditioned relations identifying which organs obstruct a target fruit. We present SG-DOR (Scene Graphs with Direction-Conditioned Occlusion Reasoning), a relational framework that, given instance-segmented organ point clouds, infers a scene graph encoding physical attachments and direction-conditioned occlusion. We introduce an \emph{occlusion ranking} task for retrieving and ranking candidate leaves for a target fruit and approach direction, and propose a direction-aware graph neural architecture with per-fruit leaf-set attention and union-level aggregation. Experiments on a multi-plant synthetic pepper dataset show improved occlusion prediction (F1=0.73, NDCG@3=0.85) and attachment inference (edge F1=0.83) over strong ablations, yielding a structured relational signal for downstream intervention planning.

Robotics.title: Intervention-Robust VLA: Diverse Demonstrations for Robot Deployment with Safety Filters
Robotics.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to 90% from 0% for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs.

Robotics.title: UNILARN: Latent Action Pretraining with Dedicated RGB, Depth, and Unified RGB-Depth Supervision
Robotics.summary: Depth provides critical geometric supervision for robot manipulation, yet existing depth-aware policies typically inject it through fused representations or auxiliary objectives, leaving its role in action learning implicit. We introduce UNILARN, a latent-action pretraining framework that explicitly preserves three complementary supervisory targets from RGB-D transitions: RGB-specific, depth-specific, and unified latent actions. RGB and depth transition embeddings are first discretized through a shared codebook, then fused and re-quantized through a separate unified codebook, preserving modality-specific dynamics while modeling their shared action semantics. These three latent-action targets provide separate pseudo-action supervision during VLA pretraining, avoiding both inconsistent independent learning and premature multimodal fusion without requiring robot action labels. The pretrained VLA is subsequently fine-tuned on executable actions and requires only RGB observations and language instructions at inference. Experiments in simulation and the real-world show improvements over RGB-based latent-action pretraining, particularly on geometry-sensitive manipulation tasks.

Robotics.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
Robotics.summary: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can transfer agile robot skills from simulation to the real world, but closing the sim-to-real gap by domain randomization requires expert physics knowledge, and simulator calibration from real data typically targets a few hand-picked parameters. Even then, simulators miss real-world effects, and environments reconstructed from onboard perception inherit sensing errors that limit policy improvement. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to calibrate simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity domains online during deployment. Residual fidelity captures sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies and perception-induced environment uncertainty. NFC operates in a latent space so that realistic environments can be sampled from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning. The framework is informative: the pretrained policy is fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected, sequential NFC seeds its proposal from the simulation-pretrained estimator, and a hallucination policy modulates posterior uncertainty following optimism in the face of uncertainty. NFC attains the most accurate posteriors among established simulation-based inference methods on five robots with up to 39 physical parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain. On a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle deployed on snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC raises success on rough terrain from 26% to 70% and reduces orientation jerk by 88%. Code and videos will be released upon publication.
Robotics.comment: The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/nfc/

Robotics.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration: Turning Field Anomalies into Simulation Fine-Tuning
Robotics.summary: A policy that transfers from simulation to a lab robot often fails in the field. Calibrating a simulator from real-world data typically targets only a few hand-picked parameters, and even calibrated simulators fail to capture unmodeled dynamics, while environments reconstructed via onboard perception inherit sensing noise and artifacts. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a framework based on conditional flow matching that infers online, directly from a robot's execution data, both simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity - the remaining dynamics discrepancy and the gap between perceived and true environment geometry. A simulation-trained anomaly detector determines when recalibration or fine-tuning is required using onboard sensory signals alone, while an exploration policy actively modulates posterior uncertainty using optimism in the face of uncertainty. Across five robot platforms with up to 39 calibrated parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain map, NFC achieves the most accurate posterior distributions compared to established simulation-based inference baselines. In physical outdoor experiments with a wheeled robot suffering an axle failure across snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC increases rough-terrain navigation success from 26% to 70% while reducing orientation jerk by 88%.
Robotics.comment: The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/nfc/

Robotics.title: FlowPAC: Flow-Guided Visual Pruning and Action Caching for Efficient VLA Inference
Robotics.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. This mismatch with dynamic robotic interactions not only degrades control performance but also causes severe hardware inefficiencies, including fragmented KV-cache layouts and wasted compute on non-critical regions. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems.

Robotics.title: Don't Test Where You Trained: Geographic Overlap Inflates End-to-End Driving Scores
Robotics.summary: In NAVSIMv1, the standard benchmark for end-to-end driving, $89.6\%$ of the test scenes lie within 4m of a training scene. We show that this geographic overlap inflates the reported scores. We propose a geographically disjoint split of NAVSIMv1 and an evaluation that compares models trained on either split on the same scenes, which neither has seen in training. All sensor-based models we test, DiffusionDrive, Latent TransFuser, and DrivoR, lose 3.4 to 6.1 PDMS points on these scenes, mainly by leaving the road and coming close to other objects, against 1.5 points for a baseline without sensors. The loss concentrates where a training drive of the original split passed the same place. At all other places, models trained on the original split are no better than those trained on the geographic split. Models trained on the original split predict road geometry that no camera can see. The gap persists when the auxiliary map loss is removed, so the models memorize locations even without being supervised to. On nuScenes, the geographic split cuts SparseDrive's mapping accuracy by $59\%$ and also degrades its planning. Driving scores on logged scenes thus partly measure how well a model remembers the test locations. We release the split to evaluate generalization to new places.

Computer Vision.title: Mesh-Free Keypoint Learning for Category-Level 6D Object Pose Estimation
Computer Vision.summary: Category-level 6D pose estimation relates partial RGB-D observations of unseen instances to a canonical frame shared across a category. Object-aware reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints retain the geometry of the visible surface. Common reconstruction targets select observed points by their distance to a registered instance surface. We present MORSE-Pose, which derives this support directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations. We map observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retain those inside a tolerance-dilated pose-and-size envelope. This construction is consistent across camera frames and metric scales. When the annotated extent bounds the object surface, the envelope conservatively contains the support of a conventional surface-distance selector. We integrate this target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context. Experiments on REAL275 and HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-based supervision at both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and viewpoint changes, and supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across benchmarks.

Computer Vision.title: Do VLMs Need to Keep Looking at Long Videos? Write It Down, Then Look Away
Computer Vision.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.

Computer Vision.title: PCRG: Training-Free Pruning and Caching of Reference Tokens for Video Generation
Computer Vision.summary: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack the variational autoencoder (VAE) latents of all references and the generated tokens into one full-attention sequence, in which reference tokens make up about half. Because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, these tokens take up an even larger share of the attention computation, yet most of them are static, smooth or irrelevant to the output. To accelerate reference-conditioned generation, we propose pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation (PCRG), a training-free, plug-and-play method that uses two signals the model already computes to assign each reference token to one of three tiers, namely pruned, cached or kept. The first is a low-level redundancy r from VAE latents, since a token whose latent barely changes over time or across its neighbors adds little new content. The second is a high-level importance g from the vision-language-model (VLM) conditioner, where the attention that the prompt and any first or last frames pay to a token tells whether the output needs to read it. Tokens that are not redundant are kept, and redundant tokens are cached if important and pruned otherwise. Pruned tokens leave the sequence before the first step with all rotary position embedding positions unchanged. Cached tokens have their keys and values computed once and reused, and kept tokens are processed as usual. On MiniMax-H3, already distilled to 8 timesteps and quantized to int8, PCRG is 1.57x faster end to end on our V2V-Bench and 1.49x faster on the public VACE-Benchmark, while the quality of VBench drops by only 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. PCRG shortens the sequence rather than changing how attention is computed or which steps are run, so it also stacks on step caching and sparse attention. On V2V-Bench it reaches 1.86x with TeaCache, 1.82x with Spark at nearly unchanged fidelity and 2.15x with Veda.

Computer Vision.title: DailyWildfireCAN: A Dataset and Benchmark for Next-Day Wildfire Spread Prediction in Canada
Computer Vision.summary: Wildfires represent a critical ecological and socio-economic challenge in Canada, where vast boreal forests and a warming climate have amplified the frequency and severity of extreme fire seasons. Predicting next-day wildfire spread can support fire management, but requires capturing complex interactions among weather, fuels, and terrain. Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach to learning these relationships from heterogeneous environmental data, yet its development and evaluation depend on representative datasets. Existing deep learning research on wildfire spread relies predominantly on US-focused datasets, leaving Canadian fire environments underrepresented. To address this gap, we present DailyWildfireCAN, a multi-modal, multi-temporal dataset and benchmark for predicting next-day wildfire spread across Canada. The dataset tracks continuous fire progression over multi-day events at a high spatial and temporal resolution of 90-m and 24-hour, respectively. This resolution preserves fine-scale information relevant to fire-edge geometry, local fuel variations, and terrain effects, supporting research toward improved daily wildfire spread forecasting. DailyWildfireCAN covers 2,440 wildfire events across eight fire seasons 2017-2024 and integrates 33 features across diverse modalities, including topography, meteorology, land cover, vegetation and forest structure, human influence indices, and satellite imagery. We establish a comprehensive benchmark comparing mono-temporal and multi-temporal prediction models, accompanied by a multi-dimensional evaluation framework assessing robustness across wildfire characteristics, geographic regions, and temporal conditions, spatial prediction quality, and sensitivity to reference label variations.
Computer Vision.comment: Preprint; under review. Project page: https://dailywildfirecan.github.io/

Computer Vision.title: SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space
Computer Vision.summary: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill$.$png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models.
