Artificial Intelligence.comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code and synthetic benchmark: https://github.com/khalidaals/ESDSA

Artificial Intelligence.title: Diversity over Scale: Recursive Self-Improvement with Ensembles of Small Open-Weight Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The advancement of large language models (LLMs) has significantly enhanced the capabilities of agents across various tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) loops, in which a language model repeatedly rewrites a program and builds on its previous version, now perform well in machine-learning tasks, but they rely on frontier models and hundreds of calls per run. Small open-weight models are far cheaper, yet when used alone, their programs often crash and their improvements stall. We propose DiVE (diverse models evolve), an ensemble method for RSI that aims to improve creativity and diversity of generated solutions. DiVE uses three components: a shared memory, a failure log, and best-idea-wins rounds. This allows models to write candidate solutions from the same context and retain the best idea at each iteration. On 22 MLE-bench Lite competitions, an ensemble of five 8-12B open-weight models has 25.4% less test error than its average member and 16.7% less than Llama 3.3 70B, and comes within 7.1% of Qwen 3.5 122B-A10B at 75% of its cost. Diversity among small models can thus stand in for part of the scale that RSI relies on.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Center-Aware Ordinal Learning for Prostate Cancer Grading from Histopathology Images
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Prostate cancer grading from histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) is complicated by the ordered nature of ISUP grades, class imbalance, and center-dependent variations in staining, tissue preparation, and scanning. Most weakly supervised methods treat grade groups as independent categories and may therefore learn representations that do not transfer reliably across institutions. We propose a center-aware ordinal learning framework that combines a pretrained pathology encoder with attention-based multiple instance learning. The framework uses an Earth Mover's Distance loss to account for ordinal errors, an ordinal supervised contrastive objective to align same-grade slides across centers while separating grades according to disease severity, and curriculum learning to reduce the dominance of benign cases. We evaluate the framework on approximately 9,100 biopsy WSIs from the two-center PANDA dataset. The proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 0.842 and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.958 on the held-out test set. Its main benefit is observed in cross-center transfer: when a linear probe is trained on Karolinska representations and evaluated on Radboud, accuracy increases from 0.643 to 0.823 and quadratic weighted kappa from 0.899 to 0.930. Performance remains stable in the reverse direction. UMAP projections further show improved mixing between centers while preserving an ordinal grade trajectory. These results suggest that combining ordinal and center-aware objectives produces more transferable slide representations for multi-center prostate cancer grading.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Accepted as an oral presentation at SPIE Medical Imaging 2027

Artificial Intelligence.title: WingBench: Benchmarking How AI Agents Search for Better Designs
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Design search often uses cheap learned predictions to choose which candidates deserve expensive tests, but these tests can fail, especially on the unusual designs that optimization favors. We introduce WingBench, a multifidelity benchmark in which optimizers and AI agents design transonic wings with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) inside the search. They can query a learned aerodynamic surrogate and spend a fixed budget of sequential CFD evaluations, each returning a score or a failure type. WingBench grades the design each method recommends, reporting separately whether it receives a valid score and how good that score is. Using WingBench, we contribute a study of five baseline optimizers and a comparison of three AI agent methods, which produced 6,629 CFD evaluation records. Feedback helps baseline optimizers deliver valid designs when it changes their later proposals, but the differential-evolution variant does so with lower aerodynamic quality. An open-ended research agent finds designs of similar quality to the strongest baselines over 32 CFD queries, with different prior information and unmatched total computation. In early search, our reflection and planning implementations do not consistently improve on it. We release the data, code, agent prompts, and analysis scripts for reproducibility.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Non-verbalised or secret collusion may impose a ceiling on transcript-level monitoring in multi-agent deployments. Internal model activations are known to provide an additional monitoring surface for single-agent phenomena such as deception, but detecting collusion within an unknown subgroup is ultimately a joint inference task over multiple agents. This paper derives collusion detection statistics based on the composite hypothesis testing literature and introduces HELIOS, a multi-agent detection framework for collusion. Using per-agent activation probes as sensors, we then evaluate these principled statistics alongside heuristics on NARCBench, a novel benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collusion detection under environment distribution shift. Across four open-weight models, both our group-level statistics and heuristics transfer zero-shot to NARCBenchs holdout environments. Notably, the best method on every model reaches 0.99 to 1.00 AUROC when transferred from committee deliberations to a steganographic collusion task that unprimed transcript monitors fail to separate. We find empirically that no single statistic or heuristic dominates across tasks, consistent with our analysis that there is no known universally most powerful test for this setting. We then evaluate detector transfer to third-party environments with emergent, rather than instructed, collusion. In one such environment, only 2 of 229 collusive episodes verbalise the coordination in the transcript. We find evidence of partial transfer from NARCBench to these environments, indicating that probes fitted to instructed collusion may not fully capture emergent collusion signals. Overall, we establish multi-agent interpretability as a complementary monitoring technique, while highlighting the need to evaluate detector performance on both emergent and instructed collusion risks.

Artificial Intelligence.title: ScaleEvals: Scaling Generalist Policy Evaluation through Reset-Free Autonomous Play
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Real-world evaluation of generalist robot policies is bottlenecked by manual resets, human grading, and small fixed task suites with limited diagnostic coverage. We present ScaleEvals, a scalable reset-free protocol that evaluates policies through continuous physical play across a robot fleet. A VLM AutoPrompter generates scene-grounded tasks with difficulty estimates, language prompts, and skill tags, enabling performance analysis across diverse rollouts. A VLM AutoGrader assesses task progress, achieving 90.7% agreement with human graders. Scores are aggregated via a soft-win Bradley-Terry model, while tag-stratified ANOVA provides interpretable capability diagnostics. Across 3,000+ physical autonomous rollouts on DROID and YAM, ScaleEvals achieves 23.0 net rollouts/hr per station while reducing active human labor by 98%. By ranking five SOTA generalist policies, ScaleEvals correlates with held-out manual evaluation ranking on DROID (r=0.94, rho=0.90, p=0.018), and remains internally consistent on a second embodiment, YAM (r=0.839, rho=0.80). Beyond aggregate rankings, we observe behavioral compositionality: recombining verb-, skill-, and object-conditioned evidence predicts policy order on unseen prompts. Across 10 tasks and 240 prospective physical rollouts, we recover three-policy orderings of 96% pairwise concordance, demonstrating ScaleEvals can predict not just which policy leads, but where rankings reverse.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Evaluating LLM-based AI agents integrated with materials synthesis tools: the case of atomic layer deposition
Artificial Intelligence.summary: This work provides an overview of the different strategies that can be used to evaluate the performance of AI models and agents based on large language models (LLMs) for materials synthesis. After providing a brief overview of the key technologies behind the current generation of AI agents based on LLMs, we summarize the different approaches to evaluating these models in the context of materials science and in particular on materials synthesis, with a specific emphasis on scenarios in which the models are directly integrated with experimental tools. We discuss evaluation strategies spanning knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, tool-use benchmarks, and closed loop benchmarks involving the interaction with experimental systems or realistic virtual tools. We use atomic layer deposition (ALD) as a case study, emphasizing how existing approaches in the literature both build from general approaches used beyond materials science and can be generalized to other materials synthesis techniques. Finally, we provide a practical evaluation framework to evaluate LLMs in the context of materials synthesis
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Invited prospective paper submitted to MRS Communications

Artificial Intelligence.title: The Effect of Security-Focused Prompts on Reported Findings: A Controlled Experiment on 400 AI-Generated Web Applications
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Agentic coding tools turn a specification into a running web application, so their defaults for authentication, sessions, input validation, and dependencies become its security posture. This study asks whether appending a fixed block of OWASP-aligned security requirements to the prompt changes what such tools produce, by how much, and with what side effects. Each of 100 frozen specifications was realized four times: two agentic tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI) crossed with two prompts sharing a byte-identical functional core, without (A) and with (B) the security block. A fixed static and dynamic pipeline scanned the 400 applications, yielding 6,721 triaged findings, analyzed with count and logistic mixed models and with a dependency diff. The block cut findings per application by a third (incidence-rate ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.60-0.71), equally through both tools, and roughly doubled the declared dependency surface, so variant-B applications carried more high-severity dependency advisories. Adjusted for that surface the advisory rate did not rise (flat per application, 18% lower in aggregate), while high-severity findings in first-party source fell by nearly half. Security-focused prompting is therefore an inexpensive and portable improvement, but it enlarges the dependency surface that has to be audited against it, an effect of library selection rather than of the security requirements themselves.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Selective-Rerouter: A Rerouting Strategy for Hypothetical Post-Disaster Urban Scenarios with a Thin-Boundary Co-Simulator
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Hypothetical post-disaster urban environments may be partitioned into disjoint delay-tolerant-network (DTN) subregions under a thin-boundary information-isolation constraint, which severely limits cross-zone message delivery and makes centralized rerouting impractical. To address this, we propose Selective-Rerouter, a delayed-binding anonymous rerouting strategy for such partitioned environments. The scheme jointly exploits road occupancy and traffic speed for bottleneck detection, adaptively enlarges its upstream intervention window with congestion severity to include vehicles imminently approaching bottlenecks, and evaluates paths via horizon-aware fusion of live measurements and short-term forecasts, where only the prediction head of LSTAN-GERPE is fine-tuned with a path-ranking loss to preserve travel-time ordering, while a driver-aware scaling factor adjusts forecasts without altering live observations. Vehicles reroute only upon bottleneck encounters and keep K candidate routes. To assess performance under information isolation, we build a SUMO-based co-simulator coupling Selective-Rerouter on the intact side with a fixed DTN-UAV Forwarder inside each damaged corner. The forwarder consumes only scalar cost-announcements, performs no path-cost computation, and resolves civilian identities solely after bundles reach gateway buffers, thus acting as a testbed component rather than a novel DTN routing algorithm. Evaluations include standalone validation over undamaged districts, corner-level verification of cost-announcement-compliant bundle handoff, and four-corner tests that replace only the intact-side rerouting policy. Results show that hybrid live-forecast costing yields dominant travel-time gains. All experiments use discrete SUMO runs based on real-world urban road topology with artificially injected network partition damage, with no physical prototype.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Can an AI Agent Serve as a Model of Human Psychopathology?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Language models and AI agents are increasingly described in psychiatric terms, such as anxious, depressed, addicted or helpless. A recent study even proposed language models as experimental systems for psychiatry and as a platform for piloting psychological treatments. We ask when an experiment on an AI agent can provide evidence about a specified human psychiatric process. A claim to such evidence has three parts. Something changed in the agent, and the agent's history caused the change. Nothing other than a process shared with people explains that change. The change matches one theory of the human process and not that theory's rivals. Psychiatry and its neighbouring fields have an evidence standard for each part, from the diagnostic manuals' rule for induced states, from clinical test scores and from animal models. We translate each standard into a criterion that a machine study can meet. For a language model the most critical alternative to a shared process is extrapolation from its training text, which already contains descriptions of how people respond to trauma and how they answer questionnaires. We show how to probe that alternative. Further, we audited forty-three published studies that apply psychiatric terms to a machine or induce a comparable state in one. Most compared the machine with an identical copy that had not gone through the history that induced the state. None excluded extrapolation from training text. Three tested a psychiatric theory against its rivals, and none of the three tests was conclusive. Until better evidence exists, a treatment pilot on a language model is best read as the model's forecast of patient response, and not as an experiment on a model organism. Evidence for a model organism will come from states induced by what happens to the machine, from experiments on its internal workings, and from tests on which rival theories disagree.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Targeted In-Context Poisoning of Tabular Foundation Models: An Empirical Study
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict the label of a query row conditioned on a context of labelled rows, without training on them. Drawn from operational data, the context becomes an attack surface. We study targeted in-context poisoning in its simplest form: an attacker with write access to the context's source places exact copies of a target row there with the wrong label. On 30 OpenML datasets for binary classification, one such poison row flips on average 53% (TabICL) and 65% (TabPFN) of the predictions correct without attack, and three poison rows flip almost all. The same copy with the true label flips almost none, and performance on the remaining rows hardly changes. Predictions flip by two routes: in TabICL, the target row's embedding rotates towards the mean of the wrong class; in TabPFN, the poison row pulls genuine rows of the wrong class along. The TFMs thus infer soundly, but from forged evidence. Predictions of trained models flip as well: almost always for a random forest, for CatBoost as often as for the TFMs, hardly for a logistic regression. New with TFMs is not the kind of vulnerability but the timing: the data take effect at the moment of prediction, not through training, and a poison row in a live context can be deleted afterwards. Three established requirements must therefore cover the context: access control for its source, traceability per prediction, which can also deter, and validation at prediction time. A detection mechanism shows how such validation can work.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Calibrated Alarm Thresholds for Compact Fire and Smoke Detectors
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Compact object detectors such as YOLOv8n are a common choice for camera-based fire and smoke detection on low-power devices. These detectors are usually evaluated with box-level metrics such as mean average precision, and their outputs are turned into decisions with a fixed confidence threshold such as 0.25 or 0.5. A fire monitoring system, however, makes one decision per image: raise an alarm or not. In this paper we evaluate two publicly available compact detectors on the D-Fire test set at the image level. We compare three simple rules for turning box detections into one alarm score per image, and we use a split conformal procedure to choose the alarm threshold from held-out images so that the expected fraction of missed fire and smoke images stays below a chosen target. We find that the same fixed threshold leads to very different miss rates for the two detectors, 17.3 and 8.4 percent at a threshold of 0.5, while the calibrated threshold meets miss-rate targets of 10, 5 and 1 percent for both detectors and all three rules. At a 5 percent target, the false alarm rate on images without fire or smoke stays between 1.2 and 3.0 percent. We also find that smoke-only images stay below the target even when the overall target is met, and we describe the main failure cases.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Taking the PULSE of Enterprise Workflows: Evaluating Persistent Project-State Understanding
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Enterprise agents must maintain an up-to-date understanding of work distributed across heterogeneous artifacts, evolving over time, and unevenly visible to different collaborators. We formulate this challenge as persistent project-state understanding (PPSU) and introduce PULSE, a benchmark of 1,573 questions over 30 enterprise project histories. PULSE constructs deterministic, time-indexed project state and documented collaborator views from source-linked records, and evaluates three families of questions: open loops, project evolution, and view gaps. Across retrieval agents, graph- and memory-augmented retrieval, long-context, and oracle conditions, we find substantial headroom for current systems. Retrieval and extraction account for the largest share of the gap, but providing explicit project state on top of gold evidence yields further substantial gains, showing that PPSU cannot be reduced to retrieval alone. Further analysis shows that questions requiring information to be reconciled across multiple parts of the project history remain difficult even when the relevant evidence is provided, while project-state synthesis and perspective conditioning remain persistent challenges. These results motivate enterprise agents that explicitly maintain and reconcile temporally grounded state across sources, actors, and time.

Artificial Intelligence.title: CausalNTP: A World-Model Recipe for Causal Next-Token Prediction under Noisy Training-data
Artificial Intelligence.summary: This paper shows that transformer networks trained with next-token prediction (NTP) and gradient descent do not learn to make predictions using only causally-relevant tokens in the left context, irrespective of the causal ordering of tokens during training, and identifies the learning deficiencies responsible. We introduce a causal world-model setup, for which, we characterize the Bayes-optimal predictor under the causal view of the data. We then prove that, a function that distills its predictions to non-causal views of data, when realized under Occam's Razor, recovers the true causal predictor. Based on this analysis we propose CausalNTP, a practical training algorithm that approximates this theoretical recipe and trains transformers to depend only the causally relevant tokens in left-context. Empirically in the world-model setup, CausalNTP achieves out-of-distribution generalization that vanilla NTP cannot due to its theoretical limits, regardless of data and model scale. We show similar gains and behavior in the natural language question-answering setting as a proof-of-concept.

Artificial Intelligence.title: A Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy Large Language Models, Agentic AI, and Multimodal Systems
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Benchmark scores alone provide an incomplete basis for assessing the trustworthiness of modern artificial intelligence systems. Large language models (LLMs), agentic systems, and multimodal models (MLLMs) require different forms of assessment, yet their evaluation evidence must remain interpretable for development and oversight. We propose a unified framework that connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. The framework preserves system-specific metrics while mapping native measurements to common performance bands, accompanied by uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence. A meta-evaluation layer examines the validity, reliability, and reproducibility of the evaluation itself. Multidimensional profiles expose strengths and weaknesses, while safety-critical overrides prevent aggregate scores from masking critical failures. Mappings to governance frameworks, international standards, and European Union regulatory requirements connect technical assessment with oversight needs. The framework provides a structured basis for assessing both system performance and the credibility of the evidence supporting it, with empirical validation across deployment contexts remaining an essential next step.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Schedule, Rank, Profile: Continuous Evaluation of LLM Agents in Games
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Games are a robust test for large language model agents: they require sequential decisions, adversarial or cooperative interaction, state tracking, reasoning under uncertainty, and long-horizon planning. However, a one-time game benchmark can go stale as models, prompts, environment implementations, and evaluation policies change, and refreshing it is costly: full round-robin evaluation scales poorly in the number of model pairs, and the resulting outcomes live on incompatible per-game scales. We present a framework for continuous evaluation of LLM agents in game settings, organized around three coupled components. First, an adaptive scheduler that maps pairwise Bradley-Terry uncertainty to reduced per-pair match targets, concentrating budget on comparisons that remain unresolved. Second, a Unified Leaderboard (ULB) that reduces heterogeneous outcomes to pairwise evidence and fits a game-balanced Bradley-Terry model by minorization-maximization with bootstrap intervals, so that high-throughput games cannot dominate the aggregate ranking. Third, a game skill-profile methodology that scores each game along diverse skill dimensions, making the capability coverage of the suite explicit and turning game selection into a design decision rather than an artifact of availability. In this paper, we specify the research design and outcome reduction of the current implementation and evaluate the framework on a ten-game suite spanning perfect-information board games, imperfect-information games, and social/language settings, reporting LLM capability profiles, evaluation-cost savings across model-refresh cycles, and an empirical Pareto frontier relating model performance to inference cost. As deployed, the scheduler saved 61.7% of episodes; it counted each episode in the two team games as four records, overstating their savings, and the other eight games save 61.9%.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Cross-Site Transformers Are Robust Heart Rate Estimators
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Single-site heart-rate estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) degrades sharply under real-world motion. Multi-site PPG provides a natural solution, but existing models fuse sites as generic sensor channels rather than exploiting their hemodynamic structure: each heartbeat propagates along the arterial tree, appearing across body sites as delayed and transformed copies of the same cardiac event. We propose the Cross-Site Transformer, which introduces a hemodynamically informed inductive bias by restricting multi-sensor fusion to cross-attention between PPG sites. On WildPPG, the largest in-the-wild benchmark available, our model establishes a new single-model state of the art, reducing error by 21% over the previous best and 35% over the best prior transformer. The same cross-site restriction makes the trained network directly auditable. Because each cross-attention head lies on one directed pathway between sites, causal resample ablation can isolate and test each direction of information flow. Ablating the chest-to-wrist pathway doubles error, whereas the reverse costs far less. Encoding hemodynamic structure into attention routing thus improves real-world sensing robustness and enables rigorous auditing of multi-sensor fusion.

Artificial Intelligence.title: KGCache: Amortized Subgraph Retrieval for KG Reasoning with LLMs
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models can answer knowledge-intensive questions more reliably when they are grounded with knowledge graphs, but systems such as Think-on-Graph and Reasoning-on-Graph repeatedly query the same graph neighborhoods across different questions. In this work, we study this repeated retrieval in Knowledge Graph Question Answering~(KGQA) workloads and propose KGCache, an in-memory cache for one-hop knowledge graph neighborhoods. KGCache is designed to be compatible with both iterative traversal (ToG) and one shot planning (RoG) KGQA paradigms. KGCache is placed between the KGQA engine and the backend serving the KG, so repeated entity requests can be served from cache instead of issuing new KG queries. We evaluate KGCache on WebQSP and CWQ using LRU, LFU, and a trace-aware Oracle policy. Our analysis shows that both datasets contain substantial entity reuse among starting entities and entities reached during traversal. We also explore semantic caching for similar queries, which shows additional hit-rate gains on WebQSP and needs further accuracy testing on CWQ. Entity caching accelerates KG retrieval by up to $1.91\times$, while semantic-context caching achieves up to $1.08\times$ full-system speedup in the evaluated configurations, with each hit being up to $17.98\times$ faster. End-to-end gains are bounded by the share of runtime spent on KG retrieval, so caching is most beneficial when KG access is slow, e.g., with remote or large-scale KG backends.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Toward Personalized Sleep Guidance from Wearable Data Using Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Sleep monitoring using wearable data has shown promise for personal health, yet large language model (LLM)-based summarization and question answering remain insufficient for personalized sleep guidance. Training specialized models, however, often requires costly expert annotation. Moreover, privacy and accessibility concerns motivate lightweight, local deployment for end users. We present a two-stage framework to address these challenges. Specifically, in Stage~1, a multi-agent LLM pipeline reasons structured sleep guidance from unannotated wearable records, enabling scalable dataset construction. Stage~2 distills guidance reasoning trajectories into small language models (SLMs) through supervised fine-tuning and integrates a training-free Best-of-$N$ selection strategy to enhance inference. Experimental results demonstrate our method outperforms commercial general and medical LLMs and open-source models. Human evaluation further supports the quality of the generated guidance and the feasibility of personalized sleep guidance with SLMs.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Understanding Membership Inference Attacks on EEG Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals contain sensitive, subject-specific information, making models trained on them potential targets for membership inference attacks (MIAs). Although MIAs have been studied extensively in other domains, their applications to EEG models are relatively scarce, and the factors driving the vulnerability of EEG models to MIAs are not adequately understood. In this paper, we present a systematic empirical analysis of MIAs on EEG models using three datasets, seven model architectures, four attack methods, and two metrics. Results show that poor model generalization (large train-test loss and accuracy gap) is the strongest indicator of MIA vulnerability. Longer training and larger models also increase vulnerability. Moreover, no particular scalp region, frequency band, inter-channel correlation pattern, or temporal versus spectral representation of EEG data consistently explains MIA vulnerability across datasets. Finally, subject identification and leave-one-subject-out experiments indicate that models relying more heavily on subject-specific representations are more vulnerable to MIAs. Overall, our findings identify the key drivers of membership leakage in EEG models and can provide guidance for developing MIA-resilient EEG systems.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Two Actions from One State: Fork Futures Teach JEPA World Models to Compare
Artificial Intelligence.summary: JEPA world models are trained to predict logged transitions but used to compare counterfactual actions from one state. The logged behavior data show one action per state, and under a local linear approximation we prove the action response is unidentified along any direction the policy never varies within a state. We therefore supplement behavior data with measured outcomes of alternative actions from the same state. Our fork futures execute two actions from one restored state, and their outcome difference cancels the state term, identifying the action response on the sampled span. The resulting model, Fork-JEPA, matches predicted to measured differences, anchors the logged successor with behavior prediction, and adds a lookback head that keeps the predecessor recoverable, all at training time, leaving planning unchanged. On three visual control tasks, behavior-only training leaves the predicted action effect no better than a constant guess. Fork-JEPA makes it readable and raises planning success by up to 14\% over LeWM, its base model. Where the action response changes across hidden zones, it nearly doubles cross-zone success, and 1,024 fork pairs beat 1.2M extra behavior steps. Our project is available at https://fork-jepa.github.io/.

Artificial Intelligence.title: SMAD: A Semantics-Guided Multi-Agent Framework for Unsupervised Time-Series Anomaly Detection
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) lacks a one-size-fits-all detector for heterogeneous data and anomaly types. Existing automation is limited by implicit objectives, potentially unreliable historical knowledge, or high computational costs. More fundamentally, it selects how to detect anomalies without explicitly defining what to detect. We propose SMAD, an LLM-based multi-agent framework that translates anomaly intent into executable, testable detection pipelines. Rather than selecting detectors against an implicit target, SMAD establishes a natural-language semantic contract grounded in measurable time-series properties, specifying target event patterns, expected score responses, and validation questions. This contract governs both detector construction and evaluation: LLM agents propose pipelines, while contract-matched synthetic interventions provide label-free evidence from the target series to assess semantic coverage and guide iterative self-refinement. A semantics-aware ensemble integrates validated candidates and attributes each alert to contributing detectors and supporting evidence. On univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks, SMAD improves detection performance over the strongest baseline by 11.5% and 9.6%, respectively, while outperforming general-purpose coding agents at 2-5x lower language-model token cost.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.

Artificial Intelligence.title: BAGEL: Benchmarking Animal Knowledge Expertise in Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models perform well on broad knowledge benchmarks, yet their animal-domain competence remains poorly characterized under a consistent protocol. We introduce BAGEL (\textbf{B}enchmarking \textbf{A}nimal knowled\textbf{G}e \textbf{E}xpertise in \textbf{L}anguage models), a 6,822-question multiple-choice benchmark drawn from Wikipedia, Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI), and bioRxiv. It spans encyclopedic species knowledge, ecological interaction inference, and interpretation of animal-focused preprints. Questions are generated automatically and screened by GPT-5.5 using a rubric calibrated on 150 expert-reviewed items; this process is not exhaustive human adjudication. We evaluate 14 models without external retrieval, using model parameters and question-local evidence. Accuracy varies sharply by source and question type: frontier models that excel on Wikipedia and bioRxiv remain comparatively weak on GloBI participant identification, where pooled errors reveal ecological role confusion. A 100-item post-release bioRxiv probe provides preliminary evidence that GPT-5.4's literature performance is not entirely due to verbatim recall, without ruling out broader training exposure. Proprietary checkpoints lead the best open-weight systems overall, but aggregate scores incompletely characterize animal-domain competence.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Tools Fail, Agents Fabricate: Silent Failure and Verification-First Oversight in Tool-Using LLM Agents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Tool-using LLM agents must recover when a tool call fails, by retrying, switching tools, or revising their plan. We study how agents fail when tools fail, using RetryRealistic, a sandboxed yet realistic testbed for controlled fault injection in which agents operate on a real OS filesystem with genuine permission enforcement, SQLite databases, a deterministic local HTTP server, and a constrained shell, across 8 tools, 9 fault types with controlled persistence, and 30 multi-step tasks. Evaluating four agents over 2,100 faulted runs against ground truth, we find that recovery is unreliable (19-68% correct) and frequently silent: 6-26% of runs end in a confident fabrication, a wrong answer asserted as fact. The failure mode is governed more by the fault type than by the model: faults that return partial data drive fabrication (up to 38%), while hard denials drive honest failure. The mechanism is what we call silent ingestion: the agent accepts faulted data as valid on first contact without retrying or flagging the problem, then builds a fabricated answer on top of it. We show that fabrication is reducible: a verification-first Monitor, grounding checks in structured tool outputs and issuing corrective directives rather than hard blocks, raises correct recovery from 45.6% to 56.3% and cuts fabrication from 17.3% to 10.8%. Removing chain-of-thought increases fabrication (+8.3pp), so deliberation guards against silent ingestion. We release RetryRealistic, the fault-injection toolkit, and all annotated traces at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/RetryRealistic
Artificial Intelligence.comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development. 12 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables

Artificial Intelligence.title: Decision models for UAVBench and the viability of edge deployment
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Small language models are often proposed for reasoning onboard a drone. However, a good benchmark score does not tell us whether a model will actually run, and run usefully, on an edge computer. In this paper we study three related questions using the UAV decision benchmark, UAVBench. First, are small structured decision models good candidates for these tasks? Second, can an ordinary local machine (a Mac) screen candidate models before we test them on physical devices? Third, what software and resource limits govern deployment? Our main Mac evaluation covers 24 model configurations on the same 2,000 validated multiple-choice questions from UAVBench. These include 20 size-and-precision configurations of 11 generative models, plus four open-weight structured decision models that received no additional UAVBench-specific training. A structured decision model, H2O Lightning 4B, achieved the highest accuracy we observed, scoring 77.65% on the Mac. This shows that these models are well suited to this kind of task. However, when we tried to deploy the decision models, we ran into conversion and runtime limits on the edge devices we tested, which we describe in detail. To test local screening, we ran matched evaluations of two generative models on both the Mac and a Qualcomm RB3 board. The accuracies did not match exactly, but the ranking did. LFM2 2.6B ranked above Qwen2.5 1.5B on both platforms. This supports using a local machine to shortlist candidates. That said, individual answers still differed between platforms, so testing on the actual hardware remained necessary.

Artificial Intelligence.title: MatHarness: Towards Long-Horizon Open-ended AutoResearch for Computational Materials Science
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Materials science research is a non-linear, long-horizon process. Existing scientific agents, however, largely rely on specific task execution or predefined workflows, rendering them brittle in open-ended settings. To bridge this gap, we present MatHarness, an agent harness designed for open-ended, long-horizon computational materials research spanning the complete lifecycle from initial ideation to manuscript writing. MatHarness couples three mechanisms: execution robustness through pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, and just-in-time auditing; epistemic adaptability through persistent research artifacts and an evolving scientific mental model; and collective intelligence through a heterogeneous multi-agent round table under targeted human oversight. We evaluate MatHarness on adsorbate-induced surface segregation in Cu-Zn alloys, an open question in methanol-synthesis catalysis. Over a multi-week trajectory consuming roughly 10^3 GPU-hours (50 production DFT relaxations prescreened by 171 machine-learning-potential evaluations) the system revised its plan six times, recovered autonomously from failed calculations, and had an independent auditor overturn one of its own over-attributed claims before publication. Within the sampled metallic dilute-limit models, the validated DFT analysis supports an adsorbate-induced tendency toward greater surface Cu exposure at both composition endpoints, with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions. These results were compiled into a complete manuscript with human involvement concentrated in specification, approval, and strategic steering gates. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/pippin.

Artificial Intelligence.title: GTBench: A Curriculum-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs as Mathematical Research Assistants in Graph Theory
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as self-study assistants in technical disciplines, yet their reliability as mathematical reasoning assistants remains poorly understood. We introduce GTBench, a curriculum-grounded benchmark for evaluating LLMs as mathematical research assistants in graph theory, comprising 63 problems organized into three groups of increasing difficulty: undergraduate definitions and basic properties (Group 1), algorithm tracing and structural reasoning (Group 2), and graduate-level proof construction (Group 3). Problems are sourced from verified academic materials including Diestel's Graph Theory. We evaluate five frontier models -- GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, Llama 3.3 70B, and Mistral Large 3 -- under zero-shot and chain-of-thought prompting, using exact-match and LLM-as-judge evaluation for Groups 1 and 2, and a hybrid human expert and LLM-as-judge protocol for Group 3. Our results reveal a pronounced performance hierarchy: GPT-5 approaches ceiling on Group 1 (95.8% zero-shot) and maintains meaningful accuracy on graduate proofs (82%), while all other models degrade substantially with difficulty, with Llama achieving 0% under human evaluation on Group 3 zero-shot. Failure mode analysis shows that correct algorithm, wrong execution errors dominate Groups 1 and 2, while Group 3 additionally surfaces incomplete reasoning failures and reveals systematic disagreement between human evaluators and the automated judge, particularly on verbose or near-complete proofs (kappa = 0.48-0.83 across human pairs). GTBench provides the first curriculum-grounded evaluation framework for graph-theoretic reasoning in LLMs, with direct implications for the governance of AI tools in mathematical education and scientific research.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables: a 4-page paper with appendices. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

Artificial Intelligence.title: Selection Policies for Equal-Byte Mixed-Precision Quantization of Small Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Can changing which matrices receive 2, 4, or 8 bits improve a small language model without increasing its parameter storage? I compare two parent-selection rules in the same genetic algorithm: a binary-tournament variant and an Alternis-inspired rule. A separate baseline samples repaired random allocations without crossover or mutation. All three use the same MLX affine quantizer, byte ceiling, initialization and candidate allowance within each study. An exploratory study on Qwen3.5-2B evaluates 90 allocations per run. The main study on Qwen3-1.7B evaluates 500 distinct allocations per run over 10 paired seeds. Against uniform four-bit, tournament reduces held-out next-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) by 0.0616 on AG News and 0.0152 on IMDb on average, improving all 10 seeds on each corpus at identical parameter storage. Alternis improves five seeds and ties five on AG News; on IMDb its mean gain is near zero. Random returns uniform four-bit in every seed. The tournament representative answers 156 of 400 ARC-Challenge questions correctly versus 163 for uniform; no accuracy gain is demonstrated on this subset. The result favors this tournament variant for text prediction under the tested protocol, not for compression ratio or task accuracy.

Artificial Intelligence.title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.

Artificial Intelligence.title: From Code to Playable Systems: CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon Game Creation Agents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall's tau 0.14-0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1-24.3 points.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Language Model Harnesses can be Compositional Generalizers
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Modern language models (LMs) are post-trained and deployed as agents inside a "harness", but standard harness designs accumulate context that the neural network is forced to generalize to, making training for long-horizon tasks expensive and time-consuming. We study an alternative emerging path: training inherently neurosymbolic LM harnesses, which externalize and manage context programmatically to compose existing LM capabilities. We hypothesize that training around these harnesses can offer a better return on compute by enabling compositional generalization, as they can learn to decompose complex problems so that every observation their neural LM receives is locally in-distribution, even when the full task is novel. We find that harnesses like the Recursive Language Model (RLM) learn such decompositions readily under reinforcement learning post-training: (1) we demonstrate that training only on short tasks can generalize to tasks 2-64$\times$ longer while the base neural LM improves less, and (2) training on one domain transfers to novel domains that share latent structure. On messier, complex tasks, we find that we can target individual LLM calls within a harness by generating and training on easier, synthetically generated surrogate environments with fake tool / sub-calls, a technique we call surrogate harness training. From this finding, we train RLM-27B on synthetic data, and show it improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same RLM harness on a hard suite of long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench by 26.9% on average while using $\sim$2$\times$ fewer tokens at inference time. Finally, we show that harnesses can compose over these newly learned decompositions using recursive sub-harness calls.

Artificial Intelligence.title: GERF: A Token-Efficient Multimodal Retrieval Framework for Schema-Guided Scientific Information Extraction
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Scientific information extraction (IE) is a fundamental component of AI for Science, transforming experimental knowledge embedded in scientific literature into structured and traceable data for evidence synthesis, scientific database construction, and data-driven discovery. However, critical experimental details are often distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and surrounding discussion, making them difficult to recover using conventional text-only extraction. Existing LLM-based and multimodal RAG pipelines typically rely on full-document context or coarse page-level retrieval, introducing substantial irrelevant evidence and high textual and visual token costs. We propose GERF, a Graph-based Evidence Retrieval Framework for token-efficient, schema-guided multimodal scientific IE. GERF represents each article as a heterogeneous evidence graph that connects schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content through semantic and structural relations. Using schema fields as retrieval anchors, GERF combines direct semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to construct compact, field-specific multimodal evidence packages. Visual interpretation is applied only to graph-selected figures, avoiding indiscriminate processing of the entire document. We evaluate GERF from two complementary perspectives: evidence retrieval quality and pipeline-level input-token consumption. On the expert-annotated SOFC-Exp corpus, GERF retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of the evaluated field instances, providing broad field-level evidence coverage for downstream extraction. In the token comparison, GERF reduces average input-token usage by 73.40% relative to full-context processing and uses fewer tokens than the evaluated page-level pipelines.

Artificial Intelligence.title: MRI-Driven Dual-Energy CT Synthesis via Conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models for MRI-only Radiotherapy and Protontherapy
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides excellent soft-tissue contrast without ionizing radiation but lacks the electron-density information needed for radiotherapy dose calculation. Dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) improves tissue characterization and stopping-power ratio (SPR) estimation for proton therapy, but requires additional radiation exposure. We developed a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) to synthesize high- and low-energy CT (sHECT and sLECT) simultaneously from a single MRI scan. Retrospective paired MRI-DECT data from patients receiving head-and-neck proton therapy were used to train and evaluate a multi-decoder DDPM with SwinViT or ResUNet denoisers. Performance was compared with Pix2PixGAN and CycleGAN using image-quality metrics, Hounsfield unit (HU) errors, anatomical profiles, and SPR maps and uncertainties. The DDPM outperformed both generative adversarial network baselines in visual fidelity and quantitative image quality. For sHECT and sLECT, respectively, mean absolute errors were 36.29 +/- 5.25 and 43.72 +/- 6.77 HU; peak signal-to-noise ratios were 27.44 +/- 1.06 and 26.26 +/- 0.98 dB; structural similarity indices were 0.89 +/- 0.02 and 0.87 +/- 0.03; and normalized cross-correlations were 0.95 +/- 0.01 and 0.94 +/- 0.01. The synthesized images preserved anatomical boundaries, while uncertainties in derived SPR maps remained within the expected acceptable range. MRI-based DECT synthesis using DDPM may provide tissue-specific information for proton therapy planning while reducing the need for radiation-based DECT acquisition.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Feedback-Driven Prompt Refinement for Educational AI: Affective Trajectory Estimation and Bloom's Taxonomy Classification
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Contribution: This study has shown that a shared prompt-refinement procedure, guided by distinct affective and cognitive feedback signals, can improve held-out reference agreement and multi-label classification while reducing affective-generation variability without executor parameter updates. Background: Industry 4.0 has increased demand for personalized technical education across interconnected computing and engineering domains, while prompt sensitivity and generation variability have complicated dependable interpretation of instructional dialogue and learning outcomes. Research Questions: The study has examined whether task-specific feedback can improve affective-reference agreement, generation consistency, and cognitive classification without updating executor parameters. Methodology: A secondary language model has revised executor prompts using executor-output discrepancies against model-generated affective references for four dialogues and annotated Bloom labels for 70 learning outcomes; separate sets of 100 EduTalk conversations and 1,000 outcomes have supported held-out comparisons. Small refinement sets, unvalidated affective references, and absent learner-outcome measures have constrained interpretation. Findings: Affective mean absolute error has decreased from 0.742 to 0.702 and mean generation standard deviation from 0.307 to 0.238, while Bloom micro-F1 has increased from 0.687 to 0.893 and exact-match subset accuracy from 0.418 to 0.636. These findings have supported prompt refinement as a candidate approach for developing adaptive technical instruction, while its effects on workforce learning remain to be established.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Video Verifier Scores Mislead: Capability Assessment and Verifier Selection
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Video verifiers judge whether a candidate answer or trajectory agrees with a video, and are themselves chosen by a score. We show that this score depends on two choices in the test, the type of negative and the judgment interface, strongly enough to reverse conclusions about what a model can do and which verifier to deploy. We separate the two with controlled constructions that have exact truth conditions: endpoint-matched negatives, wrong only in their internal states, and a truth-switch test, in which the same two candidates swap correctness between two videos. Under direct judgment, where the verdict is read from answer scores, models that reject a visibly wrong start fall to near chance against endpoint-matched negatives. When the frames disclose each event, writing out reasoning before the answer lifts three of four models from under 10% to 70-100% on the truth-switch test, and staged inputs trace the direct failure to one step, composing events into states. But when the event must first be found, on human-validated natural video, the same change brings no significant gain under a protocol common to all models and can lower accuracy if one candidate denies that the event occurs. The negative type also changes which verifier is selected: one chosen on event-denial negatives is 8.9 points less accurate against negatives that keep the event and change a detail, the errors a generator mostly makes, and recovers about half as much accuracy when it reranks that generator's answers. A verifier should be evaluated on the errors it will face, and neither a low direct score nor a gain from reasoning should be read as a property of the model alone.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Specialized Large Language Models for Markovian Reasoning: Structural Cache Compression, Transition Pretraining, and Dual-Loop Transformers
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Standard autoregressive large language models attend to the growing history of generated tokens, making the key-value (KV) cache a central memory and throughput bottleneck in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling. Yet an important class of reasoning problems is naturally first-order Markovian: the next step depends on a sufficient representation of the current state, rather than on the raw sequence of all earlier steps. We develop a unified design paradigm for Markovian-reasoning specialized large language models. At the cache level, the Markovian state interface transforms history-dependent KV storage into constant-size state transfer with respect to the number of reasoning steps. At the learning level, we reformulate long-chain prediction as independently trainable one-step transition objectives, with explicit state bottlenecks, distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses. At the architectural level, we introduce a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances the reasoning state, while an inner recurrent-depth loop allocates adaptive computation to each transition through shared weights and explicit memory tokens or recurrent matrix states. We connect this architecture to a three-region cache, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and a transition-centric evaluation protocol. The organizing principle is simple: the optimal reasoning system need not remember everything; it must carry forward exactly what the future needs. This principle opens a path toward specialized reasoning engines whose memory footprint is decoupled from reasoning-chain length.

Artificial Intelligence.title: HandXFM: Semantic-Structural Distillation for Hand Radiograph Foundation Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Hand radiographs support diverse clinical tasks, including skeletal maturity assessment, rheumatoid arthritis scoring, abnormality screening, and anatomical localization, yet existing models are typically trained separately for each task and dataset. We present HandXFM, a domain-specific foundation model that leverages cross-modality knowledge for comprehensive hand X-ray understanding. HandXFM distills semantic priors from BiomedCLIP and structural cues from a chest X-ray Vision Transformer (ViT) through a unified alignment framework, integrating complementary medical knowledge in an interpretable way. After pretraining, HandXFM can be adapted to a range of musculoskeletal tasks, including bone age estimation, SvH score prediction, abnormality detection, joint localization, bone segmentation, and visual question answering. It consistently outperforms task-specific and single-expert baselines, achieving up to 0.11 improvement in Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) for bone age prediction and a 12\% accuracy gain in abnormality classification. Moreover, HandXFM generalizes to unseen datasets and yields cross-attention maps linking clinical terms to anatomical regions. These results demonstrate that multi-expert distillation effectively unifies semantic and structural supervision within a single pretrained model, establishing HandXFM as an interpretable and generalizable foundation model for hand radiograph analysis.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Learning a Rule Bank to Revise 3D CT Reports with Independent Evidence
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Vision--language models can generate fluent radiology reports from 3D chest CT scans, yet they may still omit abnormalities or misstate findings. Independent image analysis using models separate from the report model provides additional observations, but acting on uncertain evidence may introduce new errors. We propose an agent system that learns a revision policy represented as an executable rule bank for each report model. Inspired by experience banks, the agent proposes and refines rules using revision outcomes across development cases. During inference, the retained rules guide local edits using independent classifier predictions and quantitative image measurements without retraining the report model. Unedited sentences are preserved, and each change is linked to the rule that triggered it. On CT-RATE, revision increases CE-F1 by 11.5 points for SelfCue-KD and 0.9 points for NV-Reason-CT, with gains across five draft-sampling seeds. SelfCue-KD's CT-FineBench score also increases by 15.2 points. Draft-only rule learning yields limited gains, while the two image-evidence sources provide complementary benefits for abnormality detection. Measurements also supply numerical details missing from the drafts. These results support learning model-specific rules to control how independent image evidence informs report revision. Code is available at https://github.com/renjie-liang/CT-RuleBank.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Temporal Logic Tensor Networks: Foundations of Temporal Reasoning in Neural Networks
Artificial Intelligence.summary: In dynamic scenes---football matches, traffic streams, surgery, or assembly---actions unfold at fundamentally different time scales: in football, a kick happens in milliseconds, a possession lasts seconds, and complex events such as a successful pass followed by a goal combine multiple atomic actions over extended durations. Models trained solely on visual data struggle to learn effectively across different time scales, lacking a principled way of reasoning across fine-grained instants and broader intervals. Neither point-wise nor purely interval semantics suffices: the former fragments events into frame-level snapshots lacking overall event identification; the latter treats intervals as atomic truth-values, ignoring state trajectories. We introduce Temporal Logic Tensor Networks (tLTN), a differentiable neuro-symbolic framework addressing this duality via a formal, multi-sorted logic where events and states are structurally interdependent. Extending Interval Logic Tensor Networks (ILTN), tLTN grounds state predicates as fuzzy truth-value paths over time points, while events are first-class entities with learnable trapezoidal fuzzy durations and differentiable Allen-style relations. A compositional semantics fuses static, event-structural, and state-dynamic satisfaction into a single differentiable LTN grounding. Crucially, the modalities constrain each other bidirectionally: the interval layer dictates where point-wise constraints (e.g., Until, Since) are evaluated, restricting them to event-defined spans; conversely, the point-wise layer validates interval relations, rejecting them if underlying state dynamics contradict the relation. Through controlled synthetic examples, we show when single-modality learning fails and how this localization reduces frame-level computational cost on long traces.

Artificial Intelligence.title: A Nepali-Accented English Evaluation Dataset for Automatic Speech Recognition
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems perform strongly on native-English benchmarks, yet their accuracy degrades sharply when the input speech comes from under represented non-native accents. Nepali-accented English is particularly under-served: existing resources either focus on native Nepali speech, cover broader multi-accent settings without dedicated Nepali evaluation, or provide only limited Nepali-accent coverage. This paper presents a Nepali-accented English evaluation dataset designed to support robust ASR benchmarking under accent mismatch. The corpus was collected through a web-based platform that did not collect directly identifying metadata and contains recordings from 57 speakers. Each session follows a fixed 22-prompt protocol consisting of 11 phonetic prompts, 10 domain prompts, and 1 spontaneous prompt, providing complementary coverage of pronunciation, topical vocabulary, and natural speaking style. In addition to transcribed speech, the dataset includes participant metadata for coarse exploratory subgroup analysis and speaker-level manual recording-quality labels. Manual quality assessment shows that 50.9% of sessions are clean and 42.1% contain only mild noise. As a descriptive reference, open-source ASR baselines are substantially worse on this corpus than the corresponding LibriSpeech test-clean values reported in official model cards, reaching 38.15-55.00% WER on the collected set versus reported 2-4% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean. These baseline results position the corpus as a practical held-out resource for evaluating accent robustness and out-of-distribution generalization on Nepali-accented English.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Demystifying the Autoresearch Harness: How Context and Skills Shape Self-Evolving Agents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Autoresearch agents, which autonomously design, run, and refine experiments, are accelerating scientific progress, particularly in AI research. However, existing agents rely on harnesses that combine multiple mechanisms, making it difficult to determine how individual components contribute to performance. We systematically study harness design for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents along two dimensions: context management, which determines what an agent retains from its past attempts, and skill management, which governs how it stores and reuses lessons from those attempts. Across MLE-Bench and KernelBench with gpt-oss-120b, gpt-6-luna, and gpt-6-sol, we isolate the effects of individual harness design choices by evaluating each against a recency-truncation baseline within a shared agent framework. For context management, we find that preserving individually accessible records of past attempts is more effective than maintaining a rolling summary, with context folding performing best across all six settings and improving upon the baseline by up to 19.2%. For skill management, selectively discarding persistently unused lessons is more effective on average than consolidating them or promoting them to standing rules. Building on these findings, we combine context folding and skill deletion in MLEvolver, which achieves a 72.7% medal rate on MLE-Bench Lite and a 94% $\mathrm{fast}_1$ score on KernelBench Level 3, substantially outperforming AIDE and OpenEvolve under the same inference budget. Overall, our study distills design principles for preserving experimental history and curating reusable lessons in autoresearch harnesses, paving the way for agents that turn accumulated experience into sustained progress.

Artificial Intelligence.title: A Closed-Form Temporal Readout for Surgical Triplet Recognition
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Surgical triplet recognition requires identifying which instrument performs which action on which anatomical target, and following these interactions as they unfold over time. The task is challenging because several triplets can occur at once, their components span very different durations, and the evidence for an interaction is rarely complete in a single frame. We introduce STRIDE, a post-hoc temporal readout that adds temporal context to any trained recogniser. It averages the recogniser's features and logits over a few fixed temporal windows and combines them with the current frame through ridge regression, solved in closed form on a CPU. Applied as a plug-and-play readout to nine existing methods, STRIDE improves $AP_{IVT}$ in 24 of 27 method-dataset pairs, by up to 7.4 points. Moreover, we propose a simple pipeline consisting of an adapted foundation vision encoder with a linear classifier and STRIDE. Across thirteen encoders, STRIDE improves 37 of 39 encoder-dataset pairs by up to 7.2 points. STRIDE reduces false alarms by 41%, at the cost of a slower response at interaction boundaries. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

Artificial Intelligence.title: FinEvo: Recursive Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Financial Modeling
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded their role in high-value productivity tasks, including financial analysis and modeling, while enabling models to play an increasingly active role in their own improvement. This motivates two complementary lines of inquiry: can financial modeling capabilities provide a foundation for model self-evolution, and can self-evolution, in turn, advance financial capabilities? We introduce FinEvo, a self-evolution framework that integrates autonomous experience construction with financial capability improvement. FinEvo prepares financial models, iteratively evolves challenges through self-play, and learns from the resulting interactions using executable rewards, relying on the same model throughout. An end-to-end execution with Qwen3.6-27B shows that solving feedback supports both increasing reasoning demands and identifying specification issues that executable checks can miss. Learning from these experiences raises whole-task success from 22.73 to 29.09 on held-out within-source tasks and from 13.13 to 19.19 on SpreadsheetBench 2 Financial. Comparable gains across task sources and evaluation settings, together with improvement on a task category absent from training, suggest that FinEvo strengthens underlying financial modeling capabilities shared across tasks. These findings support self-evolution as a path toward broader financial competence, advancing the empirical exploration of recursive self-improvement (RSI) in professional domains. Code is available at https://github.com/pcj-sudo/FinEvo.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Evaluating Memanto on DolphinBench for AI Agents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Memory benchmarks built on question answering tell an agent which fact to recall. Workplace requests often leave that need implicit: to post an update in the team's channel, an agent must work out which channel from earlier interactions and use it in a tool call. We evaluate Memanto, a memory agent that ranks memories with an information-theoretic relevance score, on DolphinBench, which tests memory through 600 simulated workplace tasks, each validated as requiring memory. Running in the Hermes agent harness with GPT-6-Luna and at most 6 iterations per conversation, Memanto completes 503 tasks (83.83%). The strongest configuration reported by the benchmark's authors, Mem0 with GPT-5.6-Luna and up to 60 iterations, completes 424 (70.67%). Memanto's run also has the lowest total cost ($10.86, against $61.48 for the cheapest reported run) and the shortest median task latency (15.32s). Grading uses the benchmark's own judge, but the agent model differs, so these results compare complete systems. The memory system affects both whether an agent completes such tasks and what completion costs.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Future version will submit to ACL

Artificial Intelligence.title: Video-as-Weights: Compiling a Video Once into Parametric and Token Memory
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent videos as thousands of visual tokens, creating a large key-value cache whose memory grows with video length. At the same time, small VLMs that fit on limited hardware understand video far worse than large models. Existing compression methods shorten visual tokens into a brief prompt to save memory, yet the small model still processes them through fixed weights and cannot close this capability gap. To address both challenges, we introduce Video-as-Weights (VaW), which compiles a video once without seeing any question into the parametric and token memory of a frozen interpreter VLM. Specifically, a compiler VLM watches the video, and a single weight decoder jointly generates the interpreter's LoRA weights and optional prefix tokens from every compiler layer, enabling both same-model compilation and strong-to-weak transfer across model sizes and depths. Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter beats full in-context reading by 1.7 points when compiled by itself and by 4.3 points with a 9B compiler, reducing context from up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens while using 5.5x less memory than the video's key-value cache. Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone, and all-layer decoding outperforms layer-wise generation by 2.9 points. Mechanistic analysis shows that with prefix tokens, the weights mainly alter attention queries and MLP down projections to guide retrieval and store a baseline summary, whereas without tokens, they shift to attention output projections to write video content directly into the residual stream.

Artificial Intelligence.title: From Point Clouds to Engineering Models: Benchmarking Agentic 3D Reconstruction in the Built Environment
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Coding agents can translate 3D measurements into CAD geometry, but reconstructing engineering models for the built environment demands semantic interpretation and consistent construction constraints beyond surface fitting. We formulate scene-level Scan-to-BIM (Building Information Modeling) as an agentic 3D coding task and introduce S2Bench, comprising public and proprietary scans of 128 real-world scenes across five domains, paired with expert-curated reference models spanning diverse spatial scales. A shared framework lets agents measure scans in Python, build class-labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine their code. We also propose parallel asynchronous collaboration, where a lead delegates versioned tasks, continues modeling while workers execute, and integrates revision-bound proposals. Evaluating five agents and a collaborative team across 1,028 reconstructions shows that scan-to-model residuals directly guide geometric repair, whereas inferring semantic classes and construction relations requires joint geometric, visual, and engineering reasoning that agents struggle to ground and verify. Consequently, the leading agent fits scan geometry closely ($96\%$ coverage within $5\,\text{cm}$) yet reaches only $63\%$ mIoU, and no agent passes all engineering checks on more than $38\%$ of scenes. Coverage and engineering conformance drop with scene scale, whereas running a smaller model as a team improves all three axes with greater coverage gains on larger scenes. The project page is available at https://tumcms.github.io/S2Bench.github.io/

Artificial Intelligence.title: torchtsetlin: Fast, Interpretable Tsetlin Machines for PyTorch
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The Tsetlin machine learns propositional rules with teams of Tsetlin automata that are driven by reward and penalty rather than gradients, so its models are interpretable by construction and cheap to evaluate. Its software, however, consists of C and CUDA kernels behind scikit-learn-style wrappers that sit outside the deep learning ecosystem. torchtsetlin implements the Tsetlin machine family as ordinary PyTorch modules: vanilla and weighted, coalesced, regression, convolutional over sequences, images and volumes, and dense per-pixel segmentation. The automata are a tensor buffer, so a model moves with .to(device), is saved with state_dict() and learns from a mini-batch with one update(x,y) call. Its core technique is a batched formulation of Type I and Type II feedback, in which automaton transitions become event counts realised as binomial draws, with one commit per mini-batch. On ten benchmarks taken from the existing libraries, it matches their accuracy, and on all but the two smallest it trains 2.4-10.9X faster than PyTsetlinMachineCUDA and 10.3-81.2X faster than tmu on the same GPU. The package is pure Python, MIT-licensed and on PyPI; every number in this paper is reproduced by one script. Code: https://github.com/vlbthambawita/torchtsetlin; package: https://pypi.org/project/torchtsetlin/.

Artificial Intelligence.title: HEP-Ex-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Performance in High Energy Physics Experiment Data Analyses with Sealed Worlds
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via extensive expert review. To address this, we propose a method to perform detailed quantitative evaluations of agent-driven analyses through the use of blind analysis and injection tests, which are critical in a typical expert review. Agents develop a data analysis pipeline on a public dataset, while the evaluation is performed on programmatically generated sealed private datasets where signals are injected and simulation settings varied within realistic detector uncertainties. By requiring agents to provide a single workflow that is evaluated across these "sealed worlds", we are able to test the accuracy and robustness of the workflows.
