These methods infer "better" personality and other desirable traits implicitly by ranking multiple model responses relative to each other. Recent issues with model releases highlight limitations of these existing opaque evaluation approaches: goblin-obsessed, sycophantic and generally over-the-top personalities have resulted in model rollbacks and extensive media coverage. Despite these known issues, limited public tooling exists to explicitly evaluate model personality. We introduce Feedback Forensics: an open-source toolkit to track AI personality and related behavioural traits, both those encouraged by human (or AI) feedback, and those exhibited across AI models trained and evaluated on such feedback. Feedback Forensics is adaptive and can automatically find new traits appearing in models. We demonstrate the toolkit's usefulness in two steps: (A) first we analyse the personality traits encouraged in popular human feedback datasets including MultiPref, PRISM and data from Chatbot Arena; and (B) then use our toolkit to analyse how much popular models exhibit such traits. We release (1) our Feedback Forensics toolkit alongside (2) a web app tracking AI personality in popular models and feedback datasets and (3) the underlying annotation data, see https://github.com/rdnfn/feedback-forensics.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track), v3 is the final camera-ready version

Artificial Intelligence.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use can behave inconsistently across independent runs from identical states. They may call different tools, produce contradictory outputs, or follow divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces AUC coefficient of variation (CV) by up to 30.9% on tau2-bench and 50.5% on ToolSandbox. Across Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3.5 models, RSD reduces AUC CV in seven out of eight model-benchmark settings, while improving the final task progress in all eight settings.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted as a conference paper in NeurIPS 2026. Source code is publicly available in the repository in https://github.com/SAP-samples/agent-consistency-rsd

Artificial Intelligence.title: Residual-Tail-Informed Flow Matching for Time Series Anomaly Detection
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Time series anomaly detection (TSAD) models are often trained on nominal data using average-risk objectives, which emphasize dominant normal patterns. However, real time series can contain rare but valid nominal regimes that are underrepresented in the training distribution. We show that data-space flow matching can over-penalize such rare-normal windows and assign them anomaly scores comparable to those of true anomalies. To address this, we propose Residual-Tail-Informed Flow Matching (RT-FM), an unsupervised framework that uses a temporal variational autoencoder to estimate residual latent tailness and converts it into bounded, warmup-annealed weights for training a data-space flow matching model. Experiments on seven TSAD benchmarks show that RT-FM improves rare-normal coverage while preserving strong anomaly discrimination, substantially reducing false alarms on such windows and resulting in improved aggregate detection performance. The code is available at: https://github.com/trustAIoT/RT-FM_time-series-anomaly
Artificial Intelligence.comment: IEEE International Conference on Big Data 2026 (December)

Artificial Intelligence.title: LENS: Replacing LayerNorm and Softmax in Transformers with Learnable Normalization States
Artificial Intelligence.summary: LayerNorm and attention Softmax are critical operations in Transformers. However, they cannot be efficiently mapped to General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) computations on hardware. Therefore, modern hardware accelerator designs, such as NPUs on ASIC/FPGA, consume a large amount of hardware resources or chip area to implement their specific arithmetic units. Building on previous work about LayerNorm, Softmax, and their alternatives, we introduce Learnable Normalization States (LENS), a framework that reformulates LayerNorm as tiny MLPs by abstracting a common structure from related methods and extends this method to Softmax, which moves more of the computation in Transformers to GEMM as a hardware-friendly architecture. We evaluate LENS on image classification with Vision Transformers (ViT) and autoregressive language modeling with Pythia models, including generalization tests on WikiText and LAMBADA. Across these tasks, LENS matches or exceeds baseline performance in several vision settings and retains most of the baseline performance in the remaining vision and language experiments. These findings may suggest that hand-designed normalization and attention functions are not the only choice as alternatives to LayerNorm and Softmax. LENS also provides a basis for exploring Transformer architectures for resource-limited accelerators.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Source code is available at: https://github.com/liuyh-Horizon/LENS

Artificial Intelligence.title: AutoCedar: An Agentic Framework for Verifier-Guided Access Control Policy Synthesis
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large Language Models are increasingly used to turn natural-language requirements into code. In access control, that shortcut is dangerous: a generated policy can compile and read correctly while granting access that no one approved. The difficulty is not only writing policy code. It is fixing what the requirements mean before code is written, and then checking that the final policy actually satisfies that intent. We present AutoCedar, a verifier-guided system that first turns natural-language access-control requirements into a reviewed, checkable target, and then synthesizes Cedar policies against that target. AutoCedar decomposes schema and policy authoring into small intent atoms: reviewable claims about vocabulary and behavior. Once those atoms pass mechanical validation and human intent review, the model proposes a candidate policy, the verifier checks it against the approved target, and each failure is turned into a repair signal that tells the model whether to broaden, narrow, or restructure the policy without changing the target. Because the model's work is split into small problems, each grounded in reviewed intent and backed by verifier feedback, end-to-end policy authoring becomes tractable. AutoCedar converges on all 221 tasks of CedarBench, our benchmark of authorization tasks paired with executable semantic boundaries. Across three requirements-corpus case studies covering healthcare, education, and conference management, AutoCedar converts noisy prose and extracted access-control fragments into reviewed schemas, formal checks, and a globally verified Cedar policy store for each scenario.

Artificial Intelligence.title: PEIRA: Learning Predictive Encoders through Inter-View Regressor Alignment
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Non-contrastive self-supervised learning (SSL) is an effective framework for predictive representation learning, but popular (and in practice effective) methods such as SimSiam, BYOL, I-JEPA or DINO, which rely on a form of self-distillation to train a teacher-student network, remain poorly understood as they typically do not minimize a well-defined objective. We analyze the dynamics of a variant of the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) using a regularized linear regressor to predict the learned representations of two views of the data from one another, and fully characterize its stability: non-collapsed stable equilibria align with leading nonlinear canonical correlation subspaces, while collapsed equilibria may also be stable attractors. Motivated by this result, we introduce PEIRA, a non-contrastive SSL method with an explicit objective defined through the trace of the optimal linear regressor. We show that its only stable equilibria are nontrivial global minimizers and recover the same canonical correlation subspaces, with regularization selecting the effective dimension. Experiments on ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-10 show PEIRA is competitive with VICReg and LeJEPA baselines, and qualitative empirical results support the theory. Project page: https://peira-ssl.github.io. Code: https://github.com/MichaelArbel/peira-loss (loss implementation), https://github.com/Basile-Terv/PEIRA (experiment reproduction).
Artificial Intelligence.comment: NeurIPS 2026 camera-ready. Project page: https://peira-ssl.github.io. v2: corrected assumptions in the PEIRA stability result; new results with a wider projector (k=1024, 69.17% ImageNet-1K linear probe), transfer to 8 datasets, ablations, wall-clock cost, synthetic and initialization-scale experiments; links to code

Artificial Intelligence.title: Unreasonable Confidence from Simulator Misspecification: Directional Robustness on the SPEED+ Sim-to-Real Benchmark
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Vision-based navigation systems for orbit must be trained almost entirely on synthetic imagery, because real labelled images of a given spacecraft in flight rarely exist. Benchmarks like SPEED+ are built for that situation: the training set comes from a simulator, and the test sets are real images of a satellite mockup under two kinds of lighting. That simulator approximates how light reflects off mylar and aluminium, and like every scientific simulator it is misspecified. Its error is radiometric, since it misses the specular highlights, hard shadows and sensor saturation common in real images. We probe the resulting synthetic-to-real gap, the central risk for such systems, with a deliberately simple monocular pose estimator. In a 2x2 study of backbone adaptation and photometric augmentation, trained on synthetic images and tested on both real hardware-in-the-loop domains, we find three things. (1) The model does not know it is failing: regions conformally calibrated to 90% on synthetic data cover only 9-15% of rotation errors on sunlamp and 21-38% on lightbox, so a wrong pose carries the confidence of a correct one. (2) Transfer is asymmetric: scaling data and features improved synthetic rotation error from 1.65 to 1.03 rad but moved the harshly lit sunlamp domain by only 0.05 rad, under twice its seed s.d., whereas adapting the backbone's last stage carried 63-83% of its extra synthetic gain to both real domains. (3) Once the backbone adapts, augmentation helps only in the direction it models: our photometric stack improved the diffusely lit lightbox domain from 1.17 to 0.99 rad on every seed but moved sunlamp no more than seed-to-seed variation, while with the backbone frozen it helped sunlamp more. Every post-review experiment was pre-registered, and the code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record are at https://github.com/lokindoo/spacecraft-pose-estimation.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Extended version of a paper at the Sim2Science workshop, NeurIPS 2026. Code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record: https://github.com/lokindoo/spacecraft-pose-estimation

Artificial Intelligence.title: NF-VLA: A Normalizing-Flow Baseline for Vision-Language-Action Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Autoregressive normalizing flows (NFs) provide a tractable density for learning and sampling continuous robot actions. We show that a single maximum-likelihood objective can train vision--language--action (VLA) policies competitive with leading methods on manipulation benchmarks. We present NF-VLA, which combines conditional autoregressive normalizing flows with score-based action refinement. Its deep--shallow architecture concentrates visual, language, and proprioceptive prefix conditioning in a high-capacity deep block, while unconditioned shallow blocks provide a shared invertible action transformation. The vision--language backbone and flow are jointly trained by exact maximum likelihood on Gaussian-smoothed action chunks. The same learned density supplies a single score-based correction at inference, refining generated actions to account for training-time smoothing without a separately trained denoiser. Trained on LIBERO from a pretrained vision--language backbone without robot pretraining, NF-VLA achieves 98.35\% success across the four standard suites and 72.6\% on LIBERO-Plus using the same checkpoint without further fine-tuning. Ablations show that deep-only prefix conditioning and score-based refinement both improve closed-loop success. Together, these results establish carefully structured autoregressive flows as a competitive approach to VLA control, with one learned density supporting policy training, action generation, and refinement.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Multi-output neural network surrogate for double-pulse femtosecond optothermal control of thin silicon films on fused silica
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We introduce a multi-output feedforward neural network surrogate trained on a coupled multiple-reflection and two-temperature model to map double-pulse femtosecond laser excitation (1030 nm) of crystalline silicon films on fused silica across film thicknesses (50-500 nm) and inter-pulse delays (0-10ps). Trained via Levenberg-Marquardt optimization on 2000 physical simulations, the dual-hidden-layer network ([40,30] neurons) simultaneously predicts six strongly coupled optothermal observables, peak electron temperature, peak lattice temperature, peak carrier density, minimum and maximum absorptivity and minimum refractive index achieving coefficients of determination R2 larger than 0.9998 across all targets. Evaluating a dense 200 by 200 design grid in milliseconds resolves pronounced thin-film interference fringes and carrier-induced index modulation, identifying an optimal optothermal coupling regime at d=156 nm and Dt=4.572 ps. This unified machine-learning workflow eliminates computationally expensive multi-physics runtime bottlenecks for real-time laser processing control and inverse photonic thin-film design.

Artificial Intelligence.title: A Topological Sorting Criterion for Random Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Random directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) based on imposing an order on Erdős-Rényi or scale-free graphs are widely used to generate synthetic data from causal models, in particular for evaluating causal discovery algorithms. We show that the set of nodes reachable via open paths, termed relatives, never decreases along the causal order in all DAGs. We find that it tends to increase strictly for DAGs with certain density parameters, and demonstrate that this pattern can be exploited for causal discovery via sorting by the estimated number of relatives. We note that many simulations in the literature are focused on a narrow range of parameter settings where sorting by relatives yields an excellent proxy for the causal order, and show that a strict increase of relatives leads to a singleton Markov equivalence class. We propose sampling time-series DAGs as a possible alternative and discuss implications for causal discovery and synthetic data generation. Implementations of our algorithms can be found at https://causaldisco.github.io/CausalDisco/.

Artificial Intelligence.title: LLMs Can Design Near-Optimal OR Algorithms
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can design effective algorithms for well-specified operations research (OR) problems. We study inventory control, queueing network control, and assortment optimization, using benchmark instances from recent papers in each area. We evaluate two levels of LLM use: at level 1, the model receives one problem instance and returns a solution for that instance; at level 2, it receives only the problem class description and broad parameter ranges, and returns an algorithm that maps instance parameters to solutions. Human input is minimal: we give one untuned prompt that describes the problem, and the model has access to a Python sandbox tool with a fixed compute budget. The strongest model we test, gpt-5.6-sol, matches or outperforms the best method reported in those papers on almost all evaluated instances. This holds even at level 2, where the returned algorithm is fixed before seeing the evaluation instances. Performance also improves sharply across models released less than eight months apart, suggesting that this capability is moving quickly. Thus, for the well-specified operations problems we study, a single untuned LLM query can already produce algorithms competitive with specialized methods. These results suggest that frontier LLMs can be a serious empirical baseline for algorithm design in well-specified OR problems.

Artificial Intelligence.title: SREGym: A Live Benchmark for AI SRE Agents with High-Fidelity Failure Scenarios
Artificial Intelligence.summary: AI agents are increasingly used to diagnose and mitigate failures in production systems, known as agentic Site Reliability Engineering (SRE). Current SRE benchmarks are limited to oversimplistic SRE tasks and are unfortunately hard to extend due to bespoke designs. We present SREGym, a high-fidelity benchmark for SRE agents. SREGym exposes a live system environment built atop real-world cloud-native system stacks, where high-fidelity failure scenarios are simulated through fault injectors. SREGym models the complexity of production environments by simulating (1) a wide range of faults at different layers, (2) various ambient noises, and (3) diverse failure modes such as metastable failures and correlated failures. SREGym is architected as a modular, extensible framework that orchestrates fault and noise injectors across stacks. SREGym currently includes 90 realistic, challenging SRE problems. We use SREGym to evaluate frontier agents and show that their capabilities varies significantly in addressing different kinds of failures, with up to 40% differences in end-to-end results. SREGym is actively maintained as an open-source project and has been used by researchers and practitioners.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Benchmarking LLM Inference on Desktop-Scale NVIDIA Grace Blackwell Clusters
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Two NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 systems connect directly over 200 GbE to serve larger language models and increase inference capacity, but the benefits depend on how they are deployed. We benchmark 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, 8B to 235B parameters and four weight precisions on one and two RDMA-connected systems. Using vLLM, we compare tensor parallelism (TP=2), pipeline parallelism (PP=2) and a two-replica baseline at concurrency 1 to 64, with three independent launches per configuration. TP=2 delivers a median 1.59x peak-throughput gain over one Spark, versus 1.39x for PP=2 and has higher throughput in 93 of 96 matched comparisons with separated 95% Welch intervals. It reduces unloaded inter-token latency to 0.52x to 0.73x of one Spark, whereas PP=2 provides little reduction. TP=2 also achieves the highest goodput under a strict 100 ms inter-token latency objective wherever both strategies are supported and the objective is met. For models fitting on one Spark, TP=2 generally favors low-concurrency serving, while replication offers higher throughput at high concurrency. One Spark uses less GPU energy per output token at matched concurrency. Across three precision ladders, NVFP4 reduces unloaded latency more than adding a second Spark at BF16. NCCL microbenchmarks and comparisons with an earlier TCP campaign suggest that collective communication overhead contributes to the advantage of TP=2. These results provide deployment guidance for desktop-scale inference.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 24 pages, 16 figures, 8 tables. Code and data available at https://github.com/kevinhbhimani/dgx-spark-llm-serving-benchmark Copy

Artificial Intelligence.title: Protecting Safety during Reasoning Training with Low-Rank Fisher Regularisation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models are trained to have safety guardrails, but these can be compromised while fine-tuning for new capabilities, such as reasoning. One way to mitigate this degradation is to modify the fine-tuning objective to preserve safety behaviour, but doing so effectively and efficiently remains challenging. We revisit Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which penalises parameter updates based on sensitivity estimates from the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix (FIM). While EWC provides some protection, the diagonal approximation ignores interactions between parameters. We address this limitation by exploiting recent findings that safety-relevant behaviour is located in a low-rank subspace within models. Our method, Subspace-Projected Elastic Weight Consolidation (SP-EWC), projects gradients onto this subspace to capture non-diagonal curvature efficiently. We investigate three different ways of identifying the safety subspace: through safety fine-tuning updates (LoRA), safety-related activations (ActSVD), and contrastive representations of safety and utility data (cPCA). We find that this choice substantially affects performance, with SP-EWC using cPCA comparing favourably against existing methods by better maintaining safety guardrails without introducing excessive over-refusal.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Self-supervised learning for zebrafish embryo phenotype evaluation: Systematic comparison of algorithms, label-efficient classification, and transfer learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Zebrafish embryos are a prominent model organism for image-based phenotyping and especially suited for large-scale imaging studies, for which machine learning (ML) models can automate evaluation. However, training ML models usually requires large labeled datasets, and differences in imaging conditions often impede reuse across laboratories. Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses both constraints by learning transferable representations from unlabeled images. Yet central aspects like the choice of algorithm remain underexplored for domain-specific applications. To close this gap, we benchmark popular SSL algorithms on the public EmbryoNet dataset, explore label-efficient learning, and test transfer to an unseen setting. Using representations from our strongest model, a ResNet50 network trained with SwAV, a simple linear classifier reaches 86.4% accuracy and a non-linear classifier 87.1%, rivaling the fully supervised EmbryoNet model (87.1%). The SwAV model decisively outperforms supervised training from scratch when labels are scarce (70.2% vs. 45.7% accuracy with 5% of labels). On a three-class problem (normal, dead, falsely cropped) with a small, previously unseen zebrafish toxicity dataset, recorded in a different setting, our model reaches 81.3% accuracy without retraining, while EmbryoNet achieves 75.9%. Overall, self-supervised models for zebrafish embryos seem to mostly facilitate label-efficiency and transfer to new settings rather than improving supervised results.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Axiomatic Positivstellensaetze for Function Algebras over Ordered Fields
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Positivstellensaetze furnish algebraic certificates of positivity, and hence of lower bounds and of global optimality, but the classical ones concern polynomials, whereas many problems of current interest, among them the training of neural networks, involve functions that are neither polynomial nor smooth. We isolate an axiomatic core of the constructive Positivstellensaetze of Fischer. The setting consists of an ordered field expanded by five auxiliary function symbols, subject to a few first-order axioms, together with an algebra of functions on an arbitrary set, subject to closure axioms. In this setting we prove a strict and a weak Positivstellensatz in which the witnesses are obtained by substituting the data into fixed terms that depend only on the number of constraints. The framework recovers Fischer's theorems for definable $C^r$-functions, and yields new instances: algebras of definable functions with arbitrary auxiliary functions, such as the binary step function; algebras of continuous functions, for which we give simple sufficient criteria and auxiliary functions derived from common activation functions; and algebras of continuous functions with values in an ordered field that is not closed under square roots, such as $\mathbb{Q}$. We derive certificates of lower bounds and of global optimality, and show that their expanded term length is cubic in the number of constraints for the strict certificate and quadratic for the weak one.

Artificial Intelligence.title: GNN-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Coastal Emergency Response under Extreme Water Levels
Artificial Intelligence.summary: When a storm surge approaches a coastal town, the emergency plan must be put into action quickly using water-level forecasts, flood extent, road access, vulnerable residents and shelters. Bringing this information together under time pressure is slow and depends on the duty officer's expertise. This paper is one step in a wider research line from data to safe decisions: machine learning to understand the hazard, reinforcement learning and planning to choose actions, large language models (LLMs) to explain and cross-check them, and an assurance layer that keeps people in charge. Here we address the action step on a real place. We ask whether a policy can learn the timing of emergency actions from decades of real events. Lido di Venezia is represented as a heterogeneous graph built from public elevation, road, building and census data and driven by hourly tide-gauge records from 1983 to 2024, with seven actions taken from the municipal emergency plan. A PPO policy is trained on this graph and compared, on storm windows unseen in training, with a rule-based system simulating the officer's discretionary decisions. On 18 historical test scenarios, PPO achieves a similar reduction in population exposure to the rule. With uncertain forecasts and limited protection it again performs similarly but does not outperform the tuned rule, and removing graph message passing does not substantially reduce performance. PPO therefore learns an effective protective response from an outcome-based reward alone: it is given the plan's actions and when each is allowed, but not the thresholds that tell the comparator when to act. Next steps test harder edge cases, move closer to a digital twin of the territory, and replace the simulated officer with assessment by emergency-management stakeholders, supported by LLM-based interpretation of each recommendation.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Accepted at the Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/marcellosano/coastal-emergency-drl

Artificial Intelligence.title: Re(Visiting) Time Series Foundation Models in Finance
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Financial time series forecasting is vital for trading, portfolio optimization, and risk management but is challenged by noisy, nonstationary, and heterogeneous data. Time series foundation models (TSFMs), inspired by large language models, aim to learn transferable temporal representations. Whether pre-training on massive, diverse datasets enables similar generalization to finance remains an open question. This study provides a comprehensive empirical evaluation of TSFMs in global financial markets using large-scale daily excess-return data. We assess zero-shot inference, fine-tuning, and pre-training from scratch against strong benchmarks. Off-the-shelf TSFMs generally perform poorly, while finance-native pre-training improves long-window gross portfolio performance. Larger pre-training datasets and synthetic augmentation improve selected specifications, particularly at longer input windows. Configuration changes have mixed effects across forecasting and portfolio metrics, and TSFMs do not consistently outperform strong benchmarks. These findings caution against uncritical AI adoption in finance, where insufficient validation can lead to unreliable forecasts and substantial financial losses.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Estimating Outpatient Visit Prices from Hospital Price Transparency Data using Large Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Objective: Hospital care prices in the United States have increased substantially, yet patients lack effective tools to access and compare costs. We aimed to develop and evaluate an LLM-based approach for improving access to and use of hospital price transparency (PT) data. Materials and Methods: To estimate visit prices, we used a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework to analyze PT files from three major hospitals in Maryland and the surrounding region. We compared BM25, OpenAI embedding models, and a GPT-BM25 hybrid against a no-RAG baseline for cost estimation of individual procedures and procedure groups, then evaluated the best approach for symptom-based visit cost estimation using synthetic simulations. Results: Across hospitals, the GPT-BM25 retriever achieved the best performance, with average price MAPE of 19.44% for individual procedures and 4.90% for groups, compared with 147.98% and 82.82%, respectively, for the no-RAG baseline. In simulations, our framework correctly identified approximately 50% of reference procedures and reduced MAPE relative to the LLM-only baseline at two of the three hospitals, while achieving comparable performance at the third. Discussion: Our framework uses RAG to improve care price estimation in real-world settings. Compared with the no-RAG baseline, it substantially improved cost estimates for both individual procedures and procedure groups. Improvements were smaller in synthetic simulations, likely because inferring procedures from clinical information is more complex. Practical challenges remain, including heterogeneous PT file formats, unexplained duplicate entries, and limited availability of insurer-negotiated rates. Conclusion: LLMs that effectively integrate PT data show strong potential to provide patients with more accessible and accurate healthcare cost estimates.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Microfitting: Continual Learning via Cached Test-Time Training
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Continual learning is a promising approach to specialize language models to an organization's private data. However, current methods exhibit a number of drawbacks including catastrophic forgetting, where new training updates overwrite prior knowledge. We present microfitting, which trains and caches a small adapter for each document. Each adapter is trained once, offline, on synthetic questions targeted at demonstrated base-model shortcomings and reused whenever that document is queried. This method borrows from test-time learning literature and sidesteps the problem of continual learning through parameter isolation, allowing the system to specialize on new data without overwriting prior knowledge. The process that generates adapter training data also improves over time, revising its recipe from previous outcomes and fresh examples of the target workload. On DeepSeek V4 Flash, microfitting substantially improves accuracy over the base model. In Enterprise Document Operations (EDO), an open-book Q&A environment over real-world enterprise documents, our method achieves a 38.2% relative improvement over base-model performance. Microfitting makes continual specialization practical and cost-efficient: a frozen model can adapt to an evolving private corpus overnight on local hardware, without modifying the base model or previously cached adapters.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Integrating Latent Block Models into Variational Autoencoders for Disentangled Representation Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We introduce LBM-VAE, a novel framework that integrates Latent Block Models (LBMs) into Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to jointly cluster observations and latent dimensions. Beyond its clustering capabilities, LBM-VAE provides a block-structured latent representation that naturally supports disentangled representation learning. In contrast to conventional approaches that associate each factor of variation with an individual latent dimension, our framework allows factors of variation to be encoded across groups of latent dimensions. Experimental results demonstrate the promising clustering performance of LBM-VAE, while achieving competitive results in disentangled representation learning. LBM-VAE highlights the potential of combining co-clustering and variational inference to learn structured and interpretable latent representations.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Supporting Calibrated Reliance in AI-Assisted Decision-Making: Different Strategies for Different Tasks
Artificial Intelligence.summary: As AI systems increasingly support human decision-making, a central challenge is determining what information helps people recognize when to rely on AI predictions and when to question or override them. Across three controlled human-subject studies spanning abstract visual reasoning with RAVEN matrices and deductive logical reasoning with LSAT problems, we examine how different forms of AI support affect performance in AI-assisted decision-making. A multi-stage reveal study shows that AI predictions and explanations can affect objective accuracy and subjective confidence differently. In visual reasoning, LLM explanations do not improve accuracy beyond the predicted answer alone, and no additional support format significantly outperforms prediction-only support; predicted probabilities show the highest descriptive accuracy and error recovery, while a derived selective-automation policy provides a higher-performing reference benchmark. In language-based logical reasoning, by contrast, LLM explanations yield the highest accuracy and error recovery, outperforming expert-written explanations and probability-based support. These results suggest that the effectiveness of AI support strategies depends on the task setting. Human--AI interfaces should instead be designed to support calibrated reliance and effective error recovery by matching the form of assistance to the task and the evidence available to users.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Right Goal, Wrong Body: Re-grounding Frozen VLAs under Actuation Shift
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are capable of producing desired robotic behaviors in ideal settings. However, they often fail when the robot's actuation changes at deployment. For example, remounting, mechanical wear, or command latency changes can lead to failed tasks and unsafe behaviors. To address the inevitable actuation shift, we propose ReGround, an inference-time method that keeps the VLA frozen and re-grounds its intended motion. ReGround learns the deployed robot's dynamics from task-agnostic motor babbling, and then tracks the policy's intended motion while staying close to the policy's own plan. ReGround activates only upon detecting a shift, and needs no rewards, demonstrations, or retraining. We show via two VLAs, eight LIBERO tasks, and five shift settings that ReGround can restore near-oracle success, such as raising $π_{0.5}$'s success from 0.16 to 0.90 under 400 ms latency, while remaining safer than a linear-calibration baseline. Project website and open-source code: https://umersiddique94.github.io/ReGround/.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at the SPAIS Workshop at CoRL 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: A Matrix with Steps: An Episodic and Procedural Memory Method for Tool-Using Agents and Robots
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Agents that call tools and robots that execute tasks are challenged by two shortcomings: they repeat what failed before, and they learn from runs that they only believe succeeded. We describe the construction of a memory that addresses both, built for a production agent platform. Every run is recorded as an episode, and only an outcome confirmed by an external check, a test, a tool result or a person counts; the agent's own claim never does. What is learned from episodes is kept in a memory with two parts: an associative matrix, written with the delta rule, which finds the procedure that applies to a situation; and a section of ordered, addressable step records that answers what comes after a given step, where a step is a goal of the agent, not a motion. Because the matrix sums its associations, it keeps no order and cannot return or delete a single one; it serves as the finder, and order, outcome counts and deletion live in the records. We describe how execution outcomes are stored, how episodes are recalled and used for solving tasks, and the file format that stores the memory. In simulation, a robot that judged its own success and stopped when it believed it was done reported $96\%$ of its tasks as done and solved $35\%$; with external verification it solved $79%$. In a store of $100000$ synthetic episodes ($457$MB on disk), the oldest episode was still found first, no episode from another person's memory was returned, and a success vouched for only by the model was never recalled; a lookup took $16$ms on a laptop and $40$ms on a server node (median). Task outcomes were measured up to about $10000$ confirmed records, where the exact records solved every revisit at the first attempt.

Artificial Intelligence.title: The Shadow Price of Intelligence: Quality Degradation and Retry Feedback in LLM Inference
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language model providers are compute constrained, and a common response to congestion is to degrade service: route queries to smaller models, cut reasoning budgets, or shorten context windows. A user who receives an unsatisfactory answer either retries, adding load while the system is busy, or abandons, possibly as churn. We model inference serving as a control problem in which service quality is the provider's decision. A two-regime fluid approximation with retries folded into the service rate gives closed-form trajectories and crossing times, so the dynamic program over quality tiers needs no simulation. We characterize a region in which a weaker tier uses less energy per task but more capacity per task, and show that in the fluid model reactive throttling to such a tier can keep the queue from draining. With heterogeneous customers the problem is a transportation problem with retry-inflated capacity coefficients; optimal routing follows a $cμ$-type index, and the dual of the capacity constraint gives the marginal cost of one more query by class and time. We illustrate the method on five instances calibrated to public benchmark data.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 28 pages, 12 figures. Numerical instances calibrated to public benchmark data for five LLM providers

Artificial Intelligence.title: SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations
Artificial Intelligence.summary: A coding agent working within a software organization must establish what to build, collaborate with colleagues, and verify what it delivers. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. Starting from a brief handoff, agents must recover requirements distributed across colleagues and workplace records, reconcile conflicting evidence, and implement changes evaluated by private executable tests. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Providing complete requirements upfront improves F2P by approximately 16 percentage points for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra, yet leaves complete task success unchanged. Requirement-level trajectory analysis reveals failures throughout the delivery process: Claude-Opus-5.5 directs a mean of 93% of first questions about queried cards to their accountable owners across runs but obtains only 64% of colleague-held requirements. Deferred questions go unfollowed, implementations remain incomplete even after requirements are acquired, and 31% of requirements reported as completed fail their tests. These findings highlight sustained requirement tracking, from clarification through implementation, verification, and handoff, as a key challenge for reliable autonomous software engineering.

Artificial Intelligence.title: No Certificate, No Categorical Speech Act: A Brouwerian Assertibility Constraint for Public Machine Speech
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Suppose a citizen asks a reliable AI chatbot whether a cabinet secretary engaged in serious corruption. What entitles the chatbot to answer yes or no? Drawing on Brouwer's account of constructive assertion, I argue that categorical machine speech in high-stakes domains requires an auditor-checkable and publicly contestable certificate of entitlement. Citizens expected to rely on a verdict must be able to identify and challenge the grounds on which it is issued. This requirement yields three statuses -- licensed assertion, licensed denial, and Undetermined -- that mark entitlement to categorical speech, not truth. Undetermined is neither a truth-value gap nor a tunable reject option. A design lemma shows what eliminating the third status would cost. Under stated assumptions, an interface that certifies a verdict in every case by establishing or refuting its deployed predicate provides a witnessed decision procedure on its declared scope. Where no such procedure is available, a certificate-sound interface cannot guarantee a categorical verdict for every case. I defend an output contract that keeps unsettled cases within scope and requires Undetermined whenever the available certificates fail to license exactly one side. In the corruption case, the citizen can accept a committee's finding that payments bought favorable lease terms and still ask why the materiality threshold is set at $500,000. The contract makes that choice explicit, and the certificate records how it is applied. Responsibility for defending the threshold remains with the institutions that set it, not with the machine.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Paying Creators for Training Data Can Increase AI Displacement
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Generative AI increasingly competes with creators while using their content as training data. In response, policymakers have called for platforms to compensate creators for training data use and allow opting out. We study how such policies affect creator displacement in a model of a platform where creators choose whether to contribute training data and consumers choose between purchasing from creators and prompting generative AI trained on their content. When compensation is required, the low-quality creator chooses to remain solely as a training data supplier while AI fully displaces her demand, despite AI quality and the price the platform charges for AI-generated content being identical with and without compensation. Without compensation, the risk of losing creators and their training data constrains the platform to set the price of creators' content to preserve their demand. This constraint also prevents further AI displacement as AI improves, with the platform raising AI prices while keeping creators' prices and demand unchanged to prevent exit. Compensation increases creators' payoffs and total surplus but reduces consumer surplus. Our findings highlight how compensation policies for training data can shape creators' economic roles in a future with more capable generative AI.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 53 pages, 6 figures. Previously circulated under the title "Platform Design When Creators Train Their AI Substitutes"

Artificial Intelligence.title: Subliminal Transfer of Unsafe Behaviors in AI Agent Distillation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Recent work on subliminal learning has shown that language models can transmit semantic traits through data with no apparent connection to those traits. Whether this phenomenon extends to agentic systems, where policies are learned from trajectories rather than static text, remains an open question with critical safety implications. We present the first empirical evidence that unsafe agent behaviors transfer subliminally through model distillation, demonstrated across several settings. In the primary setting, we construct a teacher agent with a deletion bias, a tendency to perform destructive file-system actions through an API-style tool interface, and distill it into a student using only trajectories from ostensibly safe tasks, with all explicit deletion keywords filtered. In the secondary setting, we replicate the threat model with shell commands, replacing API calls with shell commands and operationalizing the bias as a preference for chmod over semantically equivalent alternatives (e.g., chown, setfacl) when issuing the first permission-related command. Despite sanitation, students inherit measurable biases. Over 1,500 trials per configuration, the API student chooses a destructive action first on 35.5% of ambiguous tasks (vs. 1.2% baseline), and the Bash student's chmod-first rate reaches 30-55% (vs. 0-10% baseline). In a multi-turn environment where tool calls execute, 33.9% of student episodes end with a resource irreversibly destroyed (vs. 6.4% baseline). On TerminalBench we observe a smaller effect (7.7% vs. 0% baseline). Explicit data sanitation is therefore insufficient as a defense; mitigating behavioral bias transfer in agentic systems will require fundamentally new strategies.

Artificial Intelligence.title: How Specification Explicitness Shapes Failure in LLM-Generated Code
Artificial Intelligence.summary: When LLMs turn requirements into code, every underspecified constraint becomes behavior that the model must decide during generation. We test when specifications move beyond structure and begin to control generated behavior. In a controlled experiment, 72 participants implemented and revised Python tasks with an LLM under three levels of specification explicitness. The results show a clear break between lightweight structure and explicit behavioral obligations. Lightweight structure reduced hidden-test failures by only 8.7%. Requiring participants to specify constraints, invariants, negative requirements, edge cases, tie-breaking rules, and exception handling cut failures by 47.2% and reduced the number of distinct failure modes by 20.5%. The largest drops were in failure modes tied to implicit obligations. Invariant violations fell by 66.1%, and unsupported assumptions fell by 59.5%. After a requirement change, specifications with explicit behavioral obligations produced regressions in more submissions, but each affected submission lost less previously correct behavior. Explicit specifications also changed how developers judged generated code. Without explicit obligations, participants overestimated generated-code correctness by about 23 percentage points. With explicit obligations, they produced better code but judged it more cautiously. Thus, the lesson is sharper than "better specifications help." Lightweight structure barely helped, while explicit behavioral obligations nearly halved failures, made regressions shallower, and improved calibration.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Seeing Is No Longer Believing: Frontier Image Generation Models, Synthetic Visual Evidence, and Real-World Risk
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Image generation systems can produce plausible photographs, readable documents, and consistent depictions of people and places. Presented as records of real events, these outputs can influence decisions in news, finance, identity verification, medicine, and law. This narrative review examines public model documentation, incident reports, empirical studies, governance materials, and illustrative English and Chinese practitioner commentary available through 1 October 2026. We separate vendor capability claims, documented incidents, experimental findings, and prospective harm pathways. Realism, text rendering, reference consistency, conversational editing, search grounding, and low generation cost shape the conditions under which synthetic images acquire evidentiary weight. Documented episodes show how fabricated visuals enter public and institutional workflows, although public reporting cannot measure misuse prevalence for current releases. Comparing provider safeguards, provenance credentials, watermarks, platform labels, and statutory duties shows that origin signals do not verify a depicted event or transaction. Our framework matches artifact types and decision stakes to specific controls. Consequential decisions require authenticated source records, independent channel corroboration, and proportionate review before action.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 24 pages, 13 figures. Revised review of image-generation capabilities, synthetic visual evidence, and governance

Artificial Intelligence.title: Cyber-Secure Wearable, Ultra-Low-Power Networked Sensors for Soldier Health Monitoring: Insights from the CAPSARII project
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The CAPSARII project advances a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable platform and Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) framework to support real-time monitoring of military personnel and data-driven decision support. The architecture integrates smart-textile sensing, a body/squad area mesh, edge-deployed AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning and comparative studies. Two representative use cases--pilot fatigue and warfighters operating in harsh environments--guide requirements, validation, and interface design (including HUD and haptic feedback). As an initial step toward embedded models, we benchmark stress classification on a public wearable dataset: tree-ensemble baselines achieve state-of-the-art performance for accuracy and F1 (e.g., XGBoost: $\mathrm{Accuracy}=0.901\!\pm\!0.023$, $\mathrm{F1}=0.920\!\pm\!0.019$), while a feature-based Transformer attains the highest AUC ($0.963\!\pm\!0.025$), informing feature-engineering and compression choices for edge deployment. Building on these results, CAPSARII employs HW/SW co-design, model compression (pruning, quantization, distillation), and precision tuning to meet stringent energy and memory budgets; it further investigates Processing-in-Memory accelerators for future efficiency gains. A structured gap analysis highlights the remaining challenges: establishing validation standards for physiological signal quality and textile durability; achieving low-latency, scalable BAN/SAN communications under mobility and interference; and deploying hybrid lightweight/post-quantum cryptography with robust device identity and side-channel resilience on constrained endpoints. By consolidating these elements into a coherent, secure IoBT stack, CAPSARII delineates a practical roadmap from laboratory baselines to mission-ready soldier monitoring in both training and operational scenarios.

Artificial Intelligence.title: RoboKit: Accelerating Parallel Differentiable Optimization for Robot Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We present RoboKit, a high-performance, general-purpose toolkit for parallel differentiable optimization in robotics, built on three principles: (i) Performance and flexibility: GPU-parallel multi-seed solvers pair sampling with versatile optimizers, running 2-60$\times$ faster than task-specific baselines across seven tasks; (ii) Geometry, rendering and physics: hybrid and coarse-to-fine representations accelerate collision, differentiable rendering and simulation, optimizing 4096 grasps in 2.97 s; (iii) Integration with learning: costs are differentiable and simulation is parallel, so RoboKit both distills optimization into policies and trains RL; distilled policies run 9-240$\times$ faster at comparable accuracy, and RL reaches a GPU baseline's scores up to 2.1$\times$ sooner on the same simulator.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026. Project page: https://openrobokit.com/robokit

Artificial Intelligence.title: Do Multi-Agent LLMs Explore Each Other?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Exploration is essential for reliable autonomy in multi-agent systems, yet it remains unclear whether large language model (LLM) agents can explore effectively when interacting with one another. We show that modern LLM agents often fail to do so, exhibiting myopic and polarized interaction patterns that lead to suboptimal coordination and increased regret. We formalize this challenge as the Multi-Agent Exploration problem, modeling it as a partially observable stochastic game (POSG), in which agents must probe peers to infer their capabilities and identify effective interaction strategies. To address this, we introduce Multi-Agent Contextual Exploration (MACE), a lightweight framework that explicitly promotes exploration through structured peer selection. Across both contextual and parametric diversity settings, exploration behavior and downstream task performance substantially improve when MACE is applied. We further provide theoretical insight that MACE achieves a sublinear expected-regret bound. Overall, our results highlight a fundamental limitation of current LLM agents and underscore the importance of explicitly guided exploration for reliable multi-agent autonomy.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Anchor: Preventing Artifact Drift for Reliable Agent Verification
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Reliable evaluation of long-horizon agents requires verifiers that match what the task actually asks. Verifiable rewards have driven progress in domains like math and coding, yet building similarly reliable environments for open-ended enterprise workflows repeatedly struggles to balance realism, verifiability, and scale. This creates a validity problem we call artifact drift: when instructions, environments, oracles, and verifiers are created separately, they frequently fail to agree on what a task requires, resulting in environments that are unsolvable, reward-hackable, or inconsistent. We introduce Anchor, a benchmark-construction pipeline that formalizes domain expert specifications of business workflows into constrained optimization programs. From a single parametric specification, the pipeline jointly produces a natural-language instruction, environment configuration, solver-certified ground-truth solution, and state-based verifier. With this pipeline, altering parameters yields new tasks with controlled difficulty and known optimal solutions, producing harness-agnostic environments whose rewards depend solely on end-state business correctness. We apply Anchor to produce ERP-Bench: a benchmark of 300 long-horizon tasks spanning procurement and manufacturing workflows in a production-grade ERP system. Our pipeline organizes tasks into diverse families with calibrated difficulty profiles, and allows generated environments to evaluate coding, browser, and computer-use agents using a shared verifier. Across these harnesses, we find that frontier models follow all rules and instructions in 25.9% of trials and reach fully optimal decisions in only 17.4% of trials. Overall, Anchor and ERP-Bench offer a concrete recipe for building auditable evaluation environments whose verifiers remain aligned with the economically valuable tasks they are intended to score.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Who Verifies the Agents?

Artificial Intelligence.title: Benign Overfitting of Two-Layer ReLU Networks in Fixed Dimension through Localized Initialization
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Benign overfitting occurs when a model fits noisy training data exactly and still generalizes well. We establish this behavior for finite-width two-layer networks with the standard ReLU activation, trained by gradient flow in fixed dimension. Our data-independent initialization combines Gaussian weights with neurons initially active only on shrinking spherical caps. For uniform spherical inputs and any fixed bounded conditional response law, training and excess risks vanish in probability uniformly over all sufficiently late times. The parameters also converge, with probability tending to one, to an interpolating limit whose excess risk vanishes in probability. We use one schedule depending only on sample size and dimension. Our proof connects the network to a kernel flow whose limit combines ridge regression with localized spikes that fit the training residuals. We give explicit sample-size, width and training-time bounds.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: The results here correct and fix issues with the first version of this submission

Artificial Intelligence.title: Seeing but Not Thinking: Routing Distraction in Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have achieved remarkable performance on vision-language tasks. However, we identify a puzzling phenomenon termed Seeing but Not Thinking: models accurately perceive image content yet fail in subsequent reasoning, while correctly solving identical problems presented as pure text. Through systematic analysis, we first verify that cross-modal semantic sharing exists in MoE architectures, ruling out semantic alignment failure as the sole explanation. We then reveal that visual experts and domain experts exhibit layer-wise separation, with image inputs inducing significant routing divergence from text inputs in middle layers where domain experts concentrate. Based on these findings, we propose the Routing Distraction hypothesis: when processing visual inputs, the routing mechanism fails to adequately activate task-relevant reasoning experts. To validate this hypothesis, we design a routing-guided intervention method that enhances domain expert activation. Experiments on three multimodal MoE models across six benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements, with gains of up to 3.17% on complex visual reasoning tasks. Our analysis further reveals that domain expert identification locates cognitive functions rather than sample-specific solutions, enabling effective transfer across tasks with different information structures.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Pass the Baton: Trajectory-Relayed On-Policy Distillation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) grounds token-level supervision in the student's own trajectory, yet suffers from prefix failure: once the student commits to a wrong reasoning direction, all subsequent generation builds on this deviation, producing misdirected continuations that elicit unreliable supervision and waste compute. We identify a teacher-student continuation asymmetry on failed prefixes, where the teacher tends to redirect while the student continues along the original direction, and convert it into a label-free handoff trigger in Relay On-Policy Distillation (Relay-OPD). During training, Relay-OPD constructs relay trajectories by letting the teacher briefly take over at detected trigger points to produce a teacher leg, after which the student resumes and is optimized on the resulting trajectory. A limited relay budget concentrates intervention on critical early positions while limiting departure from the student policy. With a Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 teacher and Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B-Non-Thinking students on eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, Relay-OPD achieves the best or second-best results on every benchmark, outperforming standard OPD by +5.73% and the strongest baseline FastOPD by +1.49% on average for 1.7B, with consistent gains at 0.6B. Training trajectory length is reduced by over 50%.

Artificial Intelligence.title: HEAMS: Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 69 pages (26 main text), 6 figures, 29 tables. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams

Artificial Intelligence.title: OpenClassGen: A Large-Scale Corpus of Real-World Python Classes for LLM Research
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Existing class-level code generation datasets are either synthetic (ClassEval: 100 classes) or insufficient in scale for modern training needs (RealClassEval: 400 classes), hindering robust evaluation and empirical analysis. We present OpenClassGen, a large-scale corpus of 324,843 Python classes extracted from 2,970 engineered open-source projects. Each entry pairs a human-written class with its corresponding skeleton, which comprises class and method signatures with associated docstrings, and is enriched with 27 static code metrics covering complexity, coupling, cohesion, and inheritance properties. Unlike prior benchmarks that require repository-level context resolution, OpenClassGen provides self-contained class skeletons that serve as complete generation specifications. We demonstrate the corpus's utility by evaluating three LLMs (GPT-o4-mini, Claude-4-Sonnet, Qwen-3-Coder) on a curated, executable subset of 300 classes, enriched with test suites achieving 58% branch coverage. Results show strong semantic similarity (CodeBERTScore-F3: 0.89) but moderate functional correctness (pass rate: 0.33), with substantial variance across models. This variance, along with diverse class characteristics, confirms that OpenClassGen enables meaningful differentiation of LLM capabilities. The dataset supports diverse use cases, including fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, difficulty modelling, and failure mode analysis. The complete dataset and curation scripts are publicly available at https://zenodo.org/records/18409150.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: This paper has been accepted for publication at the 30th International Conference on Evaluation and Assessment in Software Engineering (EASE 2026) AI models/data track

Artificial Intelligence.title: Beyond Synthetic Benchmarks: Evaluating LLM Performance on Real-World Class-Level Code Generation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly from well-studied function-level code generation to emerging repository-level approaches, yet this progression reveals a critical gap: class-level code generation, which is the fundamental building block connecting individual functions to complete repositories, remains systematically underexplored. Understanding class-level capabilities is a prerequisite to repository-level success, as current approaches cannot distinguish whether failures stem from basic implementation deficiencies or sophisticated context management issues. We introduce RealClassEval, a benchmark derived from real-world open-source repositories, comprising 400 classes divided into seen and unseen partitions based on model training cutoffs. Our systematic evaluation across seven state-of-the-art LLMs reveals fundamental limitations masked by synthetic benchmarks: while LLMs achieve 84 to 89% correctness on synthetic tasks, they attain only 25 to 34% on real-world classes, with minimal distinction between seen and unseen codebases. Notably, this performance range converges with concurrent work using rich natural language descriptions and repository context, suggesting that specification complexity cannot overcome core implementation bottlenecks. Documentation provides marginal improvements (1 to 3%), while retrieval augmentation yields greater gains (4 to7%), specifically with incomplete specifications. Error analysis reveals AttributeError, TypeError, and AssertionError dominate 84% of failures, with distinct patterns between synthetic (logic-focused) and real-world (object-oriented) scenarios. These findings establish the diagnostic foundation necessary for advancing both fundamental LLM capabilities and sophisticated repository-level approaches, while providing actionable guidance for production deployment strategies.

Artificial Intelligence.title: CapCover Filter: Semantic Approximate Membership Queries over Embeddings
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Determining whether an embedding is sufficiently similar to any vector in a vector store without performing a nearest-neighbor search can substantially improve query throughput in vector-store systems. We study Semantic Approximate Membership Queries (SAMQs), which allow queries to be rejected when no indexed vector meets the requested similarity threshold, while guaranteeing no false negatives. We introduce CapCover Filter, a geometric data structure that summarizes a set of embeddings using spherical caps. Its representation is independent of the query threshold, allowing a single filter to support arbitrary thresholds without reconstruction. We evaluate alternative construction and quantization methods, compare CapCover Filter with competing filters, and measure its impact on query throughput. Across five real-world datasets, at a cosine similarity threshold of 0.95, CapCover Filter eliminates approximately 20--100\% of index accesses while using only 2\% of the raw (FP32) embedding memory. When placed before a FAISS flat index, it improves query throughput by up to 382\% and by approximately 116\% on average across the five datasets, while returning the same range-search result. We also evaluate lower similarity thresholds. Our results show that CapCover Filter can substantially improve vector-store throughput when similarity thresholds are tight, retrieval is expensive, and indexed embeddings are highly clustered. We release an optimized implementation of CapCover Filter and its evaluation framework.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Can decision models extract clinical data from cancer pathology reports? An evaluation of accuracy, calibration, and failure modes
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Decision models are a new class of language model that, instead of generating text, choose one option per question from a fixed list and return a probability for every option. They have not yet been evaluated on clinical text. We evaluated two open-weights decision models, Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B, for extracting 25 fields from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports from a single centre, against a prospectively maintained clinical database. We compared them with two generative models: Qwen3.5 9B, run locally, and GLM-5.3-flash, run through a cloud API. Tev1 reached a mean field accuracy of 0.917 (95% CI 0.913 to 0.920), the same as Qwen3.5 9B (0.918; p = 0.26), and was four times faster (15 s against 61 s per report). Nimble reached 0.862 and GLM-5.3-flash 0.986. Both decision models matched GLM-5.3-flash on simple dichotomous categories. They were weak on measurements binned into categories, on fields whose correct answer was not reported, and on some complex decisions (e.g. involved margins). We found that the main cause of the inferior performance of Nimble's came from asking 25 questions in one request: with two questions per request, its accuracy improved. Pooled over fields, the returned probabilities were well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.022 and 0.026), but they did not flag systematic errors within single fields. A simulated strategy of sending answers with a probability below 0.94 to GLM-5.3-flash raised Tev1's accuracy to 0.982, with 38% of answers escalated. Decision models can extract explicitly stated findings from pathology reports quickly on local hardware and return useful probabilities. They should be validated in the configuration in which they will be used, restricted to the fields in which they are reliable, and combined with other methods for numeric values.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Adversarial Concept Search: Predicting Compositional Errors From Feature Geometry
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Humans cannot always intuit what scenarios are most challenging to LLMs. Hoping to capture challenging edge cases, developers either design problems to be difficult for humans or curate extensive benchmarks. What if we could instead anticipate which scenarios a model will fail on? In this paper, we use an LLM's representational geometry to predict which concept combinations it will fail on. We attribute this compositional failure to interference between salient features. In tasks that require systematic composition - toy programmatic settings, multihop reasoning, multilingual factual recall - we find that when a pair of concepts is encoded near-orthogonally, the model reliably composes them. When their linear encodings are close, producing interference, the model fails to compose them. Our method reliably anticipates failure modes across different compositional tasks, without evaluating specific inputs. These results lay the groundwork to use representational geometry to identify high-risk examples, construct targeted stress tests, and provide a scalable foundation for active learning in real-world deployment.

Artificial Intelligence.title: CECAR: Cache & Expert Co-Aware Routing Accelerates On-Device Inference of MoE LLMs
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Despite growing interest in on-device LLM deployment, large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models remain impractical on resource-constrained devices, as sparse expert activation still requires all expert weights to be memory-resident. To address this, we identify three key observations for on-device MoE inference: (a) cache hit rates are fundamentally bounded even under Belady's optimal policy; (b) these bounds are insufficient for low-latency on-device inference; and (c) prior cache-aware routing based on binary cache presence can induce routing instability. Based on these insights, we propose CECAR (Cache & Expert Co-Aware Routing), a MoE inference system that jointly considers expert routing and cache management. Unlike prior cache-aware routing methods, CECAR uses an ML-based cache policy to predict the expected reuse distance of each expert and prioritizes routing and execution toward experts with smaller predicted reuse distances. On the Qwen3-30B-A3B model, CECAR achieves 12.5 tokens/s on a consumer-grade GPU with only 16 GB of VRAM, where non-resident experts are fetched from SSD, delivering a 4.5x speedup over conventional MoE inference and exceeding the decode speed of baselines that keep the entire model fully resident in DRAM. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/CECAR.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 24 pages, 5 figures, 19 tables

Artificial Intelligence.title: Locational Marginal Pricing of Compute: Co-optimizing Compute and Energy for Transparent Data Center Flexibility
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Demand from data centers and AI compute is growing rapidly and is increasing stress on the power grid. This load could be flexible through user adjustments and provide relief during energy scarcity events, yet today its flexibility is provided through utility call-ups or system-operator load shedding, and is invisible to the users whose workloads are being curtailed. In this work, we propose to quantify and couple the prices of compute and energy in a single optimization problem. The resulting compute price reflects the marginal cost of the binding constraints and decomposes into components indicating which grid, power, hardware, or service requirement causes a price surge. The economic interpretation updates the price with real-time conditions and gives users a signal for potential flexibility provision. The co-optimization ultimately connects compute and energy markets while providing a signal for relief of stress on both the grid and the compute resources.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Valid Decisions Are Not Enough: Evaluating Structural Constraints in Knowledge-Guided Generative Systems
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Knowledge-guided generative systems use explicit domain constraints to improve decision consistency and alignment with human-created solutions. However, locally valid decisions do not necessarily preserve contextual relationships in human decision-making. This paper examines when structural constraints improve or degrade agreement with human reference solutions. We introduce HARMONIX, an experimental framework using automated musical harmonization as a controlled testbed for knowledge-guided decision-making. Four configurations share the same Viterbi-based optimization mechanism: a baseline, repetition constraints, functional constraints, and their combination. Experiments cover 19,745 records and 143,634 motif pairs across training and validation partitions. Combined constraints improve reference root-interval agreement by approximately five percentage points in stable structural contexts but reduce it by nearly nine percentage points in contexts involving transposition tracking. These opposing effects are consistent across both partitions, while overall exact chord agreement changes only marginally. Contexts are identified retrospectively using reference annotations; no adaptive constraint-selection mechanism is evaluated. The findings demonstrate that interpretable constraints can introduce systematic context-specific failures concealed by aggregate accuracy metrics. They highlight the need to evaluate relationships between decisions and the contextual applicability of constraints in knowledge-guided generative systems.

Artificial Intelligence.title: MT-RGCN-DTI: A Multi-Task Relational Graph Convolutional Network for Drug-Target Interaction Prediction
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Prediction of drug-target interaction (DTI) has become a very crucial part of drug discovery. With the increase in the data volume, it has become very important to improve prediction accuracy by integrating multiple data sources. In this regard, utilising multiple resources in the form of heterogeneous information network to address DTI prediction can be rewarding. In this work, we propose a heterogeneous information network based multi-task DTI prediction model which leverages the advantages of relation graph convolutional network (RGCN). To achieve this, the model employs drug-target interaction network, drug-drug similarity network and protein-protein similarity network to construct a heterogeneous information network. Moreover, we use a knowledge graph embedding scoring functions to model interactions between drug and targets, specifically DistMult and ComplEx as decoders over the learned node representations. We performed extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and compared with state-of-the-art methods. We observed that the proposed model shows competitive performance, thereby confirming the effectiveness of our approach. The codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/Dheeran-S/MT-RGCN-DTI/.

Artificial Intelligence.title: SAFER: Navigating the Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma in World-Model-Based Planning for Autonomous Driving
Artificial Intelligence.summary: An autonomous vehicle must foresee the consequences of its actions, especially in the rare, time-critical situations where crashes happen. A world model offers this foresight, but only within the coverage of its training data, which poses an exploration-exploitation dilemma. Within this coverage a planner can hardly improve on the data, and beyond it the model's errors mislead it. Logs of competent driving rarely contain the failures that would widen the coverage, and agents that learn from interaction gain them only by failing themselves, without being shown what to do instead. We propose SAFER, a framework that learns offline from failures that others make, judged by an expert, and keeps learning online from its own driving. Offline, partially trained agents and scripted, recoverable perturbations Stage failures in simulation, and an expert Annotates every visited state with its action and value, so that much of what the planner explores is covered before it drives. In planning, a chunked latent world model Foresees the consequences fast enough for real-time use, and a risk-aware sampling-based planner Evaluates candidate maneuvers by their return minus a bounded collision penalty. Online, a loop continuously Refines the model wherever this driving leaves the coverage of the offline data.
